What you need: a Redmi phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) that supports OTG — check your model's specs before buying anything; a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any Redmi phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Redmi specifics: first, OTG is not a given on every model, and on many HyperOS phones it is off by default. Redmi phones run HyperOS — Xiaomi's Android skin, since Redmi is Xiaomi's sub-brand — and on many MIUI and HyperOS phones OTG is off unless you enable it in Settings > Additional settings > OTG (on some phones the switch is under More settings > OTG). The switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive, so enable it with the drive already attached. On some newer versions there is no OTG switch at all and OTG works directly. Spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the Note 14 Pro 4G and the Note 14 Pro 5G. If the phone ignores the drive, check Settings > Storage. Second, Redmi ships Xiaomi's apps, so the stock file manager is Mi File Manager — File Manager by Xiaomi, com.mi.android.globalFileexplorer — which handles the phone's internal storage and connected external storage, and shows banner ads while you browse your own files — and Redmi camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and the microSD slot varies by model: the Note 14 Pro 4G has a microSDXC slot (uses the shared SIM slot) while the Note 14 Pro 5G has none, so a USB drive is the plug-in storage for the 5G model, and check your own model's specs before buying a card. Third, Redmi phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB; that only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Redmi's own tools (Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — not phone-to-USB). If you want Redmi's own route, know what each tool actually does — Redmi has no phone-to-USB backup of its own; the routes on a Redmi phone are Xiaomi Cloud and Google's, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Xiaomi Cloud is Xiaomi's own cloud backup, and the one Redmi-specific route: open Settings, tap your Xiaomi account at the top, open Xiaomi Cloud, choose what to sync — gallery, contacts, messages, notes, recorder — and use the cloud backup option to save device settings and app data. It backs your photos up to Xiaomi's servers and restores them on another Xiaomi, Redmi, or POCO phone. It is a real backup — but it lives on Xiaomi's servers, needs a Xiaomi account and a connection, its free storage is limited so a large photo library needs a paid plan, and it still doesn't give you a folder of photo files on a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. Your Redmi's default gallery app is Xiaomi Gallery, not Google Photos — Google Photos integrates with it through the default-gallery access feature, so backed-up photos show up in the gallery — but either way it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the route Xiaomi's guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. And the SD-card route copies DCIM to a memory card with File Manager — a real local copy, but only some Redmi models have a microSD slot (the Note 14 Pro 4G does, the Note 14 Pro 5G does not), and the card stays in the phone (or needs a card reader to open anywhere else), not a USB drive you can plug into any computer. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — every Note 14 model in the spec tables lists OTG, but check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every Redmi phone is confirmed to have OTG — check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); forgetting the OTG switch (on many HyperOS phones OTG is off by default, and the switch turns itself off again after about 10 minutes without a drive — so a drive that worked yesterday can be ignored today; enable it in Settings > Additional settings > OTG with the drive already attached; on some newer versions there is no OTG switch at all and OTG works directly — a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; some models simply mount the drive on plug-in); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Xiaomi Cloud, Google backup, and Google Photos back your phone up to Xiaomi's or Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking an SD-card copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but only some Redmi models have a microSD slot (the Note 14 Pro 4G does, the Note 14 Pro 5G does not), the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Redmi the cloud routes are Xiaomi Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — spec tables list OTG for the 13, 12, Neo 10, and Z10 Turbo Pro, but check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, iQOO Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (not every iQOO phone is confirmed to have OTG — check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); forgetting the OTG switch (on Funtouch OS OTG is off by default, and Vivo's own FAQ says the switch turns itself off if it is not used in 5 minutes — so a drive that worked yesterday can be ignored today; enable it in Settings > More settings > OTG with the drive already attached; if there is no OTG setting at all, the phone may not support OTG); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (iQOO Cloud, Google backup, and Google Photos back your phone up to vivo's or Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup (vivo Mobile Assistant and Coolmuster Android Backup Manager back your iQOO phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on iQOO the cloud routes are iQOO Cloud, Google Photos, and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up TCL photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Google backup is the route the ZTE guides point to first: Settings > Google > Backup, Back up by Google One on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. Coolmuster Android Assistant and Coolmuster Android Backup Manager are PC tools: install one on the computer, connect the phone with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the PC — but that needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. Samsung Backup and Restore and Samsung Messages Backup are the other PC tools the ZTE guides list: they back the phone up to a computer in one click, with photos among the data types — but again, the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive. TWRP Recovery and Titanium Backup are the other routes the ZTE backup guides list: TWRP is a custom recovery that writes a whole-device backup, and Titanium Backup is a backup tool that needs a rooted phone — both are real backups, but they need a custom recovery or root and a PC or a card to hold the backup, and neither gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round); no OTG, no USB backup (on a model without working OTG — spec tables list OTG for the Axon 60, the Axon 60 Ultra, the Axon 30 Ultra, and the Blade V10, but the Blade V30, the Blade V8, the Axon 40 Lite, and the Blade A73 5G have none, so check your own model's specs before buying an adapter — a USB drive may simply never appear, and no app can change that; the cloud routes, Google Photos and Google backup, are the backup for those phones).

What to avoid: buying an adapter before checking OTG (OTG is genuinely mixed across ZTE lines — the Blade V30, the Blade V8, the Axon 40 Lite, and the Blade A73 5G have none — so check your own model's specs first, or the drive will never appear no matter what you plug in); looking for an OTG switch that isn't there (no OTG toggle turned up in ZTE's own manuals — the drive mounts on plug-in on models that support OTG, so if nothing appears, check Settings > Storage and your model's specs rather than hunting for a switch); mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy (Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup); mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy (drag-and-drop through a computer works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop tool); mistaking a PC backup for a USB backup (Coolmuster Android Assistant, Samsung Backup and Restore, and Samsung Messages Backup back your ZTE phone up to a computer — a real backup, but it lands on the PC, not on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open); mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup (copying DCIM to a memory card is a real local copy — but the card slot is mixed across ZTE models (the Axon 60 has one, the Axon 60 Ultra does not), the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between; if the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on ZTE the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this).

### Back up photos from a broken-screen phone to USB

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/broken-screen-photos-to-usb.html

A broken screen is three different problems, and only two of them have a phone-to-USB route at all: a cracked screen with dead touch, where you can still see the display; a black screen with the phone still powering on, where you cannot see anything; and a completely dead phone, where no software route exists. This article covers all three, in that order, and it is the first article in this series that is about a situation instead of a phone brand — the brand series ran to 134 articles, and a broken screen can happen to any of them. Eighteen honest caveats up front: the three scenarios need three different routes, and only the first two have a phone-to-USB route at all; an OTG mouse unlocks nothing by itself — it only lets you enter your own PIN or pattern with a cursor, and it needs a screen you can still see; one port holds either the mouse or the drive, not both — a multi-port OTG hub, or Pro&#x27;s auto-backup on connect, is what lets mouse and drive share the port; video-out needs DisplayPort Alt Mode — a USB 2.0 port physically cannot carry video, and most budget phones lack it; Samsung DeX is the best-documented video-out route — the S8 and later S series, the Note 8 and later, all Z Fold models and the A90 5G only — while the Z Flip 5 and 6 output video but run no DeX, per XDA, and the rest of the A series outputs nothing; Pixel video-out starts at the Pixel 8 — the Pixel 6 and 7 have USB 3.x ports but Google left display output switched off until the Pixel 8; OnePlus video-out is contested — the 12, 13 and Open per the usbctohdmi guide, against the 7 and newer flagships per the salivity list — so check your exact model before buying a hub; Motorola&#x27;s desktop mode is Ready For, now Smart Connect, on Edge phones, and Huawei&#x27;s is Easy Projection on Mate and P Pro phones; an on-screen prompt can block video-out — if you cannot see or tap it, the hub route stops there; Android 16&#x27;s native desktop mode is rolling out — Pixel 8, 9 and 10 with Android 16 QPR3 or later, per Rayneo — so an older Pixel mirrors instead of opening a desktop; a completely dead phone has no software route — Android Authority says so plainly — and screen replacement or professional recovery is what is left; a microSD card comes out only if the phone takes one — most high-end phones no longer do, per Android Authority — and reading the card still needs a reader and a computer; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — one notification tap, which the mouse can do — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect, but only if it was set up before the screen broke; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; check Google Photos first — the library may already be safe in the cloud — but Storage saver compresses photos, so check that setting before trusting a cloud copy; iPhones are not covered here — SnapDisk is Android only — and the iPhone OTG route varies by model, per the repair-shop guide; and the search results for this query are four results — an Android Authority generic broken-phone recovery guide, a repair-shop guide that does mention OTG-mouse unlock and copying photos to a USB drive, and two Dr.Fone guides — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide for a broken screen, and none of them mentions SnapDisk. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:First, work out which broken screen you have, because the route depends on it. Cracked screen, dead touch, display still visible: plug a USB mouse in through an OTG adapter, enter your own PIN or pattern with the cursor, then tap Backup in SnapDisk&#x27;s notification — the whole library copies to the drive oldest-first, with progress, Pause and Stop, no computer. Black screen, phone still powers on: you need a phone that supports USB-C video-out and a hub with HDMI and USB ports, so you can see the screen on a monitor and drive it with a mouse — then SnapDisk works the same way. Completely dead phone: no software route exists, so check Google Photos and the microSD card first, then a screen replacement or professional recovery. The guides that already exist do cover the OTG mouse and the video-out hub — this article is not the first guide to a broken screen — but none of them gives you the whole-library one-tap backup to a USB drive with no computer, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

Search "back up photos from a broken-screen phone to USB drive without computer" and the exact query returns four results — an Android Authority generic broken-phone recovery guide, a repair-shop guide that does mention OTG-mouse unlock and copying photos to a USB drive, and two Dr.Fone guides — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide for a broken screen, and none of them mentions SnapDisk. The second search adds three more of the same shape — a Dr.Fone ultimate guide, a Recoverit guide and a Tech Advisor guide — all routing through a computer, the cloud, or paid recovery software, not a phone-to-USB one-tap backup. FotoSafe's guide is a rival app guide, not a broken-screen guide, and VaultDrive is a rival app page, not a guide. SnapDisk's own generic guide assumes a working screen. The video-out lists — Intehill, usbctohdmi, Miracast.org, salivity, Faceofit and Rayneo — are the source for every video-out claim, and they disagree on OnePlus, which is why that claim is carried as contested.

Method 3: If the screen is black but the phone still powers on — you hear sounds, feel vibrations, the charging light comes on — the display is the problem, not the phone, and a USB-C hub with an HDMI port lets you see the screen on a monitor instead. But this only works if the phone supports video-out, and most phones do not. Check whether your phone supports video-out before buying a hub. Video-out needs DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C — a USB 2.0 port physically cannot carry video, and most budget phones lack it entirely. Plug the hub into the phone, the HDMI cable into the hub and the monitor, and the mouse into the hub&#x27;s USB port. The phone&#x27;s screen should appear on the monitor — as a mirror, or as a desktop if the phone offers one. Use the mouse on the monitor to enter your own PIN or pattern. If the phone shows an on-screen prompt asking to allow video-out, and you cannot see or tap it, the hub route stops here — that prompt is the block the repair-shop guide warns about. Plug the USB drive into the hub&#x27;s second USB port, then tap Backup in SnapDisk&#x27;s notification with the mouse. SnapDisk copies oldest-first, with progress, Pause and Stop. Wait for the copy to finish, then open a few photos on the drive before deleting anything from the phone. Which phones support video-out, from the lists: Samsung DeX runs on the Galaxy S8 and later S series, the Note 8 and later, all Z Fold models and the A90 5G only — Samsung&#x27;s own adapter page lists the S8 through S24 series, the Note 8 through Note 20 series, the Z Fold series and the Tab S4 and later — while the Z Flip 5 and 6 output video but run no DeX, per XDA, and the rest of the A series outputs nothing at all. Google Pixel video-out starts at the Pixel 8 — the Pixel 6 and 7 have USB 3.x ports but Google left display output switched off until the Pixel 8 — and Android 16&#x27;s native desktop mode, which turns the mirrored screen into a desktop with a taskbar, needs Android 16 QPR3 or later on a Pixel 8, 9 or 10, per Rayneo, so an older Pixel mirrors instead. Motorola Edge phones run Ready For, now Smart Connect; Huawei Mate and P Pro phones run Easy Projection; Sony&#x27;s Xperia 1 and 5 series, Asus ROG Phones, the LG G8, V50, V60, Velvet and Wing, and the Fairphone 5 are listed as supporting video-out too. OnePlus is contested — the 12, 13 and Open per the usbctohdmi guide, against the 7 and newer flagships per the salivity list — so check your exact model before buying a hub. Generally not supported: the Galaxy A series except the A90 5G, the Pixel 7 and every earlier Pixel, most Redmi, POCO and Realme phones, most Moto G phones, Nothing phones, and almost anything sold as a budget or entry-level phone. One reported workaround for phones without video-out is a DisplayLink dock, which renders video over plain USB — Faceofit names it as the only way an older Pixel 7 can output to a monitor — but that is a paid dongle and a workaround, not native video-out, and it is carried here as reported, not verified. If your phone is not on any video-out list, the hub will show nothing, and the realistic step is a screen replacement — once the display works again, you can unlock the phone normally and copy everything off, which is exactly why a repair often comes before the recovery itself.

What this does not do: Does not unlock your phone. A mouse, a hub and a monitor only let you enter the PIN or pattern you already know. Nothing in this article bypasses a screen lock, and no app can — if you do not know the code, the backup cannot start.; Does not install below Android 7.0. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2 instead: the file-manager copy has no version floor.; Does not work on a completely dead phone. If the phone does not power on at all, no app, adapter or hub can reach its storage. Check Google Photos and the microSD card, then a screen replacement or professional recovery.; Does not work if the phone has no video-out and no visible screen. A black screen with no DisplayPort Alt Mode leaves no way to see the phone&#x27;s display — the hub shows nothing, the mouse has nothing to click, and the backup cannot start.; Does not work if the phone does not host a drive. The phone has to support USB OTG to see the drive at all. Most Android phones do, but a phone that lists OTG No cannot mount a drive, and then neither the one-tap backup nor the file-manager copy works on it.; Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.; Does not delete photos. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Does not back up anything but photos and videos. SnapDisk copies image and video files only — no settings, no contacts, no messages, no app data.; Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. If an app keeps its photos in a private folder SnapDisk cannot read, those photos stay in the app.; Does not compress. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss..

What to avoid: Buying a single-port adapter when you need a mouse and a drive. One port holds either the mouse or the drive, not both. A multi-port OTG hub is the fix — or Pro&#x27;s auto-backup on connect, if it was set up before the screen broke, which starts the backup the moment the drive goes in.; Buying a USB-C hub for a micro-USB phone. The hub will not fit. Check the port before buying anything — a USB-C hub is the wrong adapter for a micro-USB phone, and a micro-USB OTG adapter is the wrong adapter for a USB-C phone.; Assuming your phone does video-out. Most phones do not. A USB 2.0 port physically cannot carry video, and most budget phones lack DisplayPort Alt Mode entirely — check your exact model against a video-out list before buying a hub, or the hub will show nothing.; Trusting one video-out list. OnePlus video-out is two claims — the 12, 13 and Open per the usbctohdmi guide, against the 7 and newer flagships per the salivity list — and the Miracast.org list downgrades single-source entries to disputed rather than counting them as confirmed, so check the exact model, not the brand.; Mistaking a recovery app for a backup. Dr.Fone and Recoverit are recovery tools, not backups: they run on a computer, they cost money, and they extract files after the damage — they do not copy your whole library to a drive you can keep with one tap. A backup is a plain copy on a drive; a recovery tool is the ambulance after the crash.; Mistaking screen mirroring for a desktop. A mirrored screen shows the phone&#x27;s display on the monitor — a desktop mode like DeX or Android 16&#x27;s native desktop gives you windows and a taskbar. Either one lets you tap Backup, but only the phones named in Method 3 open a desktop at all.; Paying for professional recovery before checking the cloud and the card. Google Photos on another device and the microSD card out through a reader are free, and either one may already hold the photos. Professional recovery is the last resort, not the first call — and Android Authority names it only for a completely dead phone.; Factory resetting, flashing firmware, or approving a wipe repair before the backup. Recoverit warns against it plainly: do not factory reset, flash firmware, or approve any repair that wipes the phone before you have tried the safer options. A wipe deletes the photos you are trying to save.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Photos backs your phone up to Google&#x27;s servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup. And Google Photos&#x27; &quot;Storage saver&quot; setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you&#x27;ve confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager&#x27;s Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk&#x27;s Stop button exists for exactly this.; Forgetting the phone cannot charge while the mouse occupies its only port. The repair-shop guide warns about it: a phone with one port cannot charge while the mouse is plugged in, so plan the transfer before you unplug anything — and start with a charged phone, because a dead battery mid-copy ends the backup..

If you want Blackview's own route, know what each tool actually does — Blackview's own backup guide is six generic Android ways, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Account Backup is Blackview's own first way — Settings > Google > Backup, "Back up to Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage, which Blackview's own guide says may not be sufficient for photos and videos. 2. Local Backup to Computer is Blackview's own second way — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable, open File Explorer or Finder, and copy the files to the computer's local storage or an external hard drive. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 3. Third-party backup apps is Blackview's own third way — Google One, Dropbox, MEGA, Box, Samsung Smart Switch, OneDrive, and Titanium Backup (which needs root). They are real backups — but they are cloud apps or a PC tool, not a phone-to-USB copy, and Blackview's own guide tells you to review each app's privacy policy before trusting it with your data. 4. Backup to External Storage is Blackview's own fourth way — "many Android phones support the use of a microSD card or USB OTG storage — you can use these external storage options to manually copy your important files, photos, and other data for a local backup." It is the closest thing in Blackview's own guide to this article's job — but it is a manual copy, and the manual copy is Method 2 above. 5. ADB backup is Blackview's own fifth way — enable Developer Options and USB Debugging, install Android Platform Tools on a computer, connect the phone, and run the ADB backup command. It is a real backup — but it needs a computer and command-line tools, and some apps block ADB backups. 6. Custom recovery is Blackview's own sixth way — unlock the bootloader, install TWRP, and create a full system image. It is a real backup — but it is expert level, and Blackview's own guide says it may void warranties or risk data loss if done incorrectly. Data Migration is Blackview's phone-to-phone tool — a few taps transfer all your data from an old device to a new one. It is a real transfer — but it moves data to a new phone, not to a USB drive. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Blackview phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. Google backup is the other Google route: Settings > System > Backup, Back up to Google Drive on — it backs the phone up to your Google account so you can restore app settings and data to a new phone. It is a real backup — but the backup lives in Google's cloud and restores to a phone, not a folder of photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. A spec comparison, not a guide — and the confirmation that the S98 has OTG too.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Doogee-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Doogee photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: A Doogee phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the S118 Pro lists USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, the S118 Pro manual lists OTG with reverse charging, and the S98 lists On-The-Go among its USB features — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Doogee specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current rugged models — spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the S118 Pro, the S118 Pro manual lists OTG support, and the S98 lists On-The-Go. Second, Doogee has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the per-model backup guides all point to the same three things: connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, back up to Google Drive, or use Google Photos for photos — with a microSD card as the local option; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Doogee camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The S118 Pro and the S118 both have a TF/microSD card slot up to 2 TB — on the S118 Pro the TF card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM — so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Doogee's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, per-model FAQ guides — not phone-to-USB). If you want Doogee's own route, know what each tool actually does — the per-model backup guides for the S118 Pro and the S118 all point to the same three things, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Doogee phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is what the per-model guides call the most economical method — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option the S118 manual names — move large files to an installed microSD card. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the S118 Pro's TF card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The TF card slot shares the SIM tray on the S118 Pro. The S118 Pro takes a Nano SIM card plus a TF card in the same tray, so a card and a second SIM compete for the same tray — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Doogee — the S118 Pro, S118, and S98 all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The per-model backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model FAQ for a phone-to-USB guide. The devicesfaq page for the S118 Pro is a real Doogee backup page — but its backup advice is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG reverse charging for a backup. The S118 Pro can act as a power bank and charge other devices over OTG — that is power going out of the phone, not photos. Reverse charging moves no files at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the S118 Pro and the S118 both take a card up to 2 TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. On the S118 Pro the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Doogee the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

Oukitel rugged phones (WP39, WP35, and WP33 Pro) have USB-C and OTG across the range: spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the WP39 and the WP35, and the WP33 Pro manual lists 18W reverse charging over OTG — and Oukitel has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: the per-model backup guides all point to a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos, with a microSD card as the local option. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Oukitel. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On any USB-C Oukitel, plug a USB drive in: it mounts on plug-in on most models — the WP39 and the WP35 list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the WP33 Pro manual lists 18W reverse charging over OTG — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the per-model backup guides say the most economical backup is to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, and Files by Google can access USB storage on Android 7.0 and later — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Oukitel's own backup routes work too, but they are Google backup and Google Photos, which back your photos up to Google's cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. A store spec listing, not a guide — and the confirmation that the WP100 Plus has OTG.; Cloud routes — Google Photos syncs your gallery to Google's servers, Google backup restores your data to a new phone from Google's cloud, not to a drive you hold; Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is an Oukitel-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Oukitel photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.

What you need: An Oukitel phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the WP39 and the WP35 list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG, and the WP33 Pro manual lists 18W reverse charging over OTG — so no adapter is needed for a USB-C flash drive on the current models, while a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Oukitel specifics: first, OTG is not a question on the current rugged models — spec tables list USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG for the WP39 and the WP35, the WP33 Pro manual lists OTG, and the WP210 and WP100 Plus store listings list OTG support too. Second, Oukitel has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — the per-model backup guides all point to the same three things: connect the phone to a computer and copy the files, back up to Google Drive, or use Google Photos for photos — with a microSD card as the local option; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Oukitel camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The WP39 and the WP35 both take a microSD card up to 2 TB in a hybrid slot, and the WP33 Pro takes one up to 1 TB — so a card is an option, but the card stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: Oukitel's own tools (Google backup, Google Photos, per-model FAQ guides — not phone-to-USB). If you want Oukitel's own route, know what each tool actually does — the per-model backup guides for the OT6, the OKT3, and the C32 all point to the same three things, and none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google backup is the first way the guides describe — Settings > Google > All services > Backup, "Backup by Google One" on — it backs apps, settings, photos, videos, and contacts up to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 2. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Oukitel phones: open Photos, tap your profile picture, Photos settings, Backup, and turn Backup on — it automatically backs up photos to your Google account, with 15 GB free with every Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 3. A computer copy is what the per-model guides call the most economical method — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. 4. A microSD card is the local option the spec tables name — expandable with microSD, up to 2 TB on the WP39 and the WP35 (hybrid slot), up to 1 TB on the WP33 Pro. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, the WP39's and the WP35's card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM (hybrid slot), and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The microSD card shares the SIM tray on the WP39 and the WP35. Both take a microSD card up to 2 TB in a hybrid slot, so a card and a second SIM compete for the same tray — but a card is still not a USB drive: it stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader. The WP33 Pro takes a card up to 1 TB. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any current Oukitel — the WP39, WP35, and WP33 Pro all have USB-C with OTG — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google backup and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. The per-model backup guides' most economical method backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a per-model FAQ for a phone-to-USB guide. The devicesfaq page for the OT6 is a real Oukitel backup page — but its backup advice is a computer copy, Google Drive, or Google Photos. It never describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone. The OKT3 and C32 pages say the same thing, word for word.; Mistaking OTG reverse charging for a backup. The WP33 Pro can act as a power bank and charge other devices over OTG — that is power going out of the phone, not photos. Reverse charging moves no files at all.; Mistaking a microSD copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the WP39 and the WP35 both take a card up to 2 TB, and the WP33 Pro takes one up to 1 TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. On the WP39 and the WP35 the card shares the SIM tray with the second SIM.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 17, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Oukitel the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. A TF card is the local option the FAQ pages name — "Pass media files to memory card" — the B3C takes a TF card up to 1 TB, the Air3 takes one up to 1 TB, and the B2 Ultra takes one up to 1 TB. Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Sonim-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Sonim photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Sonim Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the XP8 shipped with Android 7.0 and later ran Android 10, and the XP10 runs Android 12 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either phone, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Sonim specifics: first, OTG is confirmed on the XP8 — the user guide lists the port as "High Speed, OTG" — but the XP10 datasheet I found does not list OTG either way, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on that model; one third-party spec page claims the XP10 supports USB OTG, but Sonim's own datasheet does not say so. Second, Sonim has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — Sonim SCOUT is a device-management app, not a backup; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Sonim camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The XP8 takes a microSD card up to 128GB per Sonim's datasheet, and the XP10 takes one up to 1TB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: Method 3: Sonim's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, Sonim SCOUT, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Sonim's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Sonim backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Sonim Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Sonim SCOUT is Sonim's own preloaded app — "SonimWare's free, pre-loaded intelligent application for device configuration, management, and support". It deploys, manages, and supports the phone. It is a real tool — but it is a device-management app, not a photo backup, and it writes no photos to a USB drive. 4. A microSD card is the local option Sonim documents — the XP8 takes a card up to 128GB per Sonim's datasheet, and the XP10 takes one up to 1TB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The XP5s is not an Android phone. Sonim's XP5s runs a proprietary OS, not Android, so SnapDisk — which needs Android 7.0 or later — cannot install on it at all, even though its user manual lists OTG. The XP3 flip phones run a proprietary OS too. This article is for the Android Sonim phones (XP8 and XP10).; OTG is not confirmed on every Sonim model. The XP8 user guide lists the port as "High Speed, OTG" — but the XP10 datasheet I found does not list OTG either way, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on that model before relying on it. One third-party spec page claims the XP10 supports USB OTG, but Sonim's own datasheet does not say so. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the XP8 and the XP10, which both have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Dr.Fone's PC software backs your phone up — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The XP8 user guide and the XP10 datasheet are real Sonim pages — but the guide only lists the port as "High Speed, OTG", and the datasheet only lists the ports. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the XP8 takes a card up to 128GB, the XP10 up to 1TB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Sonim the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Sonim that is not an Android phone. The XP5s and the XP3 flip phones run a proprietary OS, not Android — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on them. If your Sonim has a 2.6-inch screen and a physical keypad with no Play Store, it is one of those handsets, not an Android phone.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up Kyocera photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/kyocera-photos-to-usb.html

Kyocera's DuraForce Android phones (Pro 2, Ultra 5G, PRO 3, and DuraSport) have USB host support on at least two of them — the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the DuraForce Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — and Kyocera has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. One honest caveat up front: the Ultra 5G and PRO 3 datasheets list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so check Settings > Storage before relying on it on those models, and the older DuraForce phones are out of scope — the original DuraForce runs Android 4.4, the DuraForce XD runs Android 5.1, and the original DuraForce PRO's spec tables list USB OTG as No. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On a Kyocera DuraForce Android phone with USB host support, plug a USB drive in: the spec tables list USB OTG as Yes for the DuraForce Pro 2, and the DuraSport's spec pages list its port as "USB Type-C, USB On-The-Go" — the Ultra 5G and PRO 3 datasheets do not list OTG either way, so test with a drive on those models — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: a file manager works — the YouTube guides' route is an OTG adapter copy with the built-in file manager, and askfilo's route is the same — but the direct route is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Kyocera's own backup advice works too, but there is none pointing at a USB drive — devicesfaq's advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser, or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud, which back your photos up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive as plain files. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. What you need: A Hammer rugged Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk) — the Blade V 5G runs Android 13, the Iron 4 runs Android 12, and the Blade 3 and the Explorer Pro run Android 10 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them, while a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Hammer specifics: first, OTG is the honest unknown on the current models — the only per-model OTG listings I found are FindPare's Yes for the Energy 18x9 and the Blade 2 Pro, and FindPare itself says its information is "not ascertained", while the Blade V 5G, Iron 4, Blade 3, and Explorer Pro spec pages list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it on any of them. Second, Hammer has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; Hammer camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The Blade V 5G takes a microSD card up to 1TB, and the Blade 3, the Iron 4, and the Explorer Pro take one up to 128GB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Third, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
Method 3: Method 3: Hammer's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Hammer's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Hammer backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Hammer Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Hammer documents — the Blade V 5G takes a card up to 1TB, and the Blade 3, the Iron 4, and the Explorer Pro take one up to 128GB — and the HAMMER 5 Smart FAQ names the SD card as an alternative to a computer copy or the cloud. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the MyPhone Hammer Blade to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the Iron 4 manual says the same: "You can transfer files between your myPhone Hammer Iron 4 and computer using a USB cable." It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.
What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; The Hammer feature phones are out of scope. The Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone at all — SnapDisk cannot install on it. If your Hammer has a keypad and an SOS button instead of a touchscreen full of apps, it is one of those handsets, not a rugged Android phone.; The oldest Hammer Android phones are out of scope. The original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0, so SnapDisk — which needs Android 7.0 or later — cannot install on them at all. If your Hammer has a micro-USB port and a 2016–2017 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current rugged phone.; OTG is not confirmed on every Hammer model. The only per-model OTG listings I found are FindPare's Yes for the Energy 18x9 and the Blade 2 Pro — and FindPare itself says its information is "not ascertained" — while the Blade V 5G, Iron 4, Blade 3, and Explorer Pro spec pages list USB-C without mentioning OTG either way, so confirm the drive mounts in Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. And one Hammer Android phone has no OTG at all: FindPare lists USB OTG as No for the Active 2 LTE. SnapDisk still needs Android 7.0 or later..
What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the Blade V 5G, the Iron 4, the Blade 3, and the Explorer Pro, which all have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Hammer's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a user manual for a phone-to-USB guide. The Iron 4 manual page and the Blade 3 datasheet are real Hammer pages — but the manual only says "You can transfer files between your myPhone Hammer Iron 4 and computer using a USB cable", and the datasheet only lists "USB Type-C, waterproof". Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the Blade V 5G takes a card up to 1TB, and the Blade 3, the Iron 4, and the Explorer Pro take one up to 128GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Hammer the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Hammer that is too old to run it — or is not an Android phone at all. The Hammer 6 LTE is a feature phone, not an Android phone, and the original Hammer Iron runs Android 4.2 and the AXE M LTE runs Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of them. If your Hammer has a keypad and an SOS button, or a micro-USB port and a 2016–2017 release date, it is one of those handsets, not a current rugged Android phone.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

### Back up FOSSiBOT photos to a USB drive (no computer)

FOSSiBOT's rugged F-series Android phones (F101, F101 Pro, F102, F107 Pro, F110 Pro 5G, F112 Pro, and F113) list USB OTG support in their spec tables, and FOSSiBOT has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos in the cloud. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.
