If you want Nomu's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Nomu backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Nomu Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Nomu documents — the S10 takes a card up to 64 GB, the S30 Mini takes one up to 64 GB, and the T18 takes one up to 32 GB, with the S10 Pro, S30, and M6 card sizes disputed between sources (up to 64 GB per PhoneMore against up to 32 GB per Smartprix on the S10 Pro; up to 64 GB per PhoneMore against up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck on the S30; up to 32 GB per Notebookcheck against up to 64 GB per unite4buy on the M6). It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the Nomu S10 to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the same advice appears on the S30 Mini page. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; Three Nomu models cannot run SnapDisk at all. The S10, the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — so SnapDisk cannot install on any of the three, even though the S20 and the S30 list OTG support. Check your own port before buying an adapter..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A micro-USB OTG adapter is what the S10 Pro, the S30 Mini, the M6, and the T18 need for a regular USB-A drive, since all four have microUSB 2.0 — so a USB-C OTG adapter is the wrong one for them. The M8 has USB-C instead, so it needs a USB-C OTG adapter for a regular USB-A drive, or a USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. A plain micro-USB charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Nomu's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a FAQ page for a phone-to-USB guide. The S10 FAQ page and the Nomu spec tables are real Nomu pages — but the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser, and the spec tables only list "USB OTG" or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support for SnapDisk support. The S20 and the S30 both list OTG support — Review Hub lists "USB OTG: YES" for the S20, and PhoneMore and Notebookcheck list OTG for the S30 — but both run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. OTG lets a file manager copy photos to a drive; it does not make the phone new enough to install SnapDisk. Test with a drive, and use Method 2 or 4 on those models.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the S10 takes a card up to 64 GB, the S30 Mini takes one up to 64 GB, and the T18 takes one up to 32 GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Nomu the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Nomu phone that cannot run it. The S10, the S20, and the S30 run Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of the three. Check Settings > About phone before installing; every other Nomu model I found runs Android 7.0.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

Neither route gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive.. None of them is a Conquest-specific phone-to-USB guide at all, and none of them offers an automated Conquest photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file. That is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What you need: A Conquest Android phone that runs Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk — the S10 runs Android 7.1, the S12 runs Android 8.1, the S12 Pro runs Android 8.1, the S16 runs Android 9.0, the S22 5G runs Android 11, and the EX201 runs Android 12 — so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the S12 and the S16, which have USB-C, while the S10 has micro USB, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on that model — and enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Four Conquest specifics: first, four models cannot run SnapDisk at all — the S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum, even though the S8 lists USB OTG support, so their photos move off the phone by file manager or computer copy instead; the S9's Android version is disputed — 5.1.1 per devicesfaq, 7.1.1 per trak.in — so check Settings > About phone on that model before installing, since SnapDisk cannot run on it if the 5.1.1 source is right. Second, OTG support is confirmed in the sources I found only on the S8, which cannot run SnapDisk — on the S10, the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201 it is unconfirmed, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it: if the drive appears, the phone hosts drives and the rest of this method works; if it never appears, the phone does not host drives and Method 4 is the route. Third, Conquest has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own — its backup advice is a computer copy or Google Drive and Google Photos; the stock photo backup is Google Photos; the stock file manager is Files by Google; Conquest camera photos live in DCIM/Camera, as on any Android phone. The S8+ takes a microSD card up to 128 GB, the S10 takes one up to 128 GB, and the S16 takes one up to 128 GB — the S16 ATEX variant takes one up to 2 TB — so a card is an option, and it still stays in the phone and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader, while a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. Fourth, SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Method 3: Conquest's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Conquest's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Conquest backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Conquest Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. A microSD card is the local option Conquest documents — the S8+ takes a card up to 128 GB, the S10 takes one up to 128 GB, and the S16 takes one up to 128 GB, with the S16 ATEX variant taking one up to 2 TB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 4. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — "connect the Conquest S8 to a computer using the USB cable and make a copy of the files using the file browser", per devicesfaq, and the same advice appears on the S8 KT35A-S8 page. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; Four Conquest models cannot run SnapDisk at all. The S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — so SnapDisk cannot install on any of the four, even though the S8 lists OTG support. Their photos move off the phone by file manager or computer copy instead.; The S9's Android version is disputed. devicesfaq lists the S9 as Android 5.1.1 with a Qualcomm Snapdragon 615, while trak.in lists it as Android 7.1.1 with a MediaTek Helio P25 — so check Settings > About phone on that model before installing; if the 5.1.1 source is right, SnapDisk cannot run on it at all.; OTG support is unconfirmed on every model that can run SnapDisk. The only Conquest model with an OTG listing in the sources I found is the S8 — FindPare lists "USB OTG: Yes" with micro USB 2.0 — and the S8 runs Android 6.0, so it cannot run SnapDisk. On the S10, the S12, the S12 Pro, the S16, the S22 5G, and the EX201, no source I found mentions OTG at all — so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; The USB port type is unconfirmed on the S22 5G and the EX201. The S10 has micro USB — the root guide for it says to connect the phone to a computer using a micro USB cable — and the S12 and the S16 have USB-C, while the S8 has micro USB 2.0. The S22 5G store listing and the EX201 spec sheet I found state no USB port type, so check your own port before buying an adapter.; The S6 comes in two variants. The original 2015 S6 has a MediaTek MT6732, 1 GB of RAM, 8 GB of storage, and a 4000 mAh battery per Ubergizmo, while the S6 OCTA has a MediaTek MT6752, 3 GB of RAM, 32 GB of storage, and a 6000 mAh battery per mobilexfiles — but both run Android 5.1, so neither can run SnapDisk..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the S12 and the S16, which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter, not a micro-USB one. The S10 has micro USB instead, so it needs a micro-USB OTG adapter. The S22 5G and the EX201 have no USB port type stated in the sources I found, so check the port first. A plain micro-USB charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. Conquest's own backup advice is a computer copy with a USB cable and a file browser — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a FAQ page for a phone-to-USB guide. The S8 FAQ page and the Conquest spec tables are real Conquest pages — but the FAQ only says to connect the phone to a computer and copy the files with a file browser, and the spec tables only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support for SnapDisk support. The S8 lists USB OTG support — FindPare lists "USB OTG: Yes" — but it runs Android 6.0, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum. OTG lets a file manager copy photos to a drive; it does not make the phone new enough to install SnapDisk. Test with a drive, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the S8+ takes a card up to 128 GB, the S10 takes one up to 128 GB, and the S16 takes one up to 128 GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On Conquest the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Installing SnapDisk on a Conquest phone that cannot run it. The S6 runs Android 5.1, and the S8, the S8+, and the S8 Pro run Android 6.0 — SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later and cannot install on any of the four. Check Settings > About phone before installing; every other Conquest model I found runs Android 7.1, 8.1, 9.0, 11, or 12, except the S9, whose Android version is disputed.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

The Land Rover Explore is a rugged outdoor phone made by Bullitt Mobile under licence from the Land Rover car brand, and Land Rover has no phone-to-USB backup tool of its own: its manual's backup is Google backup to Google's servers, and its file advice is a computer copy with a USB cable. No computer, no upload, no account. What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. Method 3: Method 3: Panasonic's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Panasonic's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Panasonic backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Android Toughbooks: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on the FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 — both take a card up to 64 GB. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the device, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the device — connect the Toughbook to a computer with a USB cable and copy DCIM to the computer. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the device. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026..

What this does not do: A few honest limits, so the automatic copy is not oversold:; Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the device is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; USB host support is unconfirmed on four models. The FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 list host-capable USB — Panasonic's own spec sheets list their micro-USB port as "option to be host" — but no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the FZ-T1, the FZ-S1, the FZ-A3, or the P-01K at all, so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; The original FZ-N1 cannot run SnapDisk at all. It runs Android 6.0.1, below SnapDisk's Android 7.0 minimum — only the FZ-N1 mk2, on Android 8.1, can. Check Settings > About phone if you are unsure which FZ-N1 you have: the mk2 has the Snapdragon 660, the original has the older quad-core chip.; Windows Toughbooks are out of scope. Most of the Toughbook line is Windows laptops, not Android devices — SnapDisk is Android-only, so no Windows Toughbook can run it. On those machines the computer copy in Method 4, with the drive plugged into the laptop itself, is the route.; The FZ-S1's microSD support is unconfirmed. The sources I found for the FZ-S1 list 64 GB of internal storage and a single USB-C port, with no microSD mention anywhere in them, so the card is not leaned on for that model — the FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 take a microSDXC card up to 64 GB, and the FZ-A3 takes microSD cards, with the capacity unconfirmed in the source found.; Most search results are about camera cards, not the Toughbook's own photos. The PetaPixel and desnoulez guides use a phone as a bridge to copy a camera's memory card to a drive — "Panasonic" there means the camera brand, not the device. This article is about the photos stored on the Toughbook itself.; The adapter differs by model. The FZ-S1 and the FZ-A3 have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into either of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on either of them. The FZ-N1 mk2, the FZ-T1, the FZ-L1, and the P-01K have a micro-USB port, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on those models. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the device to a computer, which is the opposite direction..

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the FZ-S1 and the FZ-A3, both of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the FZ-N1 mk2, the FZ-T1, the FZ-L1, and the P-01K. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the device to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your device up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the device and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a review page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Panasonic spec sheets and the Toughbook reviews are real Panasonic pages — but the spec sheets only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type, and the reviews only test the hardware. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the device.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. The FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 list host-capable USB — but no source I found mentions host or OTG support on the FZ-T1, the FZ-S1, the FZ-A3, or the P-01K. Test with a drive on those models, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a camera-card guide for a Toughbook guide. The PetaPixel and desnoulez guides are real phone-to-USB guides — but they copy a camera's memory card through a hub, with "Panasonic" meaning the camera brand. If your photos are on the Toughbook itself, the card-reader hub is the wrong tool: the drive plugs straight into the Toughbook, and Method 1 or 2 is the route.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the FZ-N1 mk2 and the FZ-L1 take a card up to 64 GB — but the card stays in the device, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the device and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On an Android Toughbook the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the device — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the device. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..

A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into the G5 and the G9, both of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the G4, the Q5, and the Q8 LTE. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The G5 manual and the Evolveo StrongPhone spec pages are real Evolveo pages — but the manual only lists an Android version and a USB connector type, and the spec pages only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. Neither of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. The G9 lists USB OTG support and the G4 lists it too — but no source I found mentions OTG on the G5, and the Q8 LTE's OTG is disputed between sources. Test with a drive on the G5, and use Method 2 or 4 on that model if the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — the G5 and the G9 take a card up to 128 GB — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 18, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On an Evolveo StrongPhone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this..


https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/faq.html

The questions a first visitor asks about backing up photos to a USB disk with SnapDisk — answered from how the app actually works in v0.1.2.

TL;DR: SnapDisk backs up your photos to a USB disk — plug it in, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

How does SnapDisk back up my photos? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" Tap Backup and your photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The progress notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice.

How much can I back up for free? The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. There is no subscription and no monthly fee — Pro is paid once.

Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. It works with the phone in airplane mode — if a backup works in airplane mode, it is offline, and SnapDisk does.

What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. A partially copied file resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over, and files that already copied are never copied twice. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup.

What disk formats work? Drives formatted exFAT have no per-file size limit. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — that only matters for very long videos. SnapDisk skips those files, lists them with the reason, and keeps going instead of failing the whole backup. NTFS has not been tested on a real disk yet, so we make no claim about it either way: not supported, not unsupported — untested.

Where do my photos go on the disk? By default SnapDisk copies from /sdcard/DCIM on your phone to /disk/DCIM on the external disk. Both folders can be changed in Settings — open the app and pick your own From and To folders. The app opened is a settings screen only; the backup itself is started from the notification.

Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the v0.1.2 APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.

Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues. If a backup fails, the app shows the full error — copy it into the issue so the cause is visible, not guessed.

If you want Oscall's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Oscall backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Oscall Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on all thirty phones — each takes a card, up to 2 TB on the newest models. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy DCIM to the computer. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG support is unstated on eight phones. The C20, C20 Pro, S60 Pro, Tiger 8, Pilot 5, Flat 3C, Flat 3C Mini and Modern 8 have no OTG listing in any source — and FindPare lists USB OTG No for the C20 Pro — so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; No covered phone runs below Android 7.0. The lowest is Android 11, so SnapDisk installs on all thirty covered Oscall phones. On a below-7.0 phone the only routes are Method 3 and Method 4 — but no Oscall phone in this article needs them for that reason.; The adapter differs by model. Twenty-six phones have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on those models. The C20 Pro, the C60 and the S60 Pro have a micro-USB port, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on those models — and the C20's port is unverified, so check it on the unit. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into twenty-six of the thirty phones, all of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the C20 Pro, the C60 and the S60 Pro. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Oscall spec pages are real Oscall pages — but they only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. Twenty-two phones list USB OTG Yes — but no source settles OTG on the C20, C20 Pro, S60 Pro, Tiger 8, Pilot 5, Flat 3C, Flat 3C Mini and Modern 8, and FindPare lists USB OTG No for the C20 Pro. Test with a drive on those eight, and use Method 3 or 4 on any model where the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — all thirty phones take a card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On an Oscall phone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.

Method 3: Method 3: Leagoo's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want Leagoo's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no Leagoo backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app, and it is the stock photo backup on Leagoo Android phones: it automatically backs up photos to your Google account. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through Google Photos instead. 2. Google Drive is the cloud backup Android names by default — "on Android devices the default built-in service is Google Drive. With Google Drive you have 15Gb free" — it backs your data up to Google's cloud. It is a real backup — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and Google accounts only offer 15 GB of free storage. 3. Google backup is what Android itself names: personal settings back up to Google's servers with a Google account, and are restored to a new phone when you sign in with that account. It is a real backup — but it backs up settings, not a folder of photo files on a drive you hold. 4. A microSD card is the local option on all sixty-three phones — each takes a card. It is a real local copy — but the card stays in the phone, and opening the card anywhere else needs a card reader. 5. A computer copy is the other way to move files off the phone — connect the phone to a computer with a USB cable and copy DCIM to the computer. It is a real backup — but it needs a PC in between, and the backup lands on the PC, not on a USB drive as plain files straight from the phone. None of them is a one-tap way to copy your camera roll to a drive. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Only the folder you pick. By default that's DCIM — your camera photos. Photos in other folders (Downloads, app folders) only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them.; Free 5 GB per run. A library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped. Pro ($9.99, one-time) removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk.; Files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped. Very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup. Reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them.; It never deletes. SnapDisk only copies. Freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself — never the other way round.; OTG support is unstated on eight phones. The KIICAA Mix, M7, M11, M9 Pro, Power 2, Power 2 Pro, Z10 and Z20 have no OTG listing in any source — and the T5c is contested, with FindPare listing OTG No against OTG Yes in three other sources — so plug a drive in and check Settings > Storage on those models before relying on it. The drive mounting is the test.; Five phones list USB OTG No. The KIICAA Power, Z7, M10, Z15 and Z9 list USB OTG No, so only Methods 3, 4 and 5 work on those five.; Thirty-three phones run below Android 7.0. The Alfa, Elite, Lead, M5, Shark, T1, Venture and Z lines below 7.0 cannot run SnapDisk at all. On a below-7.0 phone the only routes are Method 3 and Method 4 — and Method 5.; The adapter differs by model. Nine phones have a USB Type-C port, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into any of them and a regular USB-A drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter on those models. Fifty-three phones have a micro-USB port, so a regular USB-A drive needs a micro-USB OTG adapter on those models — and the Z20's port is unverified, so check it on the unit. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into nine of the sixty-three phones, all of which have USB-C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those models, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the fifty-three micro-USB models. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The Leagoo spec pages are real Leagoo pages — but they only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. Sixteen phones list USB OTG Yes — but no source settles OTG on the KIICAA Mix, M7, M11, M9 Pro, Power 2, Power 2 Pro, Z10 and Z20, the T5c is contested, and five list USB OTG No. Test with a drive on those nine, and use Method 3 or 4 on any model where the drive never mounts.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — all sixty-three phones take a card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On a Leagoo phone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.

Method 3: BQ's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want BQ's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no BQ backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app — it uploads your photos to Google's servers, and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses them. 2. Google Drive is the cloud service behind the Google backup BQ's manuals name — it backs the phone up to Google's servers with 15 GB free, not to a USB drive. 3. A microSD card is the local route — a card fits twenty-nine phones for certain, so copy DCIM to the card with the file manager, then read the card through a card reader on a computer and copy to the USB drive. BQ On is BQ's own cloud storage, which you buy — it is storage, not a USB backup. If you want a plain copy on a USB drive with no computer in between, that is Method 1 or 2, not a stock tool.

What this does not do: Photos and videos only. SnapDisk copies image and video files. Documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Google backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos.; Does not install below Android 7.0. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later, and nineteen covered BQ phones run below Android 7.0 as shipped, so SnapDisk does not install on any of them. No other BQ phone is below the floor.; Does not work if the phone does not host a drive. No BQ phone lists USB OTG No — but the V Plus and five below-floor phones (the E5 4G, the E6, the E4, the 5.7 and the 4.5) are unstated on OTG, so on those six the drive mounting is the test: plug the drive in and check the phone sees it.; Does not delete photos. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. If an app keeps its photos in a private folder SnapDisk cannot read, those photos stay in the app.; Does not compress. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into five of the thirty phones — the X2 Pro, the X2, the X Pro, the X and the C — so an adapter is only needed for a regular USB-A drive, and it must be a USB-C OTG adapter on those five, a micro-USB OTG adapter on the other twenty-five. A plain USB-C charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup. BQ On is the same idea with BQ's name on it: storage you buy, not a USB backup.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a manual page for a phone-to-USB guide. The BQ spec pages are real BQ pages — but they only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone. The BQ user manuals are the closest thing to BQ backup advice, and they name the computer copy.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. Twenty-four of the thirty phones list USB OTG Yes — but the V Plus does not list it at all, and neither do the E5 4G, the E6, the E4, the 5.7 or the 4.5. Do not assume the next BQ phone hosts a drive just because most of them do.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — twenty-nine phones take a card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On a BQ phone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive, plus BQ On — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.; Trusting one spec listing. The X2 Pro is two Android numbers — 8.0 per phonesdata against 8.1 per smartprix — the M4.5 is three — 5.0, 5.1 and 5.1.1 — the 5.7 is two — 4.1 against 4.2.1 — and the X5's card is two ceilings — 32 GB against 64 GB — so check the unit before buying a drive expecting a particular spec. The Android floor is settled on every one either way: eleven clear 7.0 and nineteen run below it on every source.

FotoSafe, "Back up Android photos to USB" — back up Android photos to a USB drive without a computer; you need Android 9 or later with USB host/OTG support, a USB drive with enough free capacity, and a data-capable OTG adapter. A rival app guide, not an HMD guide — and the source for the Android 9 floor, which all twenty clear on shipped software, with nineteen proven — OTG is contested on the Key. VaultDrive (via coticsy.com) — plug a flash drive or SSD into your iPhone or Android phone, choose what to back up and tap Start; VaultDrive copies your original photos, videos and files straight to the drive. Free to try, Pro is $19.99 once, no account; free for up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup; needs iOS 17 or later, or Android 8 or later. A rival app page, not a guide — and it says nothing about HMD. Note the split: VaultDrive needs Android 8, so all twenty clear the version floor on shipped software — and VaultDrive is proven on nineteen of them, all but the Key — while AppBrain's 12.1 floor is cleared by all twenty too. YouTube, "How to Connect USB Drive to Android Phone to Move Photos & Videos (Best Method)" — the best and most direct method for moving photos and videos from any modern Android phone to a USB drive is a USB On-The-Go connection and the phone's built-in file manager app; it needs Android 7.0 or newer, a USB flash drive and an OTG adapter. A generic Android video, not an HMD guide — and it says nothing about HMD. VaultDrive (via appbrain.com) — VaultDrive: USB Photo Backup is a photography app developed by Coticsy; 870 installs; app size 28.9 MB; needs Android 12.1+; version 1.0.7, last updated 3 November 2026; launched May 2026. An app listing, not a guide — and the source for the Android 12.1 floor, which all twenty clear — the lowest shipped version is Android 13. HMD offers no backup tool to a USB drive at all, and no bundled cloud storage of its own — HMD's own user guides point to the Google backup, Settings > System > Backup, which restores to a new phone from the cloud. Google Drive is the cloud service, and Google Photos is for photos alone — but neither writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. HMD Global is a Finnish company — Human Mobile Devices, founded in 2016, the maker of Nokia phones under licence — and its own HMD-branded smartphones started with the Pulse family on April 24, 2024. GSMChoice lists the whole HMD range, feature phones and smartphones together, and Wikipedia's HMD smartphones table lists the seventeen launched HMD smartphones; the twenty covered here are those seventeen plus the Fusion X1, the Fuse and the T21 tablet.

Method 3: HMD's own tools (Google Photos, Google Drive, or a microSD card — not phone-to-USB). If you want HMD's own route, know what each tool actually does — there is no HMD backup page pointing at a USB drive at all, and none of the stock tools writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive automatically. 1. Google Photos is Google's own photo backup app — it uploads your photos to Google's servers, and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses them. 2. Google Drive is the cloud service behind the Google backup HMD's guides name — it backs the phone up to Google's servers, not to a USB drive. 3. A microSD card is the local route — a card fits nineteen phones for certain, so copy DCIM to the card with the file manager, then read the card through a card reader on a computer and copy to the USB drive. HMD offers no bundled cloud storage of its own. If you want a plain copy on a USB drive with no computer in between, that is Method 1 or 2, not a stock tool.

What this does not do: Does not install below Android 7.0. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later, and no covered HMD phone runs below Android 7.0 as shipped — the lowest shipped version is Android 13, on the XR21, the Aura and the T21 — so SnapDisk installs on all twenty. No other HMD phone is below the floor.; Does not work if the phone does not host a drive. Nineteen covered HMD phones list USB OTG Yes, so on those nineteen the drive mounting is a formality — but the Key's OTG is contested, phonebunch Not Supported against phonepik Yes, so on the Key plug the drive in and check the phone sees it before trusting either the one-tap backup or the file-manager copy.; Does not delete photos. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Does not back up anything but photos and videos. SnapDisk copies image and video files only — no settings, no contacts, no messages, no app data.; Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. If an app keeps its photos in a private folder SnapDisk cannot read, those photos stay in the app.; Does not compress. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter you don't need — or the wrong one. All twenty phones take USB Type-C, so a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into every one of them, and a micro-USB OTG adapter is the wrong adapter for every one of them. A plain USB charging cable is not an OTG adapter: it connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction.; Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Drive and Google Photos back your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup. HMD has no bundled cloud of its own, and HMD's own guides point to the Google backup — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Mistaking a PC tool for a phone-to-USB copy. A computer copy with a USB cable moves files to a computer — but it is a copy to a computer, and the backup lands on the PC. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route, not a desktop copy.; Mistaking a spec table or a catalogue page for a phone-to-USB guide. The HMD spec pages are real HMD pages — but they only list an Android version, a chipset, or a USB connector type. None of them describes copying your camera roll straight to a USB drive from the phone. HMD's own user guides are the closest thing to HMD backup advice, and they point to the Google backup.; Mistaking OTG support on one model for OTG support on the other. Nineteen HMD phones list USB OTG Yes — but the Key is contested, phonebunch Not Supported against phonepik Yes — so do not assume the Key hosts a drive just because it clears Android 7.0, and do not assume a phone that clears Android 7.0 hosts a drive either. Plug a drive in and check, on the Key at least.; Mistaking one Vibe for the other. The Vibe name is two phones — the 2024 Vibe on Android 14 and the 2025 Vibe 5G on Android 15 — and some spec pages file the Vibe 5G under the plain Vibe name, so check which Vibe you hold before trusting a spec, an adapter or a card ceiling.; Mistaking a microSD card copy for a USB backup. Copying DCIM to a microSD card is a real local copy — nineteen phones take a card — but the card stays in the phone, and opening it anywhere else needs a card reader; a USB drive plugs into any computer as it is. And the XR21 has no card slot at all, so the card route does not exist on it.; PC-only tools when you have no computer. Drag-and-drop through a Windows PC works — but it needs the PC in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, a phone-to-USB copy is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.; Cloud backup dressed as USB backup. If the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step. Your photos sit on someone else's server, and the backup stops working the day you stop paying. On an HMD phone the cloud routes are Google Photos and Google Drive — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check.; Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete.; Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this.; Trusting one spec listing. The XR21's Android is two numbers — 13 per HMD's own datasheet against 12 per the GSMArena-derived listings — the Pulse's card is two ceilings — 256 GB per HMD's datasheet and Wikipedia against up to 1 TB per PhoneMore — the Aura's card is two ceilings — 256 GB against up to 1 TB — the Arc's card is two ceilings — 128 GB against up to 1 TB — the Vibe 5G's card is three ceilings — 256 GB against 512 GB against 1 TB — the Key's OTG is two claims — Not Supported against Yes — the Crest Max's and the Aura 2's OTG are omissions in GSMArena's USB field against Yes in other sources — and the Vibe 2's card slot is two types — a hybrid slot against a dedicated slot — so check the unit before buying a drive expecting a particular spec. The Android floor is settled on every one either way: all twenty clear 7.0 on every source.
