### Back up photos to USB when switching to a new phone

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/switching-phones-photos-to-usb.html

A new phone is the moment most people find out whether their photos were really backed up. The transfer usually works — but "usually" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and if the old phone has already been wiped or handed back for trade-in, there is no second chance. This article is about the step that comes before the transfer: a checked copy of the whole photo library on a USB drive you hold in your hand, made on the old phone, with no computer — and what to check before the old phone goes. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return a switching-specific guide — coticsy.com's "How to Back Up Your Photos Before Switching to a New Phone" — it covers the switch generally and USB copy as one manual step (exFAT, Files app, manual select/copy), and it is the best guide in the results; SnapDisk's own generic guides (transfer-photos-to-usb-automatically, usb-photo-backup) and FotoSafe's generic guide and a YouTube manual-OTG video also surface; NONE of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the phone-switch moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; SnapDisk is Android-only, so the iPhone half of a switch is the manual copy or a rival app, not SnapDisk; a transfer moves data, it is not a backup — it can be interrupted, skip items, or depend on photos that are not actually on the old phone because they live only in the cloud; the cloud-only originals trap is real in both directions — iCloud Photos with Optimize iPhone Storage keeps space-saving versions on the phone and the originals in iCloud, and Google Photos with Storage saver compresses photos larger than 16 MP down to 16 MP and videos over 1080p down to 1080p, per Google's own support page — so download the originals first; an exact file copy preserves the capture dates and locations already embedded in the originals, per the coticsy guide; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT if both phones support it, and test the drive with both phones before the switch; SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the wipe step is always yours, and always after the check; and the search results for this query are five results — SnapDisk's own generic guide, the coticsy switching guide, SnapDisk's generic USB guide, FotoSafe's generic guide, and a YouTube manual-OTG video — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the phone-switch moment. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:Back up first, transfer second, wipe last. Before you switch, plug a USB drive into the old Android phone, tap Backup in SnapDisk's notification, and the whole library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug — no computer, no upload, no account. Then run the transfer to the new phone, check that the photo count roughly matches and that older photos and long videos open at full quality, open a few photos straight from the drive, and only then wipe, sell or trade in the old phone. The switching guide that already exists — coticsy.com's — does cover the switch and USB copy as one manual step, so this article is not the first guide to switching phones — but none of the results gives you the whole-library one-tap backup to a USB drive framed for the phone-switch moment, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

Search "Back up photos to USB when switching to a new phone (no computer)" and the exact query returns five results — SnapDisk's own generic guide, the coticsy switching guide, SnapDisk's generic USB guide, FotoSafe's generic guide, and a YouTube manual-OTG video — none of them is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the phone-switch moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk. The coticsy guide DOES cover the switch generally and USB copy as one manual step (exFAT, Files app, manual select/copy), and it is the best guide in the results. FotoSafe's guide is a rival app guide, not a switching guide, and the YouTube video is a manual file-manager move. SnapDisk's own generic guides assume a working phone and say nothing about the switch moment, the transfer, or the wipe check.

Method 3: Most Android phones offer to copy apps and data from your old phone during setup, using a cable or Wi-Fi, and some manufacturers have their own transfer apps — and if your photos are backed up in Google Photos, they will be available once you sign in on the new phone. That is the transfer, and it runs after the drive copy, not instead of it: Make the drive copy first — Method 1 or 2 — and check it opens. This is the step the transfer cannot replace. During setup on the new phone, take the offer to copy from the old phone — a cable transfers the most, and some phones need an OTG adapter for it. Sign in to Google Photos on the new phone and let the library sync — but check the backup quality first, in Method 4, because a Storage saver cloud copy is not the original. Check the new phone before wiping the old one: the photo count roughly matches, older photos and long videos open at full quality — not just recent ones — and the drive copy opens. Then follow your phone maker's steps for selling or trading in a device, which include signing out of your accounts. Why the drive copy still matters when the transfer usually works: a transfer moves data, it is not a backup. It can be interrupted, it can skip items, or it can depend on photos being available that are not actually on the old phone — which is common when they live in iCloud or Google Photos. And the moment you reset the old phone, the transfer becomes the only path your photos took. The drive copy is the second path.

What this does not do: Does not transfer photos to the new phone by itself. SnapDisk copies your library to the drive — getting the photos onto the new phone is the transfer in Methods 3, 4 and 5, or a copy from the drive with the Files app or a file manager. VaultDrive does not restore the library itself either, per the coticsy guide — because the backups are plain files, you copy them onto the new phone with the steps above. Does not run on an iPhone. SnapDisk is Android only — it needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo. On the iPhone side of a switch, the copy is the manual Files-app route in Method 2, or a rival app. Does not download your cloud originals for you. If your originals live only in iCloud or Google Photos, you have to download them to the phone first — SnapDisk copies what is on the phone, and a cloud-only photo is not on the phone. Does not install below Android 7.0. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2 instead: the file-manager copy has no version floor. Does not work if the phone does not host a drive. The phone has to support USB OTG to see the drive at all. Most Android phones do, but a phone that lists OTG No cannot mount a drive, and then neither the one-tap backup nor the file-manager copy works on it. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not delete photos. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the wipe step is always yours, and always after the check. Does not back up anything but photos and videos. SnapDisk copies image and video files only — no settings, no contacts, no messages, no app data. The transfer in Methods 3, 4 and 5 is what moves those. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. If an app keeps its photos in a private folder SnapDisk cannot read, those photos stay in the app. Does not compress. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss.

What to avoid: Wiping, selling or trading in the old phone before the check. The transfer is not a backup, and once the old phone is wiped there is no second chance. Count, older photos, long videos, drive copy — then wipe. Trusting the transfer alone. A transfer can be interrupted, skip items, or depend on photos that are not actually on the old phone. The drive copy is the second path, and it is the one you hold in your hand. Trusting a cloud-only copy. Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos — larger than 16 MP resized to 16 MP, videos over 1080p resized to 1080p, per Google's support page — and iCloud Photos with Optimize iPhone Storage keeps space-saving versions on the phone. Either way the cloud copy is not the original. Download the originals first. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Reformatting erases the drive — copy existing files elsewhere before reformatting, per the coticsy guide — and test the drive with both phones before the switch. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos. FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB. Use exFAT if both phones support it — it works on iPhone and most current Android phones — and check support on both devices first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library. Make sure it is big enough for your entire library, including videos — and with room to keep backing up the new phone to the same drive afterwards. Forgetting edited versions and metadata. Retrieve cloud-only originals and preserve any edited versions or metadata you need, per the coticsy guide — an exact file copy preserves the capture dates and locations already embedded in the originals, but only if the copy holds the originals. Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Photos backs your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup. And a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone. Copy first, verify, then delete. Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this. Expecting Pro to follow you to an iPhone. SnapDisk Pro is a Google Play purchase, so it follows your Google account to another Android phone — it does not follow you to an iPhone, and SnapDisk does not run on iPhone at all. Rule of thumb: back up first, transfer second, wipe last. Make a checked copy on a drive you hold in your hand, then run the transfer, then check the new phone — count, older photos, long videos, drive copy — and only then wipe the old one. A transfer moves data; it is not a backup.

### Back up photos from an SD card to USB (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/sd-card-photos-to-usb.html

Your photos may live on a card, not in the phone — on the microSD card in the phone's slot, or on the full-size SD card in your camera. Either way the copy to a USB drive can be made with the phone alone, no computer — but the two cards are not the same job, and the guides that already exist only cover one of them. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — five of them — brightideaphotography.com, desnoulez.fr, petapixel.com, Ask Tim Grey, and goldenlenstraveler.com; all five are about a camera's memory card copied to an SSD with the phone as a bridge, by hand in the Files app; none of them is about the phone's own microSD card; none of them is a whole-library one-tap backup; and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; "SD card" means two different things here — the microSD card in your phone and the full-size SD card in your camera — and this article covers the phone's card first, then the camera's card; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the card, and choose the card's DCIM folder, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT, which the bridge guides recommend too; one USB port holds either the card reader or the drive, not both — copying straight from card to drive needs a powered hub, or two steps through the phone's storage; SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the card stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them; an iPhone has no microSD slot, so the phone's-card route is Android only, and the camera-card route on iPhone is the Files app, not SnapDisk; and a card formatted by a camera may use a folder layout other than DCIM — check the card's folders before picking, and pick the folder that actually holds the photos. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:If the card is the microSD card in your Android phone, point SnapDisk's From picker at the card's folder, plug the USB drive in, tap Backup, and the whole card copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug — no computer, no upload, no account. If the card is a camera's SD card, it needs a reader and, for a direct card-to-drive copy, a powered hub — that is the route every existing guide describes, by hand in the Files app — and SnapDisk can still do the one-tap version once the reader is plugged in, with the From picker pointed at it. Either way, open a few photos on the drive before you trust the copy, and keep the card until you have. The five guides this query already returns are all camera-card-to-SSD via a phone bridge, so this article is not the first guide to SD-card backup — but none of them covers the phone's own card, and none of them is a one-tap whole-library backup, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

Search "back up photos from SD card to USB drive without computer" and the exact query returns five results — and all five are real guides, but all five are about a camera's memory card copied to an SSD with the phone as a bridge, by hand in the Files app: brightideaphotography.com's video guide, "Back Up SD Cards Without a Laptop: Phone or iPad to SSD" (a camera card to an external drive with just a phone or tablet; the simple setup copies card to phone storage first, then phone to drive, and the better setup is a powered USB-C hub copying straight from card to SSD); desnoulez.fr's hub guide, "How to back up camera photos or SD Card without a laptop" (smartphone or tablet as a bridge between an SD or CFexpress card and an external SSD via a USB hub, copy in the Files app; featured on PetaPixel on May 11, 2025); petapixel.com's field-backup guide from May 11, 2025, "No Laptop? No Problem: How to Back Up Photos in the Field With Your Smartphone" (full-resolution RAW or JPEG files copied directly from the memory card to a solid-state drive using a USB hub connected to the phone, plus the three-copy rule: one card in the camera, one card on your person, one SSD in the checked bag); Ask Tim Grey's July 3, 2023 newsletter, "Media Card Direct to Hard Drive" (a smartphone or tablet as the intermediary for a media card to a hard drive, noting the purpose-built direct-copy drives have largely been discontinued, and naming the NewQ FileHub and the SanDisk iXpand); and goldenlenstraveler.com's travel guide, "How to Back up Photos While Traveling Without a Laptop" (exFAT SSD on a USB-C OTG adapter, SD card reader, powered hub, Files-app copy after each shoot, and always safely eject the drive). None of the five is about the phone's own microSD card, none of them is a whole-library one-tap backup, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 3: This is the bridge guides' route, and it is the one to use when the card is a camera's SD card and you want the copy to go straight from the card to the drive. It is the desnoulez and PetaPixel workflow, step for step: Connect the powered hub to the phone, and power the hub — a PD wall adapter at home, a PD power bank in the field. A powered hub gives the connected devices their own power, so the phone stays charged during a long transfer instead of draining, per the brightideaphotography guide. Insert the camera's card into the hub's SD slot, or into a card reader plugged into the hub. Plug the SSD or USB drive into the hub as well. Open the phone's file manager. The card and the drive both appear — on iPhone in the Files app, on Android in Google Files or the maker's file manager, which on Samsung can show the card and the drive side by side, per the brightideaphotography guide. Select the photos and videos on the card, tap Copy, choose the drive as the destination, and tap Paste. The files go straight from the card to the drive without ever taking up space on the phone's internal storage — that is the whole point of the hub, and it is what the simple two-step setup cannot do. Check the copy the way the bridge guides insist on: the file count and total size look right, then open a few photos and a video directly from the backup drive and make sure they actually are readable. A copy is not much use if you discover later that something went wrong, per the brightideaphotography guide — and the PetaPixel guide's version of the same rule is the three-copy habit: one card in the camera, one card on your person, one SSD in the checked bag. Safely eject everything once done, per the goldenlenstraveler guide — skipping that step risks data corruption, and a corrupted backup on the road is the costly mistake this whole workflow exists to prevent. The one-tap version of this method is SnapDisk with the From picker pointed at the reader: plug the hub in, check the phone sees the card, then in SnapDisk tap the From picker, browse to the card reader, and choose the card's folder — the picker is the system folder picker, so a mounted reader appears in it the same way the phone's own card does — and tap Backup when the drive connects. The copy then runs oldest-first with progress, Pause and Stop, and resume — the parts the Files-app copy does not give you. If the reader does not mount, the file-manager copy in the steps above is the fallback, and the hub, the reader, or the card format is the thing to check.

What this does not do: Does not read a card the phone cannot mount. The phone has to see the card at all — in its slot, or in a reader it recognises. If the card does not appear in the file manager, neither the one-tap backup nor the manual copy works on it, and the card format, the reader, or the adapter is the thing to check. Format the drive as exFAT before a trip, per the bridge guides — iOS cannot write to an NTFS drive, and a drive formatted for Windows needs checking before you rely on it in the field. Does not run the phone's-card route on an iPhone. An iPhone has no microSD slot, so there is no phone's card to back up — and SnapDisk is Android only. On the iPhone side the camera-card route is the Files app, as Methods 3 and 4 describe, or a rival app. Does not install below Android 7.0. SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2 instead: the file-manager copy has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive. Drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not delete photos. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the card keeps its photos until you delete them yourself, and that step is always yours, and always after the check. Does not back up anything but photos and videos. SnapDisk copies image and video files only — no settings, no contacts, no messages, no app data. Does not download your cloud originals for you. If your originals live only in iCloud or Google Photos, you have to download them to the phone first — SnapDisk copies what is on the phone or on the card, and a cloud-only photo is in neither place. Does not work if the phone does not host a drive. The phone has to support USB OTG to see the drive at all. Most Android phones do, but a phone that lists OTG No cannot mount a drive, and then neither the one-tap backup nor the file-manager copy works on it. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. If an app keeps its photos in a private folder SnapDisk cannot read, those photos stay in the app. Does not compress. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss.

What to avoid: Moving instead of copying. The file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step. If the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the card. Copy first, verify, then delete — the brightideaphotography guide makes the same point about the Files app's Move option. Deleting from the card before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you've confirmed the copy. Copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the card — never the other way round. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes — so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check. Unplugging mid-copy. Pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first — SnapDisk's Stop button exists for exactly this. The goldenlenstraveler guide's version is the same rule at the end: always safely eject the drive before disconnecting. Using the phone's storage as the middle step without checking the space. The two-step copy in Method 4 needs enough free space on the phone to hold everything on the card first. A big shoot will not fit — that is the brightideaphotography guide's warning, and it is the reason the hub in Method 3 exists. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos. FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB. Use exFAT — it is what every bridge guide recommends — and check the drive's format before the trip, not after you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Reformatting erases the drive — copy existing files elsewhere before reformatting, and test the drive with the phone before the trip. Buying a drive too small for the whole card. Make sure it is big enough for the entire card, including videos — and with room to keep backing up the same card afterwards. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. A charging cable connects the phone to a computer, which is the opposite direction. What you need is a data-capable OTG adapter or a USB-C drive. Assuming the card uses DCIM. A card formatted by a camera may use a folder layout other than DCIM. Check the card's folders before picking, and pick the folder that actually holds the photos — in SnapDisk and in the file manager alike. Forgetting the card in the camera. The camera-card route needs the card out of the camera and in a reader. If the card is still in the camera, there is nothing to copy — and the camera's own USB connection is a different workflow, not this one. Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy. Google Photos backs your phone up to Google's servers — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not a cloud backup. And a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Expecting Pro to follow you to an iPhone. SnapDisk Pro is a Google Play purchase, so it follows your Google account to another Android phone — it does not follow you to an iPhone, and SnapDisk does not run on iPhone at all. Rule of thumb: the card is the original — the drive is the copy, and the copy is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive and checked them. Point the From picker at the card, tap Backup, wait, check, and only then think about deleting anything from the card.

### Back up photos from a tablet to USB (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/tablet-photos-to-usb.html

A tablet is not a big phone when it comes to backup — its library is often years of family photos, many Android tablets have a microSD slot that high-end phones no longer do, older tablets still use micro-USB while newer ones use USB-C, and whether the tablet supports USB OTG varies by model. The copy itself is the same job — tablet to drive, no computer — but the port, the slot, and the size change the steps. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return real tablet guides — five of them — ceedo.com, petapixel.com, thecomputerbasics.com, ssa-digital.com, and pixoneye.com; all five are manual select-copy-paste guides, and none of them is a whole-library one-tap backup; none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; tablets differ from phones — often larger libraries, a microSD slot on many Android tablets but never on an iPad, USB-C on newer tablets and micro-USB on older ones, and OTG support that varies by model; the phone-bridge pattern from the SD-card article does not apply the same way — the tablet holds the photos itself, so the copy is direct tablet-to-drive, and the bridge only reappears for a camera card; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; an iPad has no microSD slot and SnapDisk is Android only, so the iPad route is the Files app, not SnapDisk; a tablet's photos may not all sit in DCIM — check the tablet's folders before picking, and pick the folder that actually holds the photos; and SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the tablet stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On an Android tablet, plug a USB drive in — directly if it is a USB-C drive, or through an OTG adapter — tap Backup in SnapDisk, and the whole library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug — no computer, no upload, no account. On an iPad the same copy is by hand in the Files app, because SnapDisk is Android only. The five guides this query already returns are all real tablet guides, so this article is not the first guide to tablet backup — but all five are manual select-copy-paste, and none of them is a one-tap whole-library backup, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026.

Search "back up photos from tablet to USB drive without computer" and the exact query returns five results — and four of them are real tablet guides: ceedo.com's "How To Transfer Photos From Tablet To USB Flash Drive" (Android, iPad and Windows tablets, USB-C and micro-USB, manual file-manager copy), petapixel.com's field-backup guide (a phone or tablet as a bridge for a camera card to an SSD, manual copy), thecomputerbasics.com's "Transfer Files Without a Computer" (connectors, file systems and power — a spinning hard drive may appear and then disconnect, exFAT is the format to use), ssa-digital.com's Android tablet OTG checklist (check OTG first, match the adapter to the port, some tablets need the OTG switch on in Settings), and pixoneye.com's phone-to-USB-stick guide (manual file-manager copy; its Android steps apply to a tablet with OTG, and it names ThePhotoStick Omni as a rival app-based accessory for phones). Follow-up searches add three more tablet-specific results: lenovo.com's own "USB Flash Drive for Tablets: A Comprehensive Guide" (plug-and-play, file-manager copy, a flash drive is excellent for backing up a tablet), mobilespecs.net's "How to backup ZTE Axon tablet" (Google cloud sync, TWRP, CWM, Titanium Backup, SP FlashTool, ADB — no USB drive at all), and devicesfaq.com's ZTE Axon Pad answers (connect to a computer with a USB cable, or Google cloud — no USB drive at all). None of the eight is a whole-library one-tap tablet-to-USB backup, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely inside the tablet — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive. It needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo, and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Open SnapDisk: it opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker — the defaults are From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM. If the tablet's photos live on its microSD card, tap the From picker, browse to the card, and choose the card's DCIM folder — the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in MainActivity.kt), so it reaches the card. Plug the USB drive in, tap Backup in the notification, and the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. If you unplug mid-copy the backup pauses with the full error and resumes where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size — and on a tablet with a library bigger than 5 GB that is the case Pro is for. The screenshot in the article is from SnapDisk on a phone, not a tablet — the tablet layout is unverified.

What this does not do: Does not run SnapDisk on an iPad or a Windows tablet — SnapDisk is Android only; on the iPad side the copy is the Files app, and on a Windows tablet it is File Explorer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a tablet running older Android, use the file-manager copy, which has no version floor. Does not mount a drive the tablet cannot host — without USB OTG the tablet cannot see a drive at all. Does not power a spinning hard drive by itself — a tablet supplies limited power, so a spinning drive may appear and then disconnect; use a flash drive or an SSD, or a powered hub. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README. Does not delete photos — SnapDisk only copies. Does not back up anything but photos and videos. Does not download your cloud originals for you. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Moving instead of copying — the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone. Deleting from the tablet before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; on a tablet library the copy runs long, so the pause matters more, not less. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before the trip. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a tablet library is often bigger than you think, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the ceedo guide calls the wrong adapter the number one cause of failed transfers. Assuming the tablet supports OTG — some budget or kids tablets do not, and on some the setting has to be switched on first. Assuming the photos all sit in DCIM. Mistaking a cloud backup for a photo copy — the mobilespecs and devicesfaq tablet backup guides are cloud or computer routes, and they never produce a drive you can hold. Expecting Pro to follow you to an iPad — SnapDisk Pro is a Google Play purchase, and SnapDisk does not run on iPad at all.

### Back up photos to USB when your phone battery is low

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/low-battery-photos-to-usb.html

A low battery is a clock, not a wall — the photos are still on the phone, the drive is still in your hand, and the copy is still a local one that needs no Wi-Fi and no upload. Fourteen honest caveats up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — our own offline-backup and external-drive articles, mobiletrans.wondershare.com, a Samsung community thread, and a Photostock OmniX review — plus four battery-advice guides, fonelab.com, invotech.dut.ac.za, sekin.in, and eztoolset.com; all of them are manual select-copy-paste, one-line battery advice, or a $34.99 hardware product, and none of them is a whole-library one-tap backup framed for the low-battery moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; SnapDisk's copy runs as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no low-battery run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified, and this article says so instead of promising it; the drive occupies the phone's only USB-C port — the phone cannot charge from a power bank at the same time unless the connection goes through a USB-C hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:When the battery is low and there is no charger, plug a USB drive straight into the phone and copy the photos to the drive — no computer, no upload, no account. The one-tap way is SnapDisk: plug the drive in, tap Backup in the notification, turn the screen off, and the whole library copies oldest-first in the background, with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if the phone dies. The copy is local, so switching Wi-Fi and mobile data off costs nothing and saves battery — the phone is not uploading anything. The guides this query already returns are all real guides, so this article is not the first guide to a low battery — but all of them are manual select-copy-paste, one-line battery advice, or a $34.99 hardware product, and none of them is a one-tap whole-library backup to USB framed for the low-battery moment, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 20, 2026. And two honest limits: the drive draws its power from the phone, so charge first if you can; and the drive takes the phone's only USB-C port, so the phone cannot charge from a power bank at the same time without a hub that passes power through.

Search "back up photos to USB when phone battery is low no charger" and the exact query returns five results — and the low-battery moment itself is not one of them: SnapDisk's own "How to back up photos offline on Android" (the one-tap copy, no cloud, no account, no upload — but nothing about a low battery); SnapDisk's own "How to back up photos to an external drive on Android" (the same one-tap copy to a flash drive, hard drive, or SSD, with the note that a spinning hard drive may need its own power — but nothing about a low battery either); mobiletrans.wondershare.com's "Back Up a Phone to USB Without Cloud Storage" (a manual folder copy through a USB-OTG adapter, with a computer as the fallback — and its fix to keep: keep the phone unlocked during large transfers to prevent connection pauses, which is the manual copy's battery problem in one line); the Samsung community thread "How to take pictures off phone and put on memory stick" (the manual My Files route — plug the stick in through an OTG adapter, select, Copy, choose the drive, unmount); and curatedly.co's "Photostock OmniX Review (2026)" (a $34.99 portable drive with four built-in connectors and a companion app that copies media with one tap, offline — a real one-tap product, but a product review, not a guide). A second search, for the power-bank and charge-while-copying angle, returned four more battery-advice guides: invotech.dut.ac.za's "Easy! Transfer Files From Android to USB Drive (Guide)" (the only guide with a power section — USB drives draw power from the phone, which can affect battery life during large transfers, so use a lower-power drive or connect the phone to a power source during the transfer — and its FAQ answers yes, transferring consumes significant battery, especially for large files); fonelab.com's "How to Transfer Photos from Android to Flash Drive in 3 Easy Ways" (its battery line is the one this article borrows: an OTG adapter drains your Android phone battery quickly, so charge first); sekin.in's "Transfer Photos From Android to a USB Flash Drive" (one line in the what-you-need list: a reasonably charged phone, because large transfers can take time and the phone powers the USB device); and eztoolset.com's "How to Transfer Photos from Android to a USB Drive" (its hub line is the one to keep: a USB-C hub with USB-A ports can be useful for peripherals, but may create additional power and compatibility issues). None of the nine is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the low-battery moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive. It needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo, and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Charge first if you can — the fonelab guide's advice — then check how much the photos take in Settings, then Storage; switch Wi-Fi and mobile data off, because the copy is local and SnapDisk has no internet permission, so the radios are pure battery cost; open SnapDisk — it opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker — the defaults are From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM; check From twice, because a phone's photos may not all sit in DCIM; the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in MainActivity.kt). Plug the USB drive in and tap Backup: the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. Turn the screen off — the copy is a foreground service, built to keep running with the screen off, and the screen is the biggest drain you control. One honest limit, stated plainly because it is unverified: the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no low-battery run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — if the copy pauses under battery saver, turn battery saver off for the copy and tap Resume. If the phone dies first, Method 4 is the resume: charge a little, reopen SnapDisk, tap Resume, and the copy picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. Open a few photos on the drive, then delete the originals from the phone — only now does the phone get its space back. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped — on a low battery that cap is a feature, because a short run copies the oldest 5 GB first; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss — and it copies, it never deletes.

Method 3, the power bank and the hub: the drive occupies the phone's only USB-C port, so a power bank plugged straight into the phone has nowhere to go while the drive is in. The hub gives the port back — hub into the phone, power bank into the hub's PD charging port, drive into the hub's USB-A port — then check the drive appears before tapping Backup. Two honest limits: the hub has to support data and PD pass-through, not just charging, and the hub route is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk, so test it before relying on it. Without a hub, the fonelab guide's advice stands: charge first, then copy — doing the two jobs in sequence instead of at once.

What this does not do: Does not charge the phone while the drive is plugged in — one port holds either the drive or the charger, not both, unless the connection goes through a USB-C hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk. Does not keep copying if the phone dies — the copy pauses, finished files stay on the drive, and resume picks up where it stopped after you charge a little and reopen the app. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no low-battery run has been tested. Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause — on Android 15 and later, a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2, which has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not back up anything but photos and videos. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud — download them to the phone first. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not fix a phone that will not boot. Does not work on iPhone — SnapDisk is Android only. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Starting a big copy at 5% with no plan — charge first if you can, or copy oldest-first in short runs, so even a partial run saves the earliest photos. Starting the manual copy on a low battery — the manual copy needs the phone unlocked for the whole transfer, so the screen burns the battery you are trying to save. Moving instead of copying — the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone — and on a low battery the copy is more likely to fail, not less. Deleting from the phone before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Uploading to the cloud on a low battery — a cloud backup needs Wi-Fi, upload time, and free space in the account, and the phone burns battery uploading for hours. Leaving Wi-Fi and mobile data on during the copy — the copy is local, so the radios are pure battery cost. Buying a charging-only hub and expecting data, or a hub without pass-through charging and expecting it to charge. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; in the Files app, eject the drive before unplugging it. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a low battery's library is big by definition, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the adapter has to support data transfer, not just charging. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run — a whole library is bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for.

(a complete reset is exactly what you want before giving or selling a tablet, and it is smart to remove the Google account first to avoid Factory Reset Protection complications — but its backup is a working copy you are assumed to have made already, and it says nothing about a USB drive from the phone or about SnapDisk). None of the nine is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the sell-or-trade-in moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive. It needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo, and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Check how much the photos take in Settings, then Storage; open SnapDisk — it opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker — the defaults are From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM; check From twice, because a phone's photos may not all sit in DCIM — the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in MainActivity.kt) — and repeat the copy for each folder that holds photos. Plug the USB drive in and tap Backup: the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. Turn the screen off and let it run. One honest limit, stated plainly because it is unverified: the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no selling-prep run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — if the copy pauses under battery saver, turn battery saver off for the copy and tap Resume. Wait for the copy to finish — all of it. Open a few photos on the drive, unplug the drive, and only now remove the accounts and wipe the phone. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped — a phone about to be sold often holds a library bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss — and it copies, it never deletes.

Method 3, the cloud trap: the Photos app on the phone shows the photos, and showing them feels like backing them up — it is not. Check that Backup is on in Google Photos, check the backup quality — storage saver uploads compressed copies, not the originals — check the device folders in Photos settings, Backup, Back up device folders, and check the upload actually finished on another device at photos.google.com, because seeing a photo in the Photos app on this phone proves nothing. Photos count against the shared 15 GB of free Google account storage, and if the account is full the upload stopped without telling you clearly. If anything is missing from the cloud, copy it to a USB drive first — the drive copy is the original file, byte for byte, and it does not depend on the account you are about to sign out of.

What this does not do: Does not undo a wipe or a hand-over — once the reset runs, the photos on the phone are gone, with no un-reset and no recovery, and once the phone is handed over there is no getting it back to check. Does not back up anything but photos and videos — back up settings, contacts, messages, and app data in Settings, Google, Backup, before the sale too, and export 2FA tokens and transit passes separately. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud — download them to the phone first. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no selling-prep run has been tested. Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause — on Android 15 and later, a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2, which has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not remove your accounts for you — removing the Google account and the Samsung account is your step, in Method 4, before the wipe. Does not take the SIM or microSD card out for you — a factory reset does not wipe a microSD card. Does not fix a phone that will not boot. Does not work on iPhone — SnapDisk is Android only. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Wiping before the backup finishes — the backup has to complete and be checked before the wipe, and there is no undo. Handing the phone over with your accounts still on it — Factory Reset Protection asks the next owner for your Google account password, so remove every Google account and sign out of the Samsung account before the wipe, and power the phone on before the buyer leaves to check it shows the setup welcome screen. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device — seeing photos in the Photos app on the phone proves nothing. Forgetting the device folders — Google Photos backs up the camera folder by default, and WhatsApp images, screenshots, and downloads have to be switched on separately. Leaving the microSD card in the phone — a factory reset does not wipe it. Moving instead of copying — the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move before a sale leaves photos in neither place. Deleting from the phone before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Leaving the drive plugged in during the wipe — unplug it before wiping anyway. Starting the manual copy on a big library — the manual copy needs the phone unlocked for the whole transfer and has no resume. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; in the Files app, eject the drive before unplugging it. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a phone about to be sold often holds years of photos, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the adapter has to support data transfer, not just charging. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run — a whole library is bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for.

None of the five is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup guide framed for the before-an-Android-update moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive, and it needs no Wi-Fi at all. It needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo, and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Charge first if you can — one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both. Check how much the photos take in Settings, then Storage; open SnapDisk — it opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker — the defaults are From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM; check From twice, because a phone's photos may not all sit in DCIM — the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in MainActivity.kt) — and repeat the copy for each folder that holds photos. Plug the USB drive in and tap Backup: the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. Turn the screen off and let it run. One honest limit, stated plainly because it is unverified: the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no pre-update run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — if the copy pauses under battery saver, turn battery saver off for the copy and tap Resume. Wait for the copy to finish — all of it. Open a few photos on the drive, unplug the drive, and put it somewhere safe. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped — a phone that has never been backed up often holds a library bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss — and it copies, it never deletes.

Method 3, the cloud trap: the Photos app on the phone shows the photos, and showing them feels like backing them up — it is not. Check that Backup is on in Google Photos, check the backup quality — storage saver uploads compressed copies, not the originals — check the device folders in Photos settings, Backup, Back up device folders, and check the upload actually finished on another device at photos.google.com, because seeing a photo in the Photos app on this phone proves nothing. Photos count against the shared 15 GB of free Google account storage, and if the account is full the upload stopped without telling you clearly. With no Wi-Fi the upload cannot run at all, so the drive copy comes first and the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi. If anything is missing from the cloud, copy it to a USB drive first — the drive copy is the original file, byte for byte, and it does not depend on the Wi-Fi, the account, or the subscription.

Method 4, the update itself: confirm the backup first — open a few photos on the drive — then unplug the drive, check the free space in Settings, Storage, charge the phone or plug it in, download on Wi-Fi, and tap Install when the phone can sit untouched. The phone will restart, possibly more than once — that is normal; do not hold the power button or interrupt it. After the restart, check the photos — the oldest ones, not just the most recent. If the phone will not boot, check the cloud at photos.google.com on another device, then repair — and the drive copy is the copy that survives, because it was never on the phone when the update failed.

What this does not do: Does not make the update itself safe — the backup does not fix a failed update or a bootloop, it only makes the failure survivable. Does not undo a wipe — once a factory reset runs, the photos on the phone are gone, with no un-wipe and no recovery. Does not back up anything but photos and videos — back up settings, contacts, messages, and app data in Settings, Google, Backup, before the update too. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud — download them to the phone first. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no pre-update run has been tested. Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause — on Android 15 and later, a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2, which has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not charge the phone while the drive is in the port — one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both. Does not power a portable SSD from the phone alone — a portable SSD may need a powered hub. Does not fix a phone that will not boot. Does not work on iPhone — SnapDisk is Android only. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Tapping Install before the backup finishes — the backup has to complete and be checked before the update starts, and after a wipe there is no undo. Leaving the drive plugged in during the update — unplug it before tapping Install. Starting the update on a dying battery or with no free space — charge first, check the free space in Settings, and free space only after the USB copy is verified. Interrupting the install — the phone will restart, possibly more than once, and that is normal. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device — seeing photos in the Photos app on the phone proves nothing. Forgetting the device folders — Google Photos backs up the camera folder by default, and WhatsApp images, screenshots, and downloads have to be switched on separately. Moving instead of copying — the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. Deleting from the phone before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; in the Files app, eject the drive before unplugging it. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a phone that has never been backed up holds years of photos, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the adapter has to support data transfer, not just charging. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run — a whole library is bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for. Assuming the generic guides cover the update — the FotoSafe, mefmobile.org, YouTube, umatechnology.org, and Dr.Fone guides move photos to a USB drive, but none of them says when the copy has to finish, none of them unplugs the drive before the update, and none of them checks the battery and the free space the update itself needs.

Plug the USB drive in and tap Backup: the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. Turn the screen off and let it run. One honest limit, stated plainly because it is unverified: the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no before-a-flight run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — if the copy pauses under battery saver, turn battery saver off for the copy and tap Resume. Wait for the copy to finish — all of it, the night before. Open a few photos on the drive, unplug the drive, and pack it in the carry-on — a different bag from the phone, never checked luggage. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped — a phone that has never been backed up often holds a library bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss — and it copies, it never deletes.

Method 2, by hand in the Files app: charge first, plug the drive in, open the Files app, find the photos in DCIM or Pictures, select them, tap Copy, tap the USB drive, tap Paste — and repeat for every folder that holds photos, because the Files app copies one selection at a time and a folder you forget is a folder a lost phone takes with it. Keep the phone unlocked while the copy runs — the screen stays on for the whole transfer. Copy, not Move: the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. What the manual copy does not give you is the one-tap backup: no oldest-first order, no progress bar with speed and ETA, no Pause and Stop, and no resume if the copy is interrupted.

Method 3, the cloud trap: the Photos app on the phone shows the photos, and showing them feels like backing them up — it is not. Check that Backup is on in Google Photos, check the backup quality — storage saver uploads compressed copies, not the originals — check the device folders in Photos settings, Backup, Back up device folders, and check the upload actually finished on another device at photos.google.com, because seeing a photo in the Photos app on this phone proves nothing. Photos count against the shared 15 GB of free Google account storage, and if the account is full the upload stopped without telling you clearly. With no Wi-Fi at the gate the upload cannot run at all, so the drive copy comes first and the cloud check waits for Wi-Fi. If anything is missing from the cloud, copy it to a USB drive first — the drive copy is the original file, byte for byte, and it does not depend on the Wi-Fi, the account, or the subscription.

At the airport: security X-ray does not harm a USB drive — flash memory is not affected by the X-ray dose used at security — so keep the drive accessible in the tray if security asks to see it. The drive rides in the carry-on, never in checked luggage: a checked bag can be lost, delayed, or opened, and a backup drive in a lost checked bag is a backup that flew somewhere else. Phone in pocket, drive in carry-on — two copies in two places, because two copies in the same bag is one copy. The checked-luggage SSD in the field guides is a third copy; this drive is the second copy, so it stays with you. Do not start a big copy at the gate — a boarding call cuts it off, there is no guaranteed power outlet, and there is no Wi-Fi to fall back on — and do not count on finishing in the air: the backup that counts is the one finished and checked before you board. Keep the drive with you, not in the seat pocket — a drive left in a seat pocket is a drive left on the plane.

What this does not do: Does not protect the phone from being lost or stolen — the backup copies photos, it does not keep the phone in your pocket. Does not undo a loss — once the phone is lost with photos still only on it, the photos are out of reach. Does not back up anything but photos and videos — back up settings, contacts, messages, and app data in Settings, Google, Backup, too, and export 2FA tokens and transit passes separately. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud — download them to the phone first. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no before-a-flight run has been tested. Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause — on Android 15 and later, a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2, which has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not charge the phone while the drive is in the port — one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both. Does not power a portable SSD from the phone alone — a portable SSD may need a powered hub. Does not make a checked bag safe — the drive rides in the carry-on. Does not work on iPhone — SnapDisk is Android only. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Starting the copy at the gate — a boarding call cuts it off, and there is no guaranteed power outlet or Wi-Fi to fall back on. Boarding before the copy finishes — a copy still running when the plane takes off is not a backup, and after the phone is lost there is no undo. Packing the drive and the phone in the same bag — two copies in the same bag is one copy. Putting the drive in checked luggage — a checked bag can be lost or delayed. Leaving the drive in a seat pocket — a drive left in a seat pocket is a drive left on the plane. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device — seeing photos in the Photos app on the phone proves nothing. Forgetting the device folders — Google Photos backs up the camera folder by default, and WhatsApp images, screenshots, and downloads have to be switched on separately. Moving instead of copying — the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. Deleting from the phone before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; in the Files app, eject the drive before unplugging it. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a phone that has never been backed up holds years of photos, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the adapter has to support data transfer, not just charging. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run — a whole library is bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for. Assuming the bridge guides cover the phone's library — the desnoulez.fr, PetaPixel, and brightideaphotography guides back up a camera card through the phone, but none of them copies the phone's own photos, none of them runs the night before a flight, and none of them separates the drive from the phone for the trip.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive, and it needs no Wi-Fi at all. It needs Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24 in the repo, and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Charge the phone first — one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both. Check how much the photos take in Settings, then Storage; open SnapDisk — it opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker — the defaults are From /sdcard/DCIM and To /disk/DCIM; check From twice, because a phone's photos may not all sit in DCIM — the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in MainActivity.kt) — and repeat the copy for each folder that holds photos. Plug the USB drive in and tap Backup: the library copies oldest-first in the background with live progress — percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left — and Pause and Stop. Turn the screen off and let it run. One honest limit, stated plainly because it is unverified: the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no before-lending run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — if the copy pauses under battery saver, turn battery saver off for the copy and tap Resume. Wait for the copy to finish — all of it, before the handover. Open a few photos on the drive, unplug the drive, and put it somewhere safe at home — never handed to the borrower. Free version: manual backup, up to 5 GB per run, and running it again past the cap picks up where it stopped — a phone that has never been backed up often holds a library bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for; Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase — auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies the original files as they are — no recompression, no resizing, no quality loss — and it copies, it never deletes, and it never locks.

Method 2, by hand in the Files app: charge first, plug the drive in, open the Files app, find the photos in DCIM or Pictures, select them, tap Copy, tap the USB drive, tap Paste — and repeat for every folder that holds photos, because the Files app copies one selection at a time and a folder you forget is a folder a borrower's tap takes with it. Keep the phone unlocked while the copy runs — the screen stays on for the whole transfer. Copy, not Move: the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. What the manual copy does not give you is the one-tap backup: no oldest-first order, no progress bar with speed and ETA, no Pause and Stop, and no resume if the copy is interrupted.

Method 3, the cloud trap: the Photos app on the phone shows the photos, and showing them feels like backing them up — it is not. Check that Backup is on in Google Photos, check the backup quality — storage saver uploads compressed copies, not the originals — check the device folders in Photos settings, Backup, Back up device folders, and check the upload actually finished on another device at photos.google.com, because seeing a photo in the Photos app on this phone proves nothing. Photos count against the shared 15 GB of free Google account storage, and if the account is full the upload stopped without telling you clearly. The borrower may delete a photo, so the cloud copy has to be finished and checked before the handover, not after the phone comes back. If anything is missing from the cloud, copy it to a USB drive first — the drive copy is the original file, byte for byte, and it does not depend on the Wi-Fi, the account, or the subscription.

Before you hand it over: agree what the phone is for and for how long, keep the drive at home — the borrower does not need your backup, and a drive handed over with the phone is a copy you no longer hold. Lock the borrower out of your photos with the phone's own tools: a guest profile on phones that offer one, screen pinning for the one app they need, or an app lock or a secure folder on phones that have one — the exact menu names vary by phone and not every phone offers all three, so set it up and test it before the handover. Lock the phone before you hand it over, agree the passcode or unlock steps with the borrower, and change the passcode when the phone comes home. Decide about the SIM before the handover — the borrower does not need your SIM to take a photo or use Wi-Fi — and pull it unless the lend is for calls. Do not start a big copy at the handover. When the phone comes home, check it before you delete anything from the drive.

What this does not do: Does not stop the borrower from deleting a photo — the backup copies photos, it does not keep anyone from deleting them from the phone. Does not undo a deletion — once a photo is deleted with no copy anywhere else, it is gone. Does not lock the phone or hide your photos — SnapDisk copies, it never deletes and it never locks, and there is no lock, hidden album, or guest mode in the app. Does not back up anything but photos and videos — back up settings, contacts, messages, and app data in Settings, Google, Backup, too, and export 2FA tokens and transit passes separately. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud — download them to the phone first. Does not back up photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no before-lending run has been tested. Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause — on Android 15 and later, a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer. Does not install below Android 7.0 — minSdk 24 in the repo — so on a phone running older Android, use Method 2, which has no version floor. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README; a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Does not charge the phone while the drive is in the port — one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both. Does not power a portable SSD from the phone alone — a portable SSD may need a powered hub. Does not work on a damaged port or a dead phone — never plug anything into a damaged USB port, and a dead phone is a repair-lab job only. Does not lock the phone for you — the guest profile, screen pinning, and app lock are your steps at the handover. Does not work on iPhone — SnapDisk is Android only. Does not compress — the original files are copied as they are.

What to avoid: Starting the copy at the handover — the borrower has their own errand and no reason to wait for your copy. Handing the phone over before the copy finishes — a copy still running when the borrower walks off is not a backup, and after a deletion there is no undo. Handing the drive to the borrower with the phone — a drive handed over is a copy you no longer hold. Handing the phone over unlocked with no backup. Assuming the backup keeps the borrower out of your photos — it does not, and the lock-down is a separate phone step. Leaving the SIM in the phone without deciding. Plugging anything into a damaged port. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device — seeing photos in the Photos app on the phone proves nothing. Forgetting the device folders — Google Photos backs up the camera folder by default, and WhatsApp images, screenshots, and downloads have to be switched on separately. Moving instead of copying — the Files app's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. Deleting from the phone before verifying — a backup is only a backup once you have opened photos on the drive. Unplugging mid-copy — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first; in the Files app, eject the drive before unplugging it. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos — use exFAT, and check the drive's format before you are relying on it. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library — a phone that has never been backed up holds years of photos, so check the size in Settings before you buy. Buying a charging cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port — USB-C and micro-USB do not fit each other, and the adapter has to support data transfer, not just charging. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run — a whole library is bigger than 5 GB, so it takes several taps, and that is the case Pro is for. Assuming the general guides cover the lending moment — the Techsith, Alibaba, MobileTrans, MakeUseOf, RottenWifi, and Android Central guides back up photos to the cloud, a computer, or a drive, but none of them copies the phone's library to USB in one tap, none of them keeps the drive at home while the phone goes to a borrower, and none of them says how to lock the phone down before the handover.

### Back up photos to USB before rooting your phone

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/rooting-photos-to-usb.html

Your phone is about to be unlocked and flashed, and it holds the only copy of months of photos — unlocking the bootloader wipes everything by design, and after the wipe there is no recovery. The honest caveats, up front: the exact query DOES return real guides — five of them — UMA Technology's backup-before-flashing checklist, PrivacyPortal's bootloader guide, Sod Calculator's custom-ROM guide, Awesome Android Root's unlock guide, and RottenWifi's unlock guide — and all five frame backup as a step inside a flashing or unlock guide, with computer, cloud, or manual-copy routes — and none of the five is a whole-library one-tap phone-to-USB backup framed for the before-unlock moment, and none of them mentions SnapDisk — that angle is the gap this article fills; unlocking the bootloader wipes ALL data BY DESIGN — the backup must COMPLETE and be verified on the drive BEFORE the unlock command runs, because after the wipe there is no recovery; SnapDisk backs up photos and videos ONLY — it does not back up app data, authenticator seeds, messages, or system state — so export authenticators, back up chats, and take a TWRP nandroid for a full system image separately; unplug the USB drive before flashing — the USB port is needed for the computer and fastboot — and keep the drive aside until the new ROM boots; unlocking may void the warranty, can break Play Integrity and banking apps, and some carrier variants cannot be unlocked at all — check before you start; this route is only for a phone that still works and has a dry, undamaged port — never plug anything into a damaged port, and a dead phone is a repair-lab job only; one USB-C port holds the drive OR the charger, not both — charge first, or use a powered hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk; a portable SSD may need a powered hub — the phone alone may not supply enough power for both the hub and the drive; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the screenshot below is from SnapDisk on a phone — it is the same settings screen you will see, because this article is about a phone; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the phone's storage, and choose the folder that holds the photos, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree;
