Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:You are about to unlock the bootloader — back up the whole library to USB from the phone first, before the unlock command runs: unlocking wipes everything by design, and after the wipe there is no recovery. The one-tap way is SnapDisk: plug the drive in, tap Backup in the notification, and the whole library copies oldest-first in the background, with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if anything interrupts it. The guides this query already returns are all real guides, so this article is not the first guide to backing up before flashing — and none of them is a one-tap whole-library backup of the phone's own photos to USB from the phone, for the before-unlock moment, which is the gap this article fills, as of November 21, 2026. And three honest limits: the backup has to finish and be checked before the unlock runs, because a copy still running when the wipe starts is not a backup and there is no recovery after a wipe; SnapDisk backs up photos and videos only — app data, authenticator seeds, messages, and system state need separate backups, and a TWRP nandroid is the full system image; and the drive comes out before flashing — the USB port is needed for the computer — and stays aside until the new ROM boots.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive, and it needs no Wi-Fi at all. Method 3, the cloud trap: the Photos app on the phone shows the photos, and showing them feels like backing them up — it is not. Check that Backup is on, check the quality (storage saver holds compressed copies, not originals), switch on the device folders, check the upload actually finished on another device at photos.google.com, and check the 15 GB storage. A cloud backup depends on Wi-Fi, an account, a password, and a subscription; the drive copy depends on none of those. And the cloud is not the whole pre-unlock job: authenticator seeds, chat backups, and the system image are separate.

Before you unlock: back up what SnapDisk does not — export authenticator accounts and save recovery codes, run the in-app backup for chats, back up messages, contacts, and call history. Take a TWRP nandroid (system, data, boot) for a full system image if your model can run TWRP before the unlock, and move it off the phone — a backup stored only in internal storage is deleted by the wipe. Download the ROM, the matching recovery, and the stock firmware before the wipe. Unplug the USB drive before flashing — the port is needed for the computer and fastboot — charge the phone, use a known-good data cable, and run the unlock from the guides, not from memory. Know the costs: unlocking may void the warranty, can break Play Integrity and banking apps, and can affect updates and DRM. When the new ROM boots, copy the photos back from the drive.

What this does not do: Does not back up app data, authenticator seeds, messages, or system state — photos and videos only. Does not undo a wipe. Does not unlock the bootloader, root the phone, or flash a ROM. Does not keep the drive plugged in during the flash. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud, or photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver (no WakeLock in the repo, untested). Does not run past Android 15's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause. Does not install below Android 7.0, copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive, charge the phone while the drive is in the port, or power a portable SSD from the phone alone. Does not work on a damaged port or a dead phone, does not make a locked phone unlockable, and does not work on iPhone. Does not compress.

What to avoid: Running the unlock before the copy finishes or is verified on the drive. Leaving the drive plugged in during the flash. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device. Forgetting the device folders, the authenticator exports, and the chat backups. Counting on a TWRP nandroid you have not taken. Flashing without the stock firmware at hand. Unlocking a phone that cannot be unlocked — and never paying for one-click unlock tools. Moving instead of copying. Deleting from the phone before verifying. Unplugging mid-copy. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos. Reformatting without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library, a charging cable instead of an adapter, or the wrong adapter for the port. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run.

Buying a drive too small for the whole library, a charging cable instead of an adapter, or the wrong adapter for the port. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run.

### Back up CMF Phone photos to a USB drive

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/cmf-phone-photos-to-usb.html

CMF is Nothing&#x27;s sub-brand, and its two phones — the CMF Phone 1 (2024, Dimensity 7300, 128 GB) and the CMF Phone 2 Pro (2025, Dimensity 7300 Pro, 128 or 256 GB) — run Nothing OS, the same near-stock Android skin as the main Nothing phones, with USB-C on both. The honest caveats, up front: the CMF Phone 2 Pro supports OTG on every spec source checked, but the CMF Phone 1 is disputed — GSMArena&#x27;s own review says it offers USB Host/OTG support, and Croma, MySmartPrice, Beebom, and Cashify all list OTG as supported, while GSMArena&#x27;s comparison table lists its USB as plain Type-C with no OTG and phonebunch lists OTG as Not Supported — so on a CMF Phone 1, plug a drive in and look for the mount notification before buying an adapter or counting on the one-tap route; both phones take a microSD card up to 2 TB in a hybrid slot, which is a real adjacent route — a card in the phone is storage, not a backup, and the slot holds the card or a second SIM, not both — and it is never a SnapDisk feature; Nothing&#x27;s own backup tools are Google&#x27;s — Google Photos and Google backup — which back your photos up to the cloud, not to a USB drive as plain files; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later — minSdk 24 in the repo — and it is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub; the free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice — and Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit; the screenshot below is from SnapDisk on a phone — it is the same settings screen you will see, because this article is about a phone; the From folder is a picker, not a fixed path — tap it, browse to the phone&#x27;s storage, and choose the folder that holds the photos, which the picker reaches because it is the system folder picker, verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree; drives formatted FAT32 cannot hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, per the repo README — so use exFAT; a spinning hard drive may need its own power; SnapDisk&#x27;s copy runs as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no CMF run has ever been tested, so screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified, and this article says so instead of promising it; Android 15 and later give a dataSync foreground service 6 hours in 24 hours — if the copy runs past that, Android pauses it, and opening the app resets the timer; and SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the phone stays a second copy until you have opened photos on the drive and checked them. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR:On a CMF Phone, check OTG first — the CMF Phone 2 Pro lists USB Type-C 2.0 with OTG on every spec source checked, but the CMF Phone 1 is disputed: GSMArena's review says it offers USB Host/OTG support and Croma, MySmartPrice, Beebom, and Cashify list OTG as supported, while GSMArena's comparison table lists plain USB Type-C with no OTG and phonebunch lists it as Not Supported — so plug a drive into a CMF Phone 1 and look for the mount notification before buying an adapter — then plug a USB drive in and tap Backup in SnapDisk, and the whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background, with real progress, Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug.

Search "back up photos from CMF Phone to USB flash drive without computer" and there is no CMF-specific photo-backup guide in the top results at all — the closest result is our own Nothing Phone article, which covers the CMF Phone 1 only as the OTG exception; the rest are a generic YouTube OTG walkthrough, a generic askfilo guide (curl 200, 0 SnapDisk mentions), a FotoSafe guided-app guide (curl 200, 0 SnapDisk mentions — the closest near-miss: a guided app backup, but generic Android, not CMF), a generic groovypost manual guide (curl 403, browser-verified live via search), a generic EyeFi forum thread (curl 200, 0 SnapDisk mentions), Technobezz's "Fix CMF Phone 2 Pro USB Not Recognized by PC" troubleshooting guide (curl 403, browser-verified live — a PC-connection guide, not a backup guide), and spec tables: GSMArena's CMF Phone 1 review says the port offers USB Host/OTG support (curl 200), Croma lists OTG Support Yes for the CMF Phone 1 (curl 403, browser-verified live), MySmartPrice lists USB OTG Support Yes for the CMF Phone 2 Pro (curl 403, browser-verified live), and GadgetsFocus lists USB Type-C 2.0, OTG for the CMF Phone 2 Pro (curl 200, 0 SnapDisk mentions). No top result is a CMF-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume — that angle is the gap this article fills.

Method 1: SnapDisk is the one-tap version, and it runs entirely on the phone — the photos never leave it until they are on the drive, and it needs no Wi-Fi at all. It needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24) and is not on Google Play yet, so install the v0.1.2 APK from GitHub. Check the photos size, charge first, open SnapDisk, check the From folder twice, plug the drive in, tap Backup in the notification, and the library copies oldest-first in the background with progress, Pause and Stop. Wait for the copy to finish, open a few photos on the drive to check them, then unplug the drive and put it away somewhere safe.

Method 2, by hand in Files by Google: charge first, plug the drive in, open Files by Google, find the photos in DCIM or Pictures, select them, tap Copy, paste to the drive, and repeat for every folder that holds photos. Keep the phone unlocked while the copy runs, wait for it to finish, open a few photos on the drive, then unplug the drive and put it away somewhere safe. Copy, not Move — Move deletes the originals in one step, and a failed Move leaves photos in neither place. No oldest-first order, no progress bar, no Pause and Stop, no resume.

Method 3, Nothing's own tools: CMF phones have no Nothing-owned backup for photos — the routes are Google's. Google Photos backs photos up to Google's cloud (15 GB free) and Google backup restores data to a new phone from the cloud; neither writes plain photo files to a USB drive. Nothing Gallery is a viewer arriving with Nothing OS 3.0, not a backup tool. Check photos.google.com on another device before trusting the cloud.

Method 4, the microSD route: both CMF phones take a microSD card up to 2 TB in a hybrid slot — copy photos to the card with Files by Google, no drive or adapter needed. But a card in the phone is storage, not a backup: a lost, stolen, or broken phone takes the card with it, and the hybrid slot holds the card or a second SIM, not both. It is not a SnapDisk feature — SnapDisk backs up to a USB drive, not to the card.

What this does not do: Does not settle the CMF Phone 1 OTG question for you — five sources say yes, two say no, and your own phone with a drive plugged in is the tiebreaker. Does not back up to the microSD card. Does not back up anything but photos and videos. Does not back up photos that live only in the cloud, or photos from apps that hide them. Does not promise the copy continues under battery saver (no WakeLock in the repo, unverified — lowercase, stated plainly in the article). Does not run past Android's 6-hour dataSync budget without a pause on Android 15 and later. Does not install below Android 7.0. Does not copy files over 4 GB off a FAT32 drive. Does not charge the phone while the drive is in the port. Does not power a portable SSD from the phone alone. Does not work on a damaged port or a dead phone. Does not work on iPhone. Does not compress.

What to avoid: Buying an adapter before checking OTG on a CMF Phone 1. Buying a charge-only cable and calling it an adapter. Buying the wrong adapter for the port. Trusting the cloud without checking it on another device. Forgetting the device folders. Calling the microSD card a backup. Using the hybrid slot without checking the second SIM. Moving instead of copying. Deleting from the phone before verifying. Unplugging mid-copy. Using a FAT32 drive for long videos. Reformatting the drive without copying its files off first. Buying a drive too small for the whole library. Expecting the free 5 GB cap to cover a whole library in one run.

### SnapDisk vs FotoSafe: back up Android photos to USB

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/snapdisk-vs-fotosafe.html

Two Android apps that copy your photos to a USB drive — no cloud, no account, no upload. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

TL;DR: SnapDisk and FotoSafe both back up Android photos to a USB drive offline, with no account and no subscription — and both only copy, never delete. The verified differences: FotoSafe is on Google Play today and SnapDisk is not yet (v0.1.2 — install the APK from GitHub); FotoSafe's free tier is one successful run of up to 100 media files, then its one-time Pro is required for further runs, while SnapDisk's free tier is 5 GB per run and repeatable — files already copied are never copied twice; SnapDisk Pro is $9.99 one-time, but FotoSafe's Pro price is published only in Google Play — its own site says "Google Play shows the current price" — and we could not verify a figure, so this article makes no price comparison; FotoSafe shows the planned backup before it starts, SnapDisk copies oldest-first with Pause and Stop in the progress notification, and SnapDisk checks the size of every file after copying while FotoSafe's own listing tells you to verify important backups on the drive yourself. FotoSafe needs Android 9 or later with USB host/OTG; SnapDisk needs Android 7.0 or later, so it runs on older phones FotoSafe cannot. This is the second head-to-head comparison in the series, after SnapDisk vs VaultDrive.

SnapDisk: free Android app (v0.1.2, not on Google Play yet). Plug in the disk, tap Backup in the notification, and photos copy oldest-first in the background, size-verified, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. Free: manual backup, 5 GB per run. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase for auto-backup when a disk is connected and unlimited size. No cloud, no account, no ads, and no internet permission. It needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24).

FotoSafe: FotoSafe — Photo Backup to USB (at.weidi.fotobackup), on Google Play. Connect the drive, select it as the destination in FotoSafe through Android's system picker, review the media, and start copying. Backups land in a /FotoSafe/ folder on the drive; files already backed up are skipped on later runs; a progress notification shows during longer backups, and result summaries follow each run. It works offline with no account, no ads, and no tracking, needs Android 9 or later with USB host/OTG support, and describes what it copies as photos and videos, without listing formats. Free: one successful trial run of up to 100 photos or videos. Pro is a one-time purchase that unlocks unlimited backup runs, with no subscription.

Price: both are one-time purchases, neither charges a subscription. SnapDisk Pro is $9.99 once, verified in the repo's billing code (product id pro_unlock). FotoSafe Pro is a one-time Google Play purchase with no subscription — but its price is published only in Google Play: FotoSafe's site says "Google Play shows the current price", and the Play listing text we could read shows no Pro price figure, so this article makes no price comparison rather than guessing one. Both apps are free to start.

The free tier: FotoSafe's free tier is one successful backup run of up to 100 media files — one run, not 100 files on every run — then further runs need the one-time Pro purchase. SnapDisk's free tier is 5 GB per backup run, with no file-count cap, and runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. If you want to test before you pay, FotoSafe's trial is a complete run; if you want to back up a whole library without paying, SnapDisk's repeatable 5 GB runs are the usable free tier.

Before the copy: FotoSafe shows the planned backup before it starts — destination, new files, files already backed up, and required space — then you start. It also offers an Expert mode for choosing additional folders beyond the guided flow, and its guide warns the system picker "must show USB storage, not internal storage", with a Samsung / One UI fallback documented. SnapDisk does not show a planned-backup summary before the run: pick the From and To folders in settings (the system folder picker, OpenDocumentTree in the repo), plug the drive in, tap Backup — the numbers appear once the copy is running, in the progress notification.

During the backup: SnapDisk copies oldest-first by the date the photo was taken, in the background, with Pause and Stop in the progress notification; unplug mid-copy and it pauses with the full error shown, resuming where it stopped when the disk is back; the file in flight resumes from its .part file. FotoSafe shows a visible progress notification during longer backups and result summaries after each run, and skips files already backed up on later runs — resume-by-skipping for finished files. It does not advertise Pause and Stop, states no copy order, and its own listing warns that if the phone, cable, adapter, or drive fails during a backup, the backup "may remain incomplete".

After the copy: SnapDisk checks the size of every file after copying — each copy writes to a .part file and is renamed only after the size verification passes — and files that cannot be copied (a single file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive) are skipped and listed with their reason. FotoSafe puts the check in your hands: its listing says "Please verify important backups on the destination drive", and its guide says "A completion message is useful; a real file check is better". Neither side replaces opening a few photos on the drive yourself.

Freeing up space: neither app deletes photos from your phone today. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes (the only delete calls in its source touch .part files) — so freeing space is copy to the drive, check the copy, then delete the originals yourself. FotoSafe's Play listing lists "no automatic deletion of your original files", and its guide says "Copying is not moving. Originals remain on the phone."

What to avoid: paying before trying the free run (FotoSafe's trial is one run — check the destination is the USB drive first); picking the wrong storage in the picker (phone name, "Internal storage", "Downloads", or "DCIM" at the top means cancel and start again from the USB entry); deleting before verifying; assuming the free tier covers a whole library (100 files, or 5 GB per run); assuming "offline" means the same thing everywhere (SnapDisk has no internet permission at all; FotoSafe says no cloud and no tracking, its permission set unverified); choosing on whether an app is on Play (FotoSafe is on Play today, SnapDisk is not yet — that says where to download it, not how it copies); assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off (SnapDisk's repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — unverified, stated plainly; FotoSafe's guide says keep the phone and drive connected until completion).

Rule of thumb: the app that wins is the one whose copy you trust enough to delete after. Compare the free tier, the preview, and the copy — then check the copy on the drive before you delete anything.

Moving a file off the phone frees the space in the same step. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes (the only delete calls in its source touch .part files) — so freeing space is copy to the drive, check the copy, then delete the originals yourself.

What to avoid: assuming the 10,000,000+ installs belong to the current app (they do not — the current SANDISK listing passed 1,000,000 installs in July 2026; the 10,000,000+ figure is the old Memory Zone listing, removed from Play in April 2025); buying a SanDisk drive you do not own yet just for the app (its listing promises nothing about other brands' drives — SnapDisk works with any drive Android can mount); paying before checking what the purchase buys (the SANDISK listing names no paid tier at all; SnapDisk Pro buys auto-backup on connect and unlimited size for $9.99 once — and the SANDISK app's auto-backup on connect is in its free listing); assuming "free" means the same thing on both sides (no cap stated and automatic backup included vs no ads and 5 GB per run); deleting before verifying; assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off (neither listing promises it; SnapDisk's repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — unverified, stated plainly); using a FAT32 drive for long videos (SnapDisk skips files over 4 GB and tells you; the SANDISK app's own reviewers report its copy stops entirely on such a file, with no skip — use exFAT); choosing on whether an app is on Play (the SANDISK app is on Play today, SnapDisk is not yet — that says where to download it, not how it copies); assuming contacts come along (the SANDISK app backs up contacts; SnapDisk backs up photos and videos only).

Rule of thumb: the app that wins is the one whose copy you trust enough to delete after. Compare the free tier, the preview, and the copy — then check the copy on the drive before you delete anything.

### SnapDisk vs Buffalo Photo Backup: Android USB backup

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/snapdisk-vs-buffalo.html

Two Android apps that back up your photos to a USB drive — one from Japan's biggest external-drive maker, one from a small team. Here is how they actually differ, from the facts we could verify as of November 2026.

TL;DR: SnapDisk and Buffalo Photo Backup both back up Android photos to a USB drive, and both are free to download. The verified differences: Buffalo Photo Backup is on Google Play today (updated Dec 16, 2025, Android 13 or later, rated 4.5 from 69 ratings) and SnapDisk is not yet (v0.1.2 — install the APK from GitHub, Android 7.0 or later); Buffalo Photo Backup is free with no paid tier named in its listing, while SnapDisk Pro is $9.99 one-time for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size — so there is no Pro-versus-paid price comparison to make; Buffalo Photo Backup backs up photos and videos automatically when a drive is connected, keeps the originals, copies only new photos from the second time onward, lets you view the backed-up photos in the app, and restores all or selected photos — while SnapDisk copies photos and videos only, oldest-first, and never deletes, with no restore and no in-app viewer; Buffalo Photo Backup is built for Buffalo drives — its listing names verified Buffalo SSDs, USB flash drives, and card readers — while SnapDisk works with any drive Android can mount; Buffalo Photo Backup's listing says nothing about a copy order, Pause and Stop, or per-file verification, while SnapDisk copies oldest-first with Pause and Stop in the progress notification and checks the size of every file after copying; and Buffalo Photo Backup's listing says nothing about whether the copy keeps running with the screen off, while SnapDisk copies in the background as a foreground service, though screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified. One thing to know before you search: Buffalo's app is literally named "Photo Backup" — the same words as the job — which is why this app is called SnapDisk instead. As of November 21, 2026, no SnapDisk-vs-Buffalo head-to-head comparison turned up in search — this article is the first. This is the fifth head-to-head comparison in the series, after SnapDisk vs VaultDrive, SnapDisk vs FotoSafe, SnapDisk vs Photos to USB, and SnapDisk vs SanDisk app.

SnapDisk: free Android app (v0.1.2, not on Google Play yet). Plug in the disk, tap Backup in the notification, and photos copy oldest-first in the background, size-verified, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. Free: manual backup, 5 GB per run. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase for auto-backup when a disk is connected and unlimited size. No cloud, no account, no ads, and no internet permission. It needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24).

Buffalo Photo Backup: Photo Backup (jp.buffalo.photobackup, developer BUFFALO INC.), on Google Play — updated Dec 16, 2025, Android 13 or later on a USB-C phone, rated 4.5 from 69 ratings. A free backup app from Buffalo, the No. 1 external SSD and card reader manufacturer in Japan according to a 2024 BCN survey. Open the app, connect an SSD, USB flash drive, or card reader, and backup starts automatically, keeping the original data. From the second time onward it detects newly added photos and videos, so later backups are incremental. View the backed-up photos and videos in the app, restore all or selected photos, back up photos on the phone's internal SD card, and back up to multiple storage devices — the app remembers the backup status of up to 10 devices. Free — its listing shows a price of $0 and names no paid tier. Verified devices are Buffalo SSDs, USB flash drives, and card readers.

Price: both are free to download. Buffalo Photo Backup's listing shows a price of $0, and the listing text we could read names no paid tier, no subscription, and no in-app purchase price at all. SnapDisk is free with no ads, and its Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase, verified in the repo's billing code (product id pro_unlock). No Pro-versus-paid price comparison is possible: there is no Buffalo paid tier in the listing to compare against. What the money buys on the one side where money is charged: SnapDisk's Pro buys auto-backup on connect and unlimited size instead of the 5 GB free cap. Buffalo Photo Backup's automatic backup on connect — the feature SnapDisk charges $9.99 for — is in its free listing.

The free tier: Buffalo Photo Backup's free tier is the whole feature set as its listing describes it — automatic backup of photos and videos when a compatible drive is connected, incremental backup from the second time onward, viewing backed-up photos in the app, restore of all or selected photos, and backup to up to 10 remembered storage devices — with no size or file-count cap stated. SnapDisk's free tier is 5 GB per backup run, with no file-count cap, and runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. If you own a Buffalo drive and want the whole library backed up free in one go, Buffalo Photo Backup's free tier is the usable one; if you want to back up a whole library without paying, SnapDisk's repeatable 5 GB runs are the usable free tier — Buffalo Photo Backup's is not, until your drive is a verified Buffalo one.

Before the copy: Buffalo Photo Backup is set-it-once — open the app, connect a drive, and backup starts automatically, with no folder picking and no preview in its listing: it backs up photos and videos. SnapDisk asks you to choose first: pick the From and To folders in settings (the system folder picker, OpenDocumentTree in the repo), plug the drive in, tap Backup — the numbers appear once the copy is running. Neither app shows a planned-backup summary before the run.

During the backup: Buffalo Photo Backup's automatic backup runs when the drive is connected, and from the second time onward it copies only the photos added since the last backup; its listing mentions no Pause and Stop controls, states no copy order, says nothing about whether the copy keeps running with the screen off, and says nothing about unplugging mid-backup or about files too large for the drive's format. SnapDisk copies oldest-first by the date the photo was taken, in the background, with Pause and Stop in the progress notification; unplug mid-copy and it pauses with the full error shown, resuming from its .part file when the disk is back. Files that cannot be copied — a single file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive — are skipped and listed with their reason instead of failing the whole backup. No review text was readable in the Buffalo listing this run, so no reviewer complaints are quoted; its listing says nothing about the large-file case at all.

After the copy: Buffalo Photo Backup wins on restore (all or selected photos, including ones deleted to free up space) and on viewing (connect the drive and view the backed-up photos in the app), and it remembers the backup status of up to 10 storage devices. SnapDisk has no restore feature and no in-app viewer. SnapDisk checks the size of every file after copying — each copy writes to a .part file and is renamed only after the size verification passes — and its destination mirrors the source folder structure. Buffalo Photo Backup's listing says nothing about per-file verification or the folder layout its backups land in, so neither is claimed for it. Both keep the originals, and neither backs up contacts.

Freeing up space: Buffalo Photo Backup's listing says it can help free up space, but the app itself does not say it moves or deletes files — freeing space is deleting from the phone after the backup, which is your step, and its own footnote says to back up to two or more storage devices first, just in case. SnapDisk only copies — it never deletes (the only delete calls in its source touch .part files) — so freeing space is copy to the drive, check the copy, then delete the originals yourself.

What to avoid: assuming Buffalo Photo Backup works with any drive (its verified devices are Buffalo SSDs, USB flash drives, and card readers); buying a Buffalo drive you do not own yet just for the app; paying before checking what the purchase buys (the Buffalo listing names no paid tier at all; SnapDisk Pro buys auto-backup on connect and unlimited size for $9.99 once — and Buffalo Photo Backup's auto-backup on connect is in its free listing); assuming "free" means the same thing on both sides (no cap stated and automatic backup included vs no ads and 5 GB per run); deleting before verifying (Buffalo's own listing says the same: back up to two or more devices before you delete); assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off (neither listing promises it; SnapDisk's repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — unverified, stated plainly); using a FAT32 drive for long videos (SnapDisk skips files over 4 GB and tells you; Buffalo Photo Backup's listing says nothing about files over 4 GB — use exFAT); choosing on whether an app is on Play (Buffalo Photo Backup is on Play today, SnapDisk is not yet — that says where to download it, not how it copies); reading too much into the 4.5 rating (only 69 ratings — a small base); assuming contacts come along (neither app backs them up); searching for the wrong name (Buffalo's app is literally named "Photo Backup" — that collision is why this app is called SnapDisk).

Rule of thumb: the app that wins is the one whose copy you trust enough to delete after. Compare the free tier, the preview, and the copy — then check the copy on the drive before you delete anything.

### Back up RAW photos to USB from Android — SnapDisk

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/raw-photos-to-usb.html

A RAW file is the negative — recompress it once and the edit is gone for good. Here is how to get the .dng files off your Android phone onto a USB drive byte-for-byte, and how to check every one of them arrived.

TL;DR: A RAW file is the unprocessed sensor data — the negative — and any step that recompresses it destroys the thing you shot it for, so a RAW backup has to be a byte-for-byte copy, never a re-save. SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no recompression anywhere in its copy path, and it checks the size of every file after copying. The one thing to get right is the route: the default DCIM backup reads the phone's MediaStore Images table with no MIME filter, and .dng is indexed on every phone — Android's platform map carries .dng as image/x-adobe-dng — so the default route includes them; picking the source folder with the From picker, where .dng and .raw are both in the recognised extension list, is the route for RAW files that live outside DCIM. RAW files are big — tens of megabytes each, a shoot can be gigabytes — so the free 5 GB per-run cap bites harder here than for JPEGs: repeat the run and it picks up where it stopped, or Pro ($9.99 once) removes the cap. Format the drive exFAT, because the library total is large even though a single RAW file is almost never 4 GB or more. And one honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. As of November 21, 2026, no RAW-specific phone-to-USB backup guide turned up in search — the guides that exist are generic JPEG-era photo transfer guides — so this article is the first on the RAW angle.

What the search results actually offer: the exact query returns six real guides, and every one is a generic photo transfer guide from the JPEG era — groovypost's PC-middleman and file-manager guide, robots.net's OTG-cable plus file-manager copy, FotoSafe's guided app backup through the system picker (the closest near-miss, generic Android photos, no RAW angle), Dr.Fone's four ways (Google Drive, drag-and-drop to a PC, OTG adapter, AirDroid), the Google Photos community thread answering with a manual Files-by-Google move, and the pixls.us forum thread about moving .dng files through a laptop, darktable, Nextcloud, or Syncthing — the only result that even says RAW, and not a phone-to-USB guide at all. None of the six is RAW-specific, none distinguishes a .dng from a JPEG, none warns that a recompressing step destroys a RAW file, and none mentions SnapDisk.

Why RAW changes the backup: a JPEG is a finished photo; a RAW file — usually .dng on Android, sometimes .raw — is the unprocessed sensor data plus the settings to develop it later. Recompress it once and the extra data is gone, with no undo. The cloud trap is sharper for RAW: Google Photos "Storage saver" uploads are compressed copies, not originals, and "Original quality" counts against your storage quota at tens of megabytes a shot. A USB drive holds the original file, offline, with no quota and no re-save — provided the copy itself does not touch the bytes, and SnapDisk's does not.

What you need: a phone that shoots RAW (.dng files usually in DCIM/Camera, sometimes in the camera app's own folder — check first); a USB drive sized after the count (a hundred .dng files at 25 MB each is 2.5 GB); a drive formatted exFAT (DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide is the format reference — exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac; NTFS is a Windows format most Android phones cannot open on their own); an OTG adapter for a USB-A drive, or a powered hub for a portable SSD; SnapDisk v0.1.2 (not on Google Play yet, APK from GitHub, Android 7.0 or later, no internet permission).

Method 1 — SnapDisk, one tap: plug the drive in, open SnapDisk, and pick the folders first — tap the From picker, browse to the phone's storage, and choose the folder that holds the .dng files. The From picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in the repo), and on that route SnapDisk lists files by extension, with .dng and .raw both in the list (PhotoQuery.kt). Then pick the To folder on the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and the copy runs in the background, oldest-first by date taken, with percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. If your RAW files live outside DCIM, pick the folder — the folder route does not depend on the MediaStore at all. The default route covers .dng files in DCIM too: .dng is indexed on every phone — Android's platform map carries .dng as image/x-adobe-dng. Two honest limits: the extension list does not include .tif/.tiff or .xmp sidecars (copy those by hand), and screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no wake lock, no battery-saver handling). On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34).

Method 2 — by hand in the Files app: plug the drive in, browse to the folder that holds the .dng files, select them, Copy, navigate to the USB drive, Paste. You see exactly which files you selected, and it is the fallback for the files SnapDisk's folder route does not recognise (.tif/.tiff, .xmp). What you give up is the automation: no oldest-first order, no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, no resume, and no per-file size verification. For ten .dng files that is fine; for a thousand, the one-tap route is the honest recommendation.

Method 3 — the cloud trap: open photos.google.com on a computer and look for the .dng files — if backup was off, if the device folder was never switched on, or if the uploads are "Storage saver" quality, the cloud does not hold your RAW files at all. Copy to the USB drive first, verify the .dng files on the drive, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. Never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone.

The 5 GB free cap: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run (FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB in the repo), and runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For JPEGs 5 GB is a whole library; for RAW it is a few hundred shots — a thousand .dng files at 25 MB each is 25 GB, five free runs. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock) that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit. A file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — a single RAW file is almost never that big, so this almost never fires for a .dng; what it catches is the long 4K video next to your RAW files.

What this does not do: it does not convert, develop, or edit RAW files; it does not copy .tif/.tiff RAWs or .xmp sidecars on the folder route; it backs up photos and videos only (no app data, messages, Lightroom catalogues, or presets); it never deletes anything (only .part files are ever deleted); it does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver; and it has no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied .dng files in a RAW viewer or on your computer yourself.

What to avoid: trusting the default DCIM route for RAW without checking; letting a cloud service recompress your negatives; formatting the drive NTFS; buying a drive before counting the library; deleting before verifying; assuming the .xmp sidecars came along; assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off; starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery (one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both); forgetting the videos next to the RAW files (a 4 GB-plus clip on FAT32 is skipped — use exFAT); searching for the wrong thing (the guides the search returns are generic photo transfer guides, none RAW-specific).

Rule of thumb: a RAW file is the negative — the copy has to be byte-for-byte, and the check has to be on the drive. Pick the folder, copy, open a few .dng files on the drive, then delete — that order is what keeps your negatives safe.

### Back up HEIC photos to USB from Android — SnapDisk

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/heic-photos-to-usb.html

A HEIC file is the smaller original — convert it to a JPEG once and the extra quality is gone for good. Here is how to get the .heic files off your Android phone onto a USB drive byte-for-byte, and how to check every one of them arrived.

### Back up screenshots to USB from Android — SnapDisk

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/screenshots-to-usb.html

Screenshots are the receipts, boarding passes, QR codes and chats of your phone — and they live outside DCIM, where most backup guides never look. Here is how to get them onto a USB drive byte-for-byte, and the one folder choice that would leave them behind.

TL;DR: A screenshot is a .png file, and on most Android phones it lives in Pictures/Screenshots — outside DCIM, where every camera-photo backup looks. SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no conversion — a .png stays a .png — and checks the size of every file after copying. And one honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. As of November 21, 2026, no screenshot-specific phone-to-USB backup guide turned up in search — the pages that exist are generic transfer guides that list the Screenshots folder as one row in a manual copy, and none of them offers a one-tap whole-library backup for screenshots or mentions SnapDisk — so this article is the first on the screenshot angle.

What the search results actually offer: the exact query returns four real pages worth naming, and none of them is a screenshot-specific phone-to-USB backup guide — AnExplorer's file-manager guide (its folder table lists Screenshots at /Pictures/Screenshots/, 100 MB–2 GB, as one row in a manual transfer), UMA Technology's full guide (a manual folder-by-folder copy that tells you to split the transfer into folders "such as: Camera 2024, Camera 2025, Camera 2026, Screenshots, WhatsApp, Videos", and names Pictures/Screenshots as where screenshots live), Dr.Fone's four generic routes (Google Drive, drag-and-drop to a PC, an OTG adapter, AirDroid — no screenshot angle; its only screenshot mentions are links to a separate article about how to take one), and WikiTechLibrary's whole-phone backup guide (a manual file-manager copy, folder by folder — DCIM, Downloads, Documents, Screenshots, WhatsApp — which does suggest FolderSync to automate folder sync, a general-purpose sync tool configured per folder, not a one-tap whole-library backup with progress and verification). None of the four distinguishes the default route that provably includes screenshots from the DCIM folder route that provably misses them on most phones, none warns that the obvious folder to pick is the wrong one, and none mentions SnapDisk.

Where screenshots live — and why that decides the backup: on a Pixel and most phones running close-to-stock Android, screenshots are saved to Internal storage → Pictures → Screenshots; on a Samsung Galaxy phone, to DCIM → Screenshots by default — inside the camera folder, not outside it. Both locations are stated in the transfer guides themselves. That is the reverse of the HEIC and RAW problem: for .heic files the default route is the uncertain one and the folder route is the certain one; for .dng files the default route is certain too: .dng is indexed on every phone — Android's platform map carries .dng as image/x-adobe-dng, while for screenshots the default route is the certain one — the MediaStore Images table indexes .png on every Android phone, and the query carries no folder filter and no MIME filter — and the uncertain route is the folder route, and only in one configuration: a DCIM folder picked as From on a phone whose screenshots live outside DCIM. A screenshot is a .png on most Android phones — lossless, pixel for pixel what was on the screen — and .png is in SnapDisk's recognised extension list (PhotoQuery.kt), alongside .jpg, .jpeg, .heic, .heif, .dng and .raw; a few phones save screenshots as .jpg instead, and .jpg is in the same list. A typical screenshot is a few hundred kilobytes to a couple of megabytes, so a thousand of them is roughly half a gigabyte to two gigabytes.

What you need: an Android phone with screenshots on it (check Pictures/Screenshots, or DCIM/Screenshots on a Samsung); a USB drive sized after the count (a thousand screenshots is roughly half a gigabyte to two gigabytes); a drive formatted exFAT (DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide is the format reference — exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac; NTFS is a Windows format most Android phones cannot open on their own); an OTG adapter if the drive is USB-A; and SnapDisk v0.1.2 (not on Google Play yet — the APK from GitHub; Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24; no account, no cloud, no ads, no internet permission).

Method 1 — SnapDisk, one tap: plug the drive in, leave the From folder unpicked — the default — and tap Backup in the notification. The default run reads the phone's MediaStore Images table and the Video table with no folder filter and no MIME filter (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, called from BackupService when no From folder is picked), so the screenshots copy along with the camera photos, oldest-first, as .png files, with a progress notification (percent, copied/total, speed, ETA) plus Pause and Stop. To copy screenshots only, tap the From picker and choose Pictures/Screenshots — the picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in the repo), and the folder route walks the folder you picked, subfolders included, copying every file whose extension is in the list. Picking Pictures as From covers the Screenshots subfolder too. The trap is picking DCIM as From: the folder route walks only the tree you picked, so on a Pixel or stock-Android phone a DCIM pick leaves every screenshot behind, silently, while the run still says done — on a Samsung the same pick includes them, because Samsung saves screenshots in DCIM/Screenshots by default. If you pick a folder, pick Pictures — never DCIM alone — unless you have checked that your screenshots live inside DCIM. Honest limits: no screenshots-only mode on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no wake lock, no battery-saver handling, no screenshot run ever tested). On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). Fair comparison: WikiTechLibrary's guide suggests FolderSync to automate folder sync to an OTG drive — a real automation that covers the Screenshots folder too — but it is a general sync tool configured per folder, with no oldest-first order across the library, no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, and no per-file size verification with .part resume.

Method 2 — by hand in the Files app: plug the drive in, browse to Pictures/Screenshots (or DCIM/Screenshots on a Samsung), select the screenshots, Copy, navigate to the USB drive, Paste. You see exactly which files you selected, and it is the fallback for the configuration SnapDisk's folder route gets wrong. Two screenshot-specific warnings: copy, do not share — messaging apps recompress images before sending, so the file that arrives is not pixel-exact; and do not use Move — Move deletes the originals as the copy goes, and an interrupted Move leaves screenshots split between phone and drive with no record of which is which. What you give up is the automation: no oldest-first order, no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, no resume, and no per-file size verification. For a hundred screenshots that is fine; for a thousand, the one-tap route is the honest recommendation.

Method 3 — the cloud trap: Google Photos backs up the camera folder, and the Screenshots folder is a separate toggle under Photos settings → Backup → Back up device folders — and whether that toggle is on varies by phone and app version. Reminari's guide says other device folders, Screenshots included, "often need switching on by hand"; MakeUseOf's guide to the same settings says that on the version it tested, Screenshots is "by default, already selected". Both cannot be the rule for your phone, so check photos.google.com instead of assuming. Even when the toggle is on, the cloud is the wrong place for screenshots twice over: every screenshot uploads and counts against your Google Account storage, and Google's own help page says Storage saver uploads "may be compressed into a different image format, like a .jpg" — a screenshot saved as a JPEG is no longer the pixel-exact original. Copy to the USB drive first, verify the .png files on the drive, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. Never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone.

The 5 GB free cap: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run (FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB in the repo), and runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For screenshots, 5 GB goes a very long way: a thousand screenshots is roughly half a gigabyte to two gigabytes, a whole screenshot library in a single free run. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock) that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit. A file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — a single screenshot never reaches that, but the long 4K video next to it might, and exFAT removes the problem.

What this does not do: it does not convert screenshots — to anything; it does not copy screenshots only on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); it does not keep a screenshot's context (a screenshot of a boarding pass is a picture of the pass, not the pass itself); it does not read or index screenshots (no OCR, no search inside the images); it backs up photos and videos only (no app data, messages, browser tabs, notes, or clipboard history); it never deletes anything (only .part files are ever deleted); it does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver; and it has no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied .png files in a viewer or on your computer yourself.

What to avoid: picking DCIM as the From folder and assuming the screenshots came along; assuming your screenshots are in Pictures/Screenshots without checking (Samsung saves them in DCIM/Screenshots by default); trusting Google Photos without checking the Screenshots toggle; letting a cloud service recompress your originals (Storage saver may convert to .jpg); sharing a screenshot when you meant to copy it (messaging apps recompress images); using Move instead of Copy in the Files app; formatting the drive NTFS; buying a drive before counting the library; deleting before verifying; assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off; starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery (one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both); and searching for the wrong thing (the pages the search returns are generic transfer guides that list the Screenshots folder as one row in a manual copy — none of them is a screenshot backup guide).

Rule of thumb: a screenshot is the paper trail of your phone — the copy has to be byte-for-byte, and the check has to be on the drive. Leave From unpicked, or pick Pictures — never DCIM alone — copy, open a few .png files on the drive, then delete. That order is what keeps your screenshots safe.

A motion photo looks like an ordinary .jpg — and that is the trap. Inside the file, after the still image, sits a few seconds of video. Anything that re-saves, recompresses or shares the photo strips the clip, and the still that comes back looks fine. Here is how to get motion photos onto a USB drive with the motion still inside them.

TL;DR: A motion photo is one file — a .jpg still with a few seconds of video appended inside it. Google's Motion Photo format 1.0 says so in plain words: a motion photo is a single file that contains a still photographic image and a short video, which includes audio recording. Pixel calls it Motion or Top Shot and names the files MVIMG_… or ….MP.jpg; Samsung calls it Motion photo and saves the same single-file form, with a MotionPhoto_Data marker before the clip. That is the whole trap: the file looks like an ordinary photo, so anything that re-saves it — Google Photos Storage saver, WhatsApp, an editor that exports a fresh still — strips the clip and hands you back a still that looks fine. SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no conversion, so the clip survives — but only if the copy is byte-for-byte. The certain route is the folder route: pick DCIM as the From folder and the tree walk copies every motion photo, .jpg or .heic, because both extensions are in the recognised list. The default run covers JPEG motion photos too — they are .jpg files, MediaStore indexes .jpg on every phone, and the query carries no folder filter and no MIME filter — but if your Pixel saves motion photos as .heic, the default route is device-dependent, the same HEIC rule as the HEIC article. Motion photos are bigger than stills — each file carries a few seconds of video as well as the photo — so count the DCIM/Camera folder first and divide by the 5 GB free per-run cap. Format the drive exFAT, because the 4K videos sitting next to your motion photos are the ones that hit the FAT32 4 GB limit. And one honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. None of the five distinguishes a byte-for-byte copy from a re-save, none warns that the obvious tools strip the clip, and none mentions SnapDisk.

What a motion photo actually is: one file. Google's Motion Photo format 1.0 defines it as a single file containing a still photographic image and a short video, which includes audio recording — the primary still image (JPEG, HEIC or AVIF) with the video file appended to it, and XMP metadata in the still describing where the video starts. The clip is usually about three seconds, roughly a second and a half either side of the shutter. Pixel names files MVIMG_… on older Pixels or PXL_….MP.jpg from 2021 on; Samsung keeps a plain date name like 20230712_154210.jpg, with a MotionPhoto_Data tag before the video and a SEF trailer. Viewers that do not know about motion photos stop reading at the end of the JPEG image and show the still. That single-file shape is the opposite of the iPhone's: an iPhone Live Photo is two files, the still and a separate .mov clip — the WL-191 article, where the .mov companion copies as a second file. On Android there is no second file to miss; the risk runs the other way, the one file gets re-saved and the clip is stripped. Motion photos live in DCIM/Camera alongside the ordinary stills, so a DCIM pick covers them. Check motion is actually on before you start: Samsung switches Motion photo off by itself in high-resolution modes such as 50MP and 200MP, and in Portrait, Panorama and Hyperlapse modes, and it can stop saving clips when storage is almost full. And check the format: the spec allows HEIC and AVIF primaries as well as JPEG, and Pixel motion photos can be .heic in some configurations — if yours are .heic, the HEIC rule applies instead of the JPEG one, and the folder route is the certain one.

What you need: an Android phone with motion photos on it (Pixel Motion/Top Shot, Samsung Motion photo — and check it is actually on); a USB drive sized after the count (a motion photo is bigger than a still alone, so add up DCIM/Camera first and divide by 5 GB); a drive formatted exFAT (DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide is the format reference — exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac; NTFS is a Windows format most Android phones cannot open on their own); an OTG adapter if the drive is USB-A; and SnapDisk v0.1.2 (not on Google Play yet — the APK from GitHub; Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24; no account, no cloud, no ads, no internet permission).

Method 1 — SnapDisk, one tap: plug the drive in, tap the From picker, browse to the phone's storage, and choose DCIM — or DCIM/Camera, for motion photos only. The From picker is the system folder picker (OpenDocumentTree in the repo), and the folder route walks the folder you picked, subfolders included, copying every file whose extension is in the list — both .jpg and .heic are in it (PhotoQuery.kt), so a DCIM pick copies every motion photo in the tree whatever its primary format. Then pick the To folder on the drive and tap Backup. The default run — leave From unpicked — covers JPEG motion photos too: with no From folder picked, SnapDisk reads the phone's MediaStore Images table and the Video table with no folder filter and no MIME filter (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, called from BackupService when no From folder is picked), and a JPEG motion photo is a .jpg file, which every Android MediaStore indexes. But the default route is the uncertain one for .heic motion photos: whether a given phone's MediaStore indexes .heic is device-dependent, the HEIC article's finding. So the rule is the same as the HEIC article's: if you do not know the format, pick the folder. The motion survives because the copy never touches the file's bytes: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte with no transcoding step, and checks the size of every file after copying, renaming the .part file to the final file only after the size verification passes. The check that matters: open a copied motion photo on a computer and it shows only the still — that does not mean the motion is gone, most computer viewers stop at the end of the JPEG image and never look for the clip. To prove the clip survived, copy one file back to the phone and open it in Google Photos or Samsung Gallery — it plays as a motion photo again — or drop it on one of the free in-browser extractor tools, which read the embedded clip and save it as an MP4 without uploading the file. Honest limits: no motion-only mode on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no wake lock, no battery-saver handling, no motion-photo run ever tested). On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). Fair comparison: VaultDrive is on Google Play today, shows the size before you start, has backup reminders, folders by date or by album, an App Lock, and incremental backups on Pro — and its Live Photos section promises both parts of an iPhone Live Photo, saved side by side — but its page promises nothing about Android motion photos at all. If those features are what you want, VaultDrive is the honest pick at $19.99 once for Pro Lifetime against SnapDisk's $9.99 once. What SnapDisk adds is the oldest-first order across the whole library, the detailed progress notification with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification with .part resume, a free tier of 5 GB per run against VaultDrive's 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and the folder route that provably keeps the clip, whatever the format.

Method 2 — by hand in the Files app: plug the drive in, browse to DCIM/Camera, select the motion photos, Copy, navigate to the USB drive, Paste. Check the sizes against the phone, and copy one file back to the phone and open it in the Gallery to confirm it still plays. The manual route is also the fallback for the photos MediaStore does not index: the default run reads the MediaStore Images table with no format filter, so a .heic motion photo is included like any .jpg on a phone whose MediaStore indexes .heic — but whether a given phone's MediaStore indexes .heic is device-dependent, the HEIC article's finding, so on a phone that does not index it the folder route is the fallback; and a photo in a folder MediaStore skips, for example a folder containing a .nomedia file, never reaches the default run either, and the way to copy it is to select it by hand in DCIM/Camera and copy it the same way.

Method 3 — the cloud trap: Google Photos backs up the camera folder, and a motion photo uploaded at Original quality keeps its clip — the extractor sources say motion photos downloaded in original quality keep their video. But the default is not Original quality: Google's own help page says Storage saver uploads "may be compressed into a different image format, like a .jpg", and the extractor sources say Google Photos in storage-saver quality usually removes the clip. So the cloud copy of a motion photo is only as good as the quality setting it was uploaded at. One more cloud detail: a motion photo downloaded from Google Photos in original quality sometimes arrives as a ZIP with a separate MP4 already extracted — that is Google splitting the file for you on download, not a second file you missed. A burst looks like one photo — and that is the trap. Behind the single thumbnail in your gallery sit dozens of individual files, and the one you want is frame 37 of 60. Here is how to get every frame of a burst onto a USB drive, and how to prove they all arrived.

The default run covers .dng bursts too: .dng is indexed on every phone — Android's platform map carries .dng as image/x-adobe-dng — so an Expert RAW burst frame is in the result set by construction as well. The frames survive because the copy never touches the files' bytes: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte with no transcoding step, and checks the size of every file after copying, renaming the .part file to the final file only after the size verification passes. The check that matters: count, do not look — open the backup folder on the drive and count the files, the number should match the frame count on the phone, the "1/60" the gallery showed you. Honest limits: no burst-only mode on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no wake lock, no battery-saver handling, no burst run ever tested). On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). Fair comparison: VaultDrive's page — read in full this run — says nothing about burst photos at all, no burst line anywhere on it, so it is not a burst guide either; what it does have, and what is genuinely burst-relevant, is a choose-photos feature (back up just the photos and videos you pick) — if you want one burst and nothing else, picking it in VaultDrive is the honest route, and its folders-by-date-or-album and incremental backups on Pro are real wins SnapDisk does not have — but its free tier is the burst trap: 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and one 100-frame burst eats half of that in a single backup, against SnapDisk's 5 GB per run with no file count. VaultDrive is on Google Play today at $19.99 once for Pro Lifetime against SnapDisk's $9.99 once. What SnapDisk adds is the oldest-first order across the whole library, the detailed progress notification with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification with .part resume, and the folder route that provably copies every frame, whatever the format.

Method 2 — by hand in the Files app: plug the drive in, browse to DCIM/Camera, select the burst frames, Copy, navigate to the USB drive, Paste. The file manager shows you the individual files, not the gallery's single thumbnail — so you can see the frame count as you select, which is the check the gallery hides from you. Three burst-specific warnings: copy in the Files app, do not share from the Gallery — sharing a burst hands the cover frame, or the few frames you picked, to another app, not the whole burst; do not delete the stack before opening it — the stack controls include deleting multiple photos at once, so one careless delete can take the whole burst; and do not use Move — an interrupted Move leaves burst frames split between phone and drive with no record of which is which. What you give up is the automation: no oldest-first order, no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, no resume, and no per-file size verification. For one burst that is fine; for a season of them, the one-tap route is the honest recommendation. The manual route is also the fallback for the photos MediaStore does not index: the default run reads the MediaStore Images table with no format filter, so a .dng burst frame is included like any .jpg — but a frame in a folder MediaStore skips, for example a folder containing a .nomedia file, never reaches the default run, and the way to copy it is to select it by hand in DCIM/Camera and copy it the same way.

Method 3 — the cloud trap: Google Photos backs up the camera folder, and a burst uploaded there keeps its frames — the grouped photos are saved in the Camera folder and backed up as default. But the default is not Original quality: Google's own help page says Storage saver uploads "may be compressed into a different image format, like a .jpg" — and a burst frame re-saved at reduced quality is a worse frame, with no way back to the original. One more cloud detail, because it confuses people with bursts specifically: the gallery shows one thumbnail for the whole burst, and the stack controls include deleting multiple photos at once — so the cloud copy is one careless delete away from losing frames you never reviewed. Google Photos does let you save all the frames from a burst from inside the stack — but that is a manual step per burst, and it only helps if you do it before you delete anything. The order matters: copy to the USB drive first, count the files on the drive against the phone, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. Never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone.

The 5 GB free cap: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run (FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB in the repo), and runs can be repeated — files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For bursts, 5 GB does not go as far as it does for single shots: one hold is dozens of files, and a season of bursts is hundreds or thousands of frames. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock) that auto-starts the backup on connect and removes the size limit. The count to do before you start is the library size: open the Files app, look at the DCIM/Camera folder size, divide by 5 GB, and that is how many free runs the library needs. A file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — a single burst frame never reaches that, but the long 4K video next to it might, and exFAT removes the problem.

What this does not do: it does not pick the best frame for you (SnapDisk copies files — every frame of every burst, oldest-first; choosing the keeper is the gallery's job); it does not turn a burst into a GIF or a video (the frames stay individual .jpg files — that is a separate tool's job, on a copy); it does not copy bursts only on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); it does not convert bursts — to anything (converting a frame loses quality — that is your editor's job, on a copy); it does not read or index bursts (no best-frame detection, no search inside the frames); it backs up photos and videos only (no app data, messages, browser tabs, notes, or clipboard history); it never deletes anything (only .part files are ever deleted); it does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver; and it has no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied .jpg files in a viewer or on your computer yourself.

What to avoid: assuming one thumbnail is one photo (a burst is dozens of files wearing one thumbnail — count the files on the drive, not the thumbnails in the gallery); deleting the stack before opening it (the stack controls include deleting multiple photos at once); sharing the cover when you meant to copy the burst (Share hands one frame to another app); assuming the default run missed the burst because the gallery shows one item (check the file count on the drive); letting Storage saver recompress the frames (Storage saver uploads "may be compressed into a different image format, like a .jpg"); using Move instead of Copy in the Files app; formatting the drive NTFS; buying a drive before counting the library; deleting before verifying (and for a burst, the check is the frame count on the drive); assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off; starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery (one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both); and searching for the wrong thing (the pages the search returns are generic transfer guides, our own general articles, and one forum thread — none of them is a burst backup guide).

Rule of thumb: a burst is dozens of files wearing one thumbnail — the copy has to get every frame, and the check has to count frames, not thumbnails. Pick DCIM/Camera as From, copy, count the files on the drive against the phone, then delete. That order is what keeps your bursts safe.

A slow-motion video looks like a special file — and that is the trap. It is an ordinary .mp4, and the slow part is a note inside the file, not a second file. Anything that re-saves or re-encodes it can drop the note, and the video that comes back plays at full speed. Here is how to get slow-motion videos onto a USB drive with the slow part still inside them.

TL;DR: A slow-motion video is not a special file. Your phone records it as an ordinary .mp4 (or .mov) in DCIM/Camera — the slow part is a note inside the file, a segment of slow-motion playback metadata, not a second file and not a different format. Samsung's own support page says Slow Motion plays back up to 8 times slower than normal, and Super Slow-mo up to 32 times slower — the slowness is playback, and the file is a normal video. That decides the backup: anything that copies the file byte-for-byte keeps the slow part, and anything that re-saves or re-encodes it can drop it. SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no conversion, so every slow-motion clip arrives intact. Both routes are certain for .mp4 and .mov — the default run reads the phone's MediaStore Video table with no folder filter and no MIME filter, and .mp4 and .mov are both indexed on every phone — and the folder route (pick DCIM/Camera as From) is the certain one for every format in the list. The check that matters: copy one clip back to the phone and watch it play in slow motion, or compare size and duration — and do not expect the slow part to survive on every player, because a player that does not read the metadata plays the file at full speed. What a slow-motion video actually is: a normal video file with a note inside it. Your phone records it as an ordinary .mp4 — on some phones, a .mov — saved in DCIM/Camera like every other video the camera shoots, and the slow part is metadata: a record of which segments of the track play back slowly. Android's own media library names the thing directly — SlowMotionData, which "holds information about the segments of slow motion playback within a track" — and Samsung stores the same information in an smta metadata box inside the file. The file is not a different format, and there is no second file holding the slow part. The slowness is playback: the camera shoots at a high frame rate and the player stretches it out. Samsung's own support page says Slow Motion allows you to record a video then play it back up to 8 times slower than normal, and Super Slow-mo plays videos back 32 times slower than normal videos — and its community explains how: Super Slow-mo shoots at 960 frames a second, and when it is played back at 30 frames a second, that is 32 times slower. One second of recording at 960 frames a second becomes about 32 seconds of playback. The slow part is also an edit choice, not a fixed property of the file: Samsung's support page walks you through choosing the portion of the video you want in slow motion with sliders at the bottom of the screen, then choosing Export or Save — the file holds the whole recording, and the slow segment is the part you picked. Two things follow: the file is big for its length (a second of Super Slow-mo holds 960 frames, where a second of ordinary video holds 30), and the risk is not that the file gets left behind — it is a .mp4 in DCIM/Camera — but that the file gets re-saved. A copy that streams the bytes keeps the metadata note; a share, an edit, or a re-encode that writes a fresh file may not. That is the opposite of the burst article's risk, where many files hide behind one thumbnail — here one file hides a note inside it, the same shape as the motion photo in the WL-193 article. The check is different too: for a burst you count files, for a slow-motion clip you watch it play. One more form: Instant Slow-mo — on newer Samsung phones, the Gallery app can slow down any video while you touch and hold the screen, generating the slow motion on playback, and the original file is untouched; if you save that slow-mo clip from the Gallery, it becomes a new .mp4 file, and that new file copies like any other video.

What you need: an Android phone with slow-motion videos on it (Samsung Galaxy: Camera app, More, Slow Motion or Super Slow-mo, then record — then check the count in the Gallery); a USB drive sized after the count (slow-motion files run large, so add up DCIM/Camera first and divide by 5 GB); a drive formatted exFAT (DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide is the format reference — exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac; NTFS is a Windows format most Android phones cannot open on their own); an OTG adapter if the drive is USB-A; and SnapDisk v0.1.2 (not on Google Play yet — the APK from GitHub; Android 7.0 or later, minSdk 24; no account, no cloud, no ads, no internet permission).

A panorama looks like an ordinary wide photo — and that is the trap. For a plain sweep it is just pixels, but for a Photo Sphere the spin is a note inside the file, and anything that re-saves it can drop the note and leave you with a flat strip. Here is how to get panoramas onto a USB drive with the spin still inside them.

TL;DR: A panorama is an ordinary wide .jpg in DCIM/Camera. A plain sweep is just pixels — no special format — and a Photo Sphere is the same .jpg with a note inside it: XMP metadata in Google's Photo Sphere namespace, GPano:ProjectionType equirectangular and the crop fields, that tells the viewer to wrap the image into a sphere you can look around in. That decides the backup: anything that copies the file byte-for-byte keeps the spin, and anything that re-saves or recompresses it can drop the metadata — and a panorama that loses it comes back as a flat wide strip. SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no conversion, so every panorama arrives intact. Both routes are certain for .jpg panoramas — the default run reads the phone's MediaStore Images table with no folder filter and no MIME filter, and .jpg is indexed on every phone — and the folder route (pick DCIM/Camera as From) is the certain one for every format in the list. Panoramas run larger than ordinary stills — one panorama write-up puts a standard panorama at five to ten megabytes and a photosphere of the same scene at fifteen to twenty-five — so count the DCIM/Camera folder first and divide by the 5 GB free per-run cap, and format the drive exFAT, because the long 4K videos sitting next to your panoramas can pass the FAT32 4 GB limit. The check that matters: copy one panorama back to the phone, open it in Google Photos, and look for the sphere viewer — and do not expect the spin to survive on every viewer, because a viewer that does not read the GPano tags shows a flat strip while the file is still intact. One honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. What the search results actually offer: The exact query returns real pages — and none of them is a panorama-specific phone-to-USB backup guide.
