That is the gap this article fills: a phone-to-USB backup that treats a panorama as what it is — an ordinary .jpg, with a note inside it when it is a Photo Sphere — with the route that provably copies it unchanged.

What a panorama actually is: A panorama is a wide .jpg with, sometimes, a note inside it. There are two kinds, and the difference between them is the whole article. The first is the plain sweep: you pan left to right, the phone stitches one row of frames into a rectilinear or cylindrical projection and saves it flat. That file is a standard wide JPEG with no spherical metadata at all — the panorama-ness is just pixels, a very wide image, and any viewer that can open a .jpg can open it. The second is the Photo Sphere: the phone guides you through a grid of overlapping shots, stitches them into an equirectangular projection — a sphere flattened into a rectangle, the same way a map of the earth gets stretched at the poles — and embeds XMP metadata that tells the viewer to wrap it back into a sphere. Google's own Photo Sphere XMP page says the metadata lives in the Google Photo Sphere namespace, http://ns.google.com/photos/1.0/panorama/, embedded inside the image file according to the Adobe XMP standard, and that the GPano parameters — ProjectionType equirectangular, the compass heading, the crop fields — are what make a viewer display it as a photo sphere rather than a flat image. When Google Photos detects the GPano metadata in a JPEG, it adds a small sphere icon, and tapping it switches to a gyroscope-driven mode where you tilt and rotate the phone to look around. The numbers make the shape concrete. A standard panorama is one row of frames stitched into a strip; a photosphere is a grid of overlapping shots across several rows, stitched into a full sphere. One panorama write-up puts a standard panorama at five to ten megabytes, and a photosphere of the same scene at fifteen to twenty-five — partly because it holds more total pixel data across the grid, and partly because the equirectangular projection is inherently less efficient at storing detail. On a Pixel 9, the panorama mode changed shape: Google's own blog says panorama mode used to work via video — the camera scanning the scene as you move — and now uses the HDR+ photo pipeline, stacking the photos and all their data together into a stitched panorama, with full 360 capabilities and even vertical panoramas. The file that comes out is still a .jpg in DCIM/Camera, whatever the pipeline behind it. Two things follow from that shape, and they decide the backup. First, the file is big for a still: a panorama holds many frames' worth of pixels, so a panorama library adds up faster than a library of ordinary stills — and the 5 GB free cap below bites sooner than it does for stills, though far later than it does for video. Second, the risk is not that the file gets left behind — it is a .jpg in DCIM/Camera, and every route in this article copies .jpg files — but that the file gets re-saved. A copy that streams the bytes keeps the GPano note; a share, an edit, or a re-encode that writes a fresh file may not. That is the same shape as the slow-motion article's risk, where one file hides a note inside it, and the opposite of the burst article's risk, where many files hide behind one thumbnail — here one file hides a note inside it, the same shape as the motion photo in the WL-193 article, where one .jpg hides a video inside it. The check is different too: for a burst you count files, for a panorama you open it in the viewer and look for the spin. One more form to know about, because it confuses people: a panorama that opens flat is not necessarily broken. A viewer that does not read the GPano tags shows the equirectangular image as a flat wide strip — stretched at the poles, distorted, looking wrong — and that proves nothing about the file. The metadata may still be inside it, and the same file opened in Google Photos on the phone may spin perfectly. The check is the phone's own Google Photos, which reads the note — not a computer viewer, which usually does not.

What you need: An Android phone with panoramas on it. On a Pixel, open the Camera app, tap Panorama, and sweep — or, on a Pixel 9 and later, follow the dots the camera shows you, pausing on each one while it snaps. On a Samsung Galaxy, open the Camera app, tap More, then Panorama, and sweep. Then check the count: open a panorama in Google Photos and look for the sphere icon — so you know which files are the Photo Spheres before you back them up. If a panorama opens as a flat wide strip with no sphere icon, it was a plain sweep, and no backup can make it spin.; A USB drive with enough free space. Count first: panoramas run larger than ordinary stills — a standard panorama is a few megabytes, a photosphere several times that — so add up the DCIM/Camera folder in the Files app before you buy the drive, and divide by 5 GB to know how many free runs the library needs.; A drive formatted exFAT. The format reference for this article is DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide: exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac. FAT32 cannot hold a single file of 4 GB or more — a single panorama never reaches that, but the long 4K videos sitting next to your panoramas can, and exFAT is the practical format for the whole folder. NTFS is a Windows format that most Android phones cannot open on their own — do not use it for a phone backup drive.; An OTG adapter if your drive is USB-A. A dual USB-C drive plugs straight in; a standard USB-A stick needs a data-capable OTG adapter. A portable SSD may need a powered hub — the phone alone may not supply enough power for the drive.; and SnapDisk v0.1.2. Not on Google Play yet — install the APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24 in the repo). No account, no cloud, no ads, and no internet permission — your photos physically cannot leave the phone.

Method 1: SnapDisk — the phone, one tap: This is the route this article is for, and for .jpg panoramas both routes are certain — which is the honest centre of this article, and different from the HEIC article, where only the folder route was certain for .heic. The default run — leave From unpicked — reads the phone's MediaStore Images table with no folder filter and no MIME filter, verified in the repo as PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, called from BackupService when no From folder is picked — and a panorama is a .jpg file, which every Android MediaStore indexes, so it is in the result set by construction. The folder route — tap the From picker, browse to the phone's storage, and choose DCIM or DCIM/Camera — is the certain one for every format in the list: the From picker is the system folder picker (verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree), the tree walk recurses into subfolders, and it copies every file whose extension is in the list. .jpg is in that list, verified in the repo's PhotoQuery.kt, so a DCIM pick copies every panorama in the tree whatever its kind — plain sweep or Photo Sphere alike. Then pick the To folder on the drive, in the same picker, and tap Backup. The copy runs in the background: oldest-first by the date the photo was taken, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. There is no format split to know about here, and that is the point: a panorama is a .jpg, and .jpg is the one format every route covers. The default run is certain for panoramas for the same reason it is certain for ordinary stills — the MediaStore Images table holds every .jpg on the phone, panorama or not, because nothing in the row marks a file as a panorama. The folder route is certain in every case, and the default route is certain for .jpg. That is the whole rule, and it is simpler than the other format articles' rule because the common case here — .jpg — is covered by both routes. The spin survives because the copy never touches the files' bytes. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — there is no transcoding step anywhere in its copy path — and it checks the size of every file after copying, renaming the .part file to the final file only after the size verification passes. A panorama that arrives on the drive is the same .jpg that left the phone, GPano metadata included. And here is the check that matters, because it is the one most people get wrong for panoramas: open it in the viewer, do not just look at the thumbnail. Copy one panorama back to the phone, open it in Google Photos, and look for the sphere viewer — tilt the phone and watch the scene move. Or, if you would rather not copy it back, compare the file size and dimensions on the drive against the phone: a matching size and matching dimensions mean the file arrived whole, and a whole file carries its metadata with it. A panorama that opens as a flat strip on a computer does not prove the spin is gone — most computer viewers do not read the GPano metadata, so they show the flat equirectangular image while the note is still inside it. The phone's own Google Photos is the check, because it reads the note. This article does not promise the spin survives on every viewer on every computer — that is a property of the viewer, not of the file — and it says so instead of promising it. Two honest limits on this route. First, there is no panorama-only mode on the default run: it copies the whole library, oldest-first, panoramas mixed in with stills and ordinary videos in date order. If you want panoramas only, that is what the DCIM/Camera pick is for — and even then, the pick copies every photo in the folder, panorama and ordinary alike; there is no way to pick only the panoramas except by selecting them by hand in Method 2. Second, screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified: SnapDisk copies as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no panorama run has ever been tested, so this article says so instead of promising it. Keep the phone awake for the run, or check it. On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, so a very long copy can be paused by Android itself, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). One fair comparison, because the search surfaced a rival that does part of this right: VaultDrive's page — read in full this run — says nothing about panoramas at all, not one panorama line anywhere on it, so it is not a panorama guide either. What it does have, and what is genuinely panorama-relevant, is a choose-photos feature: back up just the photos and videos you pick. If you want a handful of panoramas and nothing else, picking them in VaultDrive is the honest route, and its "Original quality, byte for byte" line — HEIC, ProRAW, ProRes and 4K video copied as they are, never compressed or re-encoded — is the same byte-for-byte promise this article makes, plus "Dates and places kept" — the capture date, location and camera details inside each photo stay intact — which is the metadata promise in another form, and folders by date or album and incremental backups on Pro, which are real wins SnapDisk does not have. But its free tier is a softer trap for panoramas than for bursts or slow motion: 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and a panorama collection is usually dozens of files, not hundreds, so the 200-file cap rarely bites — the 2 GB cap is the one that can bite a big photosphere library, against SnapDisk's 5 GB per run with no file count. VaultDrive is on Google Play today at $19.99 once for Pro Lifetime against SnapDisk's $9.99 once. What SnapDisk adds is the oldest-first order across the whole library, the detailed progress notification with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification with .part resume, and this article's rule: both routes provably copy every panorama, because a panorama is a .jpg.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed): If you would rather not install anything, the Files app does the same copy by hand — and for panoramas it has one advantage: you see exactly which files you selected. Plug the drive in, open Files by Google (or your phone's file manager), browse to DCIM/Camera, long-press one panorama, tap the rest, tap Copy, navigate to the USB drive, and tap Paste. The file manager shows you the individual .jpg files, not the gallery's panorama badge — so you can see the file sizes as you select, which is the check the gallery hides from you. Panoramas are the wide ones: in list view, a panorama's dimensions give it away, and its file is several times an ordinary still. Check the drive afterwards: compare the file sizes and dimensions against the phone, and copy one panorama back to the phone and open it in Google Photos to confirm the spin arrived. Three warnings specific to panoramas on this route. First, copy in the Files app — do not share from the Gallery. Sharing a panorama from the Gallery hands the file to another app, and what that app does with it — re-encode it, strip the metadata, save a fresh file — is out of your control. Copy in the Files app moves the file itself; Share hands the file to another app. Second, do not use Move. The guides that suggest Move are telling you to delete the originals as the copy goes — and a Move that is interrupted halfway leaves some panoramas on the drive, some on the phone, and no record of which is which. Copy, verify, then delete — that order is what keeps your panoramas safe. Third, do not judge the copy by opening it on the computer. Most computer viewers do not read the GPano metadata, so a perfectly good copy opens as a flat wide strip on a computer — and that proves nothing about the file. The check is the phone's Google Photos, which reads the note. What you give up is everything SnapDisk automates. There is no oldest-first order — you copy in whatever order you selected. There is no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, and no resume: if the drive is unplugged mid-copy, you start that file again and work out yourself which panoramas already arrived. There is no per-file size verification, and no skipped-file list — a file that does not fit, or a copy that silently stops, fails quietly. For a few panoramas that is fine. For a library of them, the manual route is an afternoon of tapping and checking, and the one-tap route is the honest recommendation. The manual route is also the fallback for the one thing SnapDisk's default run cannot do: copy panoramas only. If you want just the panoramas and nothing else, select them by hand in DCIM/Camera and copy them the same way.

Method 3: the cloud trap — check Google Photos before you trust it: Before you trust the cloud with panoramas, check what it actually holds. Google Photos backs up the camera folder, and a panorama uploaded there keeps its file — but the default is not Original quality. Google's own help page says Storage saver uploads "may be compressed into a different image format, like a .jpg" — and it says more that bites panoramas specifically: photos larger than 16 MP are resized to 16 MP. A panorama is a wide, high-resolution image, often over 16 MP, so Storage saver resizes it — and a re-save that writes a fresh file has no reason to preserve the GPano metadata that makes it spin. Whether the spin survives a Storage saver re-encode is not something this article promises either way — no panorama run through the cloud has ever been tested here — so the rule is the same as for every other format in this series: copy to the drive first, at original quality, and check the copy, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. The setting is one tap in Photos settings — easy to have wrong for years without noticing, because the panorama looks identical as a flat strip. One more cloud detail, because it confuses people with panoramas specifically: the spin is metadata, and metadata is the first thing a re-encode drops. A panorama that comes back from the cloud as a flat strip may have lost the note, or may be opening in a viewer that never read it — and from the phone alone you cannot tell which. That is why the check in this article is a copy back to the phone and an open in Google Photos, not a glance at a thumbnail. Copy to the USB drive first, open one panorama on the phone and watch it spin, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. And never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone. Check the drive copy, watch it spin, then delete — that order is what keeps your panoramas safe.

The 5 GB free cap, and why panoramas feel it less than video: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — verified in the repo as FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB — and runs can be repeated. Files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For panoramas, 5 GB goes further than it does for video: a panorama library is usually dozens of files at a few megabytes each — a standard panorama five to ten megabytes, a photosphere fifteen to twenty-five — so a whole panorama collection is often hundreds of megabytes, not gigabytes, and one free run covers it. The cap bites when the library mixes panoramas with the long 4K videos sitting next to them in DCIM/Camera, which is what the folder route copies too. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock, verified in the repo's billing code) that auto-starts the backup when a disk is connected and removes the size limit, so a whole season copies in one run. The cap is per run, not per library, and that distinction is what matters here: the free version can finish any panorama library if you run it again, because files already copied are never copied twice. The count to do before you start is the library size: open the Files app, look at the DCIM/Camera folder size, divide by 5 GB, and that is how many free runs the library needs. Do the arithmetic before you plug the drive in, not halfway through the copy. One more size note: a file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — verified in the repo's BackupService. A single panorama never reaches that, but a long 4K video sitting next to your panoramas can — and that file is skipped and listed, the panoramas around it copy normally, and the fix is the same exFAT format recommended above.

What this does not do: It does not convert your panoramas — to anything. SnapDisk copies the .jpg exactly as it is. Converting a panorama to a smaller file, or to any other format, re-encodes it — and a re-encode is exactly the step that can drop the GPano metadata. That is your editor's or your computer's job, on a copy, never on the only original.; It does not stitch panoramas for you. Stitching is the camera's job — the sweep, the dots, the HDR+ pipeline — not SnapDisk's. SnapDisk copies the finished .jpg files; it does not make them.; It does not extract the sphere to a flat image. The spin stays inside the .jpg, as metadata — flattening it is a separate tool's job, on a copy, never on the only original. The backup's job is to keep the original intact.; It does not copy panoramas only on the default run. The default run copies the whole library, oldest-first, panoramas mixed in with stills and ordinary videos in date order. Panoramas only is the by-hand pick in Method 2 — and even then, you select them one by one in the file manager.; It does not promise the spin plays on every viewer. A viewer that does not read the GPano metadata shows a flat wide strip — the file is intact, the viewer just does not apply the spin. The check is the phone's own Google Photos, which reads the note.; It does not read or index your panoramas. There is no panorama detection and no search inside the files — SnapDisk copies files, and finding one panorama among a thousand .jpg files is your file manager's job, on the drive, after the copy.; It does not back up anything but photos and videos. No app data, no messages, no system state — and no browser tabs, notes, or clipboard history. Those live in the app's own storage, not in the photo folders, and they need their own backup.; It does not delete anything. SnapDisk only copies — the only delete calls in its source touch .part files, never your photos — so freeing space is a two-step flow you do yourself: copy to the drive, open one panorama on the phone and watch it spin, then delete the originals from your phone. That flow is covered step by step in How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive.; It does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver. No wake lock, no battery-saver handling in the repo, no panorama run ever tested — stated plainly above, not promised. Keep the phone awake for the run.; and It does not restore or view your photos. There is no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied .jpg files in a viewer or on your computer yourself. The SnapDisk vs VaultDrive comparison covers what the rivals add here, and what they charge for it.

What to avoid: Assuming a panorama is a special format. A panorama is an ordinary wide .jpg — and a Photo Sphere is the same .jpg with a note inside it. The backup does not need to understand panoramas — it needs to copy the file without changing it.; Sharing the panorama when you meant to copy it. Sharing from the Gallery hands the file to another app, which may re-encode it and drop the metadata. Copy, verify, then delete.; Formatting the drive NTFS. Most Android phones cannot open NTFS on their own. Panoramas run larger than ordinary stills — a photosphere can be fifteen to twenty-five megabytes. Count the DCIM/Camera folder first, then buy the size, and divide by 5 GB to know how many free runs the library needs.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you have confirmed the copy — and for a panorama, the check is opening it in Google Photos and watching it spin. Copy, watch it spin, then delete from the phone — never the other way round.; Assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off. Unverified — no wake lock, no battery-saver handling. Keep the phone awake for the run or check it.; Starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery. A timelapse video looks like a mistake — a few seconds of video for hours of recording — and that is the trap. It is an ordinary .mp4, and the speed is baked into the frames, not stored as a note. Anything that copies the file keeps it fast. Here is how to get timelapse videos onto a USB drive with the speed still in them.

TL;DR: A timelapse video is not a special file. Your phone records it as an ordinary .mp4 in DCIM/Camera — the camera captures frames at a frequency much lower than the rate they are played back at, as Google's own Pixel time-lapse page puts it, and the finished clip is a normal video whose frames are spaced out. There is no metadata note holding the speed, unlike a slow-motion clip, where the slow part is a note inside the file — so there is nothing for a copy to lose, and even a re-encode keeps the speed; what a re-encode can change is the resolution, not the pace. That decides the backup: anything that copies the file byte-for-byte keeps the timelapse, and SnapDisk copies byte-for-byte with no conversion, so every timelapse arrives intact. Both routes are certain for .mp4 and .mov — the default run reads the phone's MediaStore Video table with no folder filter and no MIME filter, and .mp4 and .mov are both indexed on every phone — and the folder route (pick DCIM/Camera as From) is the certain one for every format in the list. A timelapse covers hours in a short clip, so the file is small for the time it spans and the 5 GB free per-run cap bites later than it does for slow motion — but a long 4K timelapse is still a large file, so count the DCIM/Camera folder first and divide by 5 GB, and format the drive exFAT, because a long 4K clip can pass the FAT32 4 GB limit. The check that matters: play one clip and watch it run fast — any player plays a timelapse fast, because the speed is in the frames, not in a note a player has to read. One honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. That is the gap this article fills: a phone-to-USB backup that treats a timelapse clip as what it is — an ordinary file with the speed baked into its frames — with the route that provably copies it unchanged.

What a timelapse video actually is: A timelapse video is a normal video file whose frames are spaced out. Your phone records it as an ordinary .mp4 saved in DCIM/Camera like every other video the camera shoots, and the speed is in the frames themselves: the camera captures individual frames at a frequency much lower than the rate they are played back at — Google's own Pixel time-lapse page says exactly that — and plays them back at normal speed, so hours of real time become seconds of video. There is no second file holding the speed, and — this is the point the whole article turns on — there is no metadata note holding it either. The numbers make the shape concrete. On a Pixel, open the Camera app, switch to video mode, and tap Time Lapse — Google's own page lists the settings you get there: the interval between frames, the resolution (720p, 1080p, 4K), and the speed, 5x or 120x. At 120x, twenty minutes of recording becomes a ten-second clip, as Android Authority's walkthrough of the Pixel mode records. On a Samsung Galaxy, open the Camera app, tap More, then Hyperlapse — Hyperlapse is Samsung's name for the same mode — and pick a speed: 4x, 8x, 16x, and sometimes 32x, as the Samsung guides list them. HowToGeek's Hyperlapse walkthrough puts the file plainly: recording a hyperlapse is just like recording any other video — tap the shutter, let it roll, tap again to stop, and the finished clip is saved to the gallery. One distinction worth knowing: a hyperlapse is a timelapse where the camera moves a long distance while recording — all hyperlapses are timelapses, but not all timelapses are hyperlapses — and either way the file that comes out is an ordinary video. Two things follow from that shape, and they decide the backup. First, the risk is not that the file gets left behind — it is a .mp4 in DCIM/Camera, and every route in this article copies .mp4 files — and it is not that the speed gets dropped, because there is no note to drop. That is the opposite of the slow-motion article's risk, where one file hides a note inside it that a re-encode can strip, and the opposite of the panorama article's risk, where a Photo Sphere hides GPano metadata that a re-save can drop. A timelapse survives even a re-encode with its speed intact — what a re-encode changes is the resolution and the quality, not the pace. Second, the real risk is human: the clip looks wrong. A few seconds of video for hours of recording reads as a broken or failed recording, and the mistake is deleting it as one — or sharing it from the Gallery and getting back a re-encoded copy at lower resolution, which still plays fast but is no longer the original file. The check is different too: for a slow-motion clip you watch it play slowly in the phone's Gallery, because only a player that reads the metadata applies the slow part — for a timelapse you just play it, on any player, because the speed is in the frames and every player plays it fast. One more form to know about, because it confuses people: a timelapse made from an ordinary video afterwards. Third-party apps can take a normal clip and speed it up into a timelapse — and the file that comes out is, again, an ordinary .mp4 with the speed baked into the frames. The point is the same either way: what you back up is files, and the speed lives in the frames, never in a separate timelapse format or a metadata note.

What you need: An Android phone with timelapse videos on it. On a Pixel, open the Camera app, switch to video mode, and tap Time Lapse — speeds from 5x to 120x. On a Samsung Galaxy, open the Camera app, tap More, then Hyperlapse, and pick 4x, 8x, 16x or 32x. Then check the count: open a clip and watch it run fast, so you know which files are the timelapses before you back them up. If a clip plays at normal speed, it was not recorded as a timelapse, and no backup can make it fast.; A USB drive with enough free space. Count first: a timelapse covers hours in a short clip, so the file is small for the time it spans — but a long 4K timelapse is still a large file, and one timelapse guide notes that recording an hour in 4K can take 3–5 GB of storage — so add up the DCIM/Camera folder in the Files app before you buy the drive, and divide by 5 GB to know how many free runs the library needs.; A drive formatted exFAT. The format reference for this article is DriveForge's exFAT-vs-FAT32-vs-NTFS guide: exFAT has no 4 GB per-file limit and is read and written by current Android phones, Windows, and Mac. FAT32 cannot hold a single file of 4 GB or more — a long 4K timelapse can reach that — and exFAT is the practical format for the whole folder. NTFS is a Windows format that most Android phones cannot open on their own — do not use it for a phone backup drive.; An OTG adapter if your drive is USB-A. A dual USB-C drive plugs straight in; a standard USB-A stick needs a data-capable OTG adapter. A portable SSD may need a powered hub — the phone alone may not supply enough power for the drive.; and SnapDisk v0.1.2. Not on Google Play yet — install the APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later (minSdk 24 in the repo). No account, no cloud, no ads, and no internet permission — your photos physically cannot leave the phone.

Method 1: SnapDisk — the phone, one tap: This is the route this article is for, and for timelapse clips both routes are certain — which is the honest centre of this article, and different from the HEIC article, where only the folder route was certain for .heic. The default run — leave From unpicked — reads the phone's MediaStore Video table with no folder filter and no MIME filter, verified in the repo as PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, called from BackupService when no From folder is picked — and a timelapse clip is a .mp4 or .mov file, which every Android MediaStore indexes, so it is in the result set by construction. The folder route — tap the From picker, browse to the phone's storage, and choose DCIM or DCIM/Camera — is the certain one for every format in the list: the From picker is the system folder picker (verified in the repo as OpenDocumentTree), the tree walk recurses into subfolders, and it copies every file whose extension is in the list. Both .mp4 and .mov are in that list, verified in the repo's PhotoQuery.kt, so a DCIM pick copies every timelapse clip in the tree whatever its format. Then pick the To folder on the drive, in the same picker, and tap Backup. The copy runs in the background: oldest-first by the date the video was taken, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, plus Pause and Stop. There is no format split to know about here: the default run is certain for .mp4 and for .mov — both are indexed on every phone, .mov as video/quicktime in Android's platform MIME map — so whichever your phone saves timelapse as, the default run covers it. The folder route is certain in every case too. That is the whole rule, and it is simpler than the HEIC article's rule because the common case here — .mp4 and .mov alike — is covered by both routes. The speed survives because the copy never touches the files' bytes. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — there is no transcoding step anywhere in its copy path — and it checks the size of every file after copying, renaming the .part file to the final file only after the size verification passes. A timelapse clip that arrives on the drive is the same .mp4 that left the phone, frames spaced out exactly as recorded. And here is the check that matters, because it is the one most people get wrong for timelapse: play it, do not just look at it. Play one clip back on the phone and watch it run fast — or, if you would rather not copy it back, compare the file size and duration on the drive against the phone: a matching size and a matching duration mean the file arrived whole. Unlike the slow-motion check, this one cannot fail by player: any player plays a timelapse fast, because the speed is in the frames, not in a note a player has to read. A timelapse that plays at normal speed on the drive would mean the file itself was changed — the check is the file, not the player. This article does not promise a shared or re-encoded copy is the original — that is a property of the share, not of the file — and it says so instead of promising it. Two honest limits on this route. First, there is no timelapse-only mode on the default run: it copies the whole library, oldest-first, timelapse clips mixed in with stills and ordinary videos in date order. If you want timelapse clips only, that is what the DCIM/Camera pick is for — and even then, the pick copies every video in the folder, timelapse and ordinary alike; there is no way to pick only the timelapses except by selecting them by hand in Method 2. Second, screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified: SnapDisk copies as a foreground service — the mechanism Android gives a copy that must keep running with the screen off — but the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling, and no timelapse run has ever been tested, so this article says so instead of promising it. Keep the phone awake for the run, or check it. On Android 15 and later a dataSync foreground service gets 6 hours in 24 hours, so a very long copy can be paused by Android itself, and opening the app resets the timer (WL-34). One fair comparison, because the search surfaced a rival that does part of this right: VaultDrive's page — read in full this run — says nothing about timelapse at all, not one timelapse line anywhere on it, so it is not a timelapse guide either. What it does have, and what is genuinely timelapse-relevant, is a choose-photos feature: back up just the photos and videos you pick. If you want a handful of timelapse clips and nothing else, picking them in VaultDrive is the honest route, and its "Original quality, byte for byte" line — HEIC, ProRAW, ProRes and 4K video copied as they are, never compressed or re-encoded — is the same byte-for-byte promise this article makes, plus folders by date or album and incremental backups on Pro, which are real wins SnapDisk does not have. But its free tier is a softer trap for timelapse than for slow motion: 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and a timelapse collection is usually a handful of clips, not hundreds, so the 200-file cap rarely bites — the 2 GB cap is the one that can bite a long 4K timelapse, against SnapDisk's 5 GB per run with no file count. VaultDrive is on Google Play today at $19.99 once for Pro Lifetime against SnapDisk's $9.99 once. What SnapDisk adds is the oldest-first order across the whole library, the detailed progress notification with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification with .part resume, and this article's rule: both routes provably copy every clip, because a timelapse is a .mp4 with the speed baked into the frames.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed): If you would rather not install anything, the Files app does the same copy by hand — and for timelapse it has one advantage: you see exactly which files you selected. Plug the drive in, open Files by Google (or your phone's file manager), browse to DCIM/Camera, long-press one timelapse clip, tap the rest, tap Copy, navigate to the USB drive, and tap Paste. The file manager shows you the individual .mp4 files, not the gallery's timelapse badge — so you can see the file sizes as you select, which is the check the gallery hides from you. Check the drive afterwards: compare the file sizes and durations against the phone, and play one clip on the phone and watch it run fast to confirm the speed arrived. Three warnings specific to timelapse on this route. First, copy in the Files app — do not share from the Gallery. Sharing a timelapse clip from the Gallery hands the file to another app, and what that app does with it — re-encode it at lower resolution, save a fresh file — is out of your control. The speed would survive, because it is in the frames, but the file that comes back may not be the original. Copy in the Files app moves the file itself; Share hands the file to another app. Second, do not use Move. The guides that suggest Move are telling you to delete the originals as the copy goes — and a Move that is interrupted halfway leaves some clips on the drive, some on the phone, and no record of which is which. Copy, verify, then delete — that order is what keeps your timelapse clips safe. Third, do not judge the copy by the file size. A timelapse is short — a few seconds for hours of recording — so a small file is normal, and a small file is not a failed copy. The check is playing it: a timelapse that runs fast is a timelapse that arrived. What you give up is everything SnapDisk automates. There is no oldest-first order — you copy in whatever order you selected. There is no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, and no resume: if the drive is unplugged mid-copy, you start that file again and work out yourself which clips already arrived. There is no per-file size verification, and no skipped-file list — a file that does not fit, or a copy that silently stops, fails quietly. For a few clips that is fine. For a library of them, the manual route is an afternoon of tapping and checking, and the one-tap route is the honest recommendation. The manual route is also the fallback for the clips MediaStore does not index: the default run reads the MediaStore Video table with no format filter, so a .mov timelapse clip is included like any .mp4 — but a clip in a folder MediaStore skips, for example a folder containing a .nomedia file, never reaches the default run, and the way to copy it is to select it by hand in DCIM/Camera and copy it the same way.

Method 3: the cloud trap — check Google Photos before you trust it: Before you trust the cloud with timelapse, check what it actually holds. Google Photos backs up the camera folder, and a timelapse clip uploaded there keeps its file — but the default is not Original quality. Google's own help page says Storage saver stores photos and videos "at a slightly reduced quality" — and it says more that bites timelapse specifically: videos higher than 1080p will be resized to high-definition 1080p, and "some information, like closed captions, might be lost". A 4K timelapse backed up at Storage saver comes back as a 1080p file — still fast, because the speed is in the frames and a resize changes resolution, not frame spacing — but no longer the original file. Whether the speed survives a Storage saver re-encode is not something this article promises either way — no timelapse run through the cloud has ever been tested here — so the rule is the same as for every other format in this series: copy to the drive first, at original quality, and check the copy, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. The setting is one tap in Photos settings — easy to have wrong for years without noticing, because the clip still plays fast at 1080p. One more cloud detail, because it confuses people with timelapse specifically: the speed is in the frames, and the resolution is the thing a re-encode changes. A timelapse that comes back from the cloud looking soft or low-resolution has not lost its speed — it has lost its pixels — and from the phone alone you cannot tell whether the file on the cloud is the original or a resized copy. That is why the check in this article is a copy to the drive first and a play on the phone, not a glance at a cloud thumbnail. Copy to the USB drive first, play one clip and watch it run fast, and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. And never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone. Check the drive copy, watch it run fast, then delete — that order is what keeps your timelapse clips safe.

The 5 GB free cap, and why a timelapse feels it less: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — verified in the repo as FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB — and runs can be repeated. Files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For timelapse, 5 GB goes further than it does for ordinary video, and much further than for slow motion: a timelapse covers hours in a short clip, so the file is small for the time it spans — where a second of Super Slow-mo holds 960 frames, a timelapse holds a few frames for a whole minute of real time. A whole timelapse collection is often one free run. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock, verified in the repo's billing code) that auto-starts the backup when a disk is connected and removes the size limit, so a whole season copies in one run. The cap is per run, not per library, and that distinction is what matters here: the free version can finish any timelapse library if you run it again, because files already copied are never copied twice. The count to do before you start is the library size: open the Files app, look at the DCIM/Camera folder size, divide by 5 GB, and that is how many free runs the library needs. Do the arithmetic before you plug the drive in, not halfway through the copy. One more size note: a file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — verified in the repo's BackupService. A single timelapse rarely reaches that, but a long 4K one can — and that file is skipped and listed, the clips around it copy normally, and the fix is the same exFAT format recommended above.

What this does not do: it does not convert timelapse clips — to anything (converting a clip re-encodes it, and a re-encode is exactly the step that can drop the resolution, even though the speed survives); it does not slow a timelapse down, or make ordinary videos into timelapses (turning an ordinary clip into a timelapse is the camera's Time Lapse mode — or an editor's speed change, on a copy — not SnapDisk's job); it does not split a timelapse into still frames (the frames stay inside the .mp4 — extracting them is a separate tool's job, on a copy, never on the only original); it does not copy timelapse clips only on the default run (the whole library copies, oldest-first); it does not promise a shared copy is the original (sharing hands the file to another app, which may re-encode it at lower resolution — the speed survives, because it is in the frames, but the pixels may not); it does not read or index timelapse clips (no timelapse detection, no search inside the clips); it backs up photos and videos only (no app data, messages, browser tabs, notes, or clipboard history); it never deletes anything (only .part files are ever deleted); it does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver; and it has no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied .mp4 files in a viewer or on your computer yourself.

What to avoid: assuming timelapse is a special format (a timelapse clip is an ordinary .mp4 with the speed baked into the frames — the backup does not need to understand timelapse, it needs to copy the file without changing it); mistaking a timelapse for a broken clip (a few seconds of video for hours of recording is the point, not a failed recording — play it before deleting anything); sharing the clip when you meant to copy it (Share hands the file to another app, which may re-encode it at lower resolution); judging the copy by the file size (a timelapse is short, so a small file is normal — the check is playing it, not weighing it); letting Storage saver resize the 4K timelapses (Google Photos Storage saver resizes videos higher than 1080p to 1080p — Google's own words — copy to the drive first, at original quality); using Move instead of Copy in the Files app; formatting the drive NTFS; buying a drive before counting the library; deleting before verifying (and for a timelapse clip, the check is playing it and watching it run fast); assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off; starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery (one USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both); and searching for the wrong thing (the pages the search returns are generic transfer guides, our own general articles, and two OTG walkthrough videos — none of them is a timelapse backup guide).

Rule of thumb: a timelapse video is an ordinary .mp4 with the speed baked into the frames — there is no note to lose, so the copy just has to be byte-for-byte, and the check has to prove the clip still plays fast. Pick DCIM/Camera as From, copy, play one clip back on the phone and watch it run fast, then delete. That order is what keeps your timelapse clips safe.

One copy of your photos is not a backup — it is a hope. The 3-2-1 rule says keep three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one off-site. Here is how to do that for Android photos with a USB drive, no computer, and no cloud account you did not choose.

TL;DR: The 3-2-1 rule is three copies, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy kept somewhere else — the same rule NIST describes in its 3-2-1 guidance, and the same one CISA tells small businesses to follow. For an Android phone owner it maps cleanly: the phone itself is copy 1, a USB drive is copy 2 on different media, and a second drive kept elsewhere — or a cloud copy — is the off-site copy 3. The USB copy is the one this article is about, because it is the copy the search results make hardest: every 3-2-1 guide that turns up for Android photos routes it through a computer — plug the phone in with a cable, drag DCIM to the computer, then copy that folder to a drive — or through the cloud, or through a manual file-manager copy on the phone. None of them offers the USB copy as a one-tap whole-library copy straight from the phone to the drive, with no computer anywhere in the chain, and none of them mentions SnapDisk. SnapDisk is that copy: plug the drive in, tap Backup, and the whole library copies oldest-first in the background, with progress, Pause and Stop, per-file size verification, and resume where it stopped — free up to 5 GB per run, Pro $9.99 once for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. The honest trade-off is copy 3: SnapDisk is offline-only — it holds no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave the phone — and it has no cloud step, so the off-site copy is a second drive kept at a relative's home, at work, or in a safe deposit box, or a cloud backup you run yourself. One honest limit: screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified — the repo holds no wake lock and no battery-saver handling — so keep the phone awake for the run or check it. Its step-by-step is a cable: connect the phone to the computer, choose File Transfer, open File Explorer, copy DCIM and the rest, paste them onto the computer, external SSD, or USB flash drive. Its own recommendation is "USB backup Android to a computer". No SnapDisk mention anywhere on the page, and no one-tap whole-library copy. Revaults' "How to back up your photos and documents (the 3-2-1 rule)" states the rule the same way — the original plus two backups, two kinds of storage, one away from home — and its local backup is the same shape: connect the phone to a computer, copy the photos and files to a folder, then copy that folder to an external drive or a USB stick. Its off-site copy is a cloud account or a second drive kept at a relative's home, a workplace, or a safe deposit box. No SnapDisk mention, no one-tap copy. Sync by Miciniti's "The 3-2-1 Backup Rule, Explained for Normal People" maps the rule onto two saved tasks — a Backup task to a USB or external drive for copy 2, a second Backup task to a cloud drive for copy 3 — which is the closest any rival comes to an app doing the USB copy, but it is a task you set up and run by hand, not a one-tap whole-library copy, and its USB and external drives sit behind a paid upgrade. GadgetsNow's "How to Back Up All Your Photos Without Paying for Extra Cloud Storage" starts the same way — transfer the photos to a laptop or desktop with a USB cable first, then copy them to an external hard drive or a USB drive — and its 3-2-1 section repeats the rule without changing the route. TechCity's "Complete Phone Backup Guide: Never Lose Your Photos Again" states the 3-2-1 strategy up front — phone as one copy, a cloud service as the off-site copy, a computer or external hard drive as the third — and its five methods are Google Photos, iCloud, back up to your computer, OneDrive, and Samsung Smart Switch: cloud and PC, no phone-to-USB copy at all, no SnapDisk mention. The second phrasing — 3-2-1 backup redundancy for Android photos to a USB flash drive, no computer — returns the same shape from the other side, and still nothing on the narrow angle. Sync by Miciniti's Android photos guide says the safest setup is two of three routes — Google Photos, a cloud drive, or an SD card or USB drive — and its USB route is again a saved Backup task you run by hand. The third phrasing, checked this run to pin down the remaining names, returns more of the same: TechBulletinNow's phone-and-computer guide (cloud, computer, external drive), PengJiangWen's TechLife guide (cloud copy two, computer copy three), TechBuniyaad's "How To Back Up Your Phone Properly" (cloud for the daily copy, local to a computer once a month), Dr.Fone's Android backup guide (its own PC tool plus Google Backup), and Techwire's phone guide (cloud, then an external drive or computer every few months). Not one of them offers a one-tap whole-library phone-to-USB copy, and not one of them mentions SnapDisk. VaultDrive's own page — read in full this run — says nothing about 3-2-1 at all, not one occurrence anywhere on it, so it is not a 3-2-1 guide either. That is the gap this article fills: 3-2-1 where copy 2 is the whole library, one tap, phone straight to USB, no computer.

The 3-2-1 rule, in plain English: Three copies of anything you cannot replace. Two different kinds of storage. One copy kept somewhere else. That is the whole rule, and every page in the search above states it the same way — the only thing they disagree on is what the copies sit on. The numbers defend against three different ways of losing photos, and each number answers one of them. Three copies protects you if one copy fails: a phone dies, a drive corrupts, a cloud account locks you out — two copies left is still a backup, one copy left is a hope. Two kinds of storage protects you if one kind of device has a fault: two folders on the same laptop are not two kinds of storage, and neither are two drives in the same drawer from the same batch. One copy off-site protects you from the thing that takes a whole location at once: a fire, a flood, a burglary — the copies in the house go together, and only the copy somewhere else survives. For a phone owner the mapping is the one this article uses throughout. Copy 1 is the phone itself — the originals, in DCIM/Camera and Pictures, the copy you look at every day. Copy 2 is a USB drive — a different kind of storage from a phone, a copy you can hold, that needs no account and no internet. Copy 3 is the off-site copy — a second drive kept at a relative's home, at work, or in a safe deposit box, or a cloud backup you run yourself. The rule does not care which cloud, or which drive, or which app made copy 2 — it cares that the three copies are really three, that two kinds of storage are really two, and that one copy is really somewhere else. Two traps hide inside that sentence. The first is sync pretending to be backup: a synced photo library is not a second copy, because deleting a photo in one place can delete it everywhere — Google Photos itself documents that deleting a photo in Google Photos also deletes the copy on the device. The second is two copies that are really one: a phone and a drive that always sit in the same bag, or a phone and a computer that always sit in the same room, fail together in the same theft or the same fire. The rule is only satisfied when the copies are independent — different media, different places — and the rest of this article is the routine that keeps them that way. One more thing the rule does not say, because people read it into it: it does not say the copies have to be made the same way, or at the same time, or by the same tool. Copy 2 can be a one-tap app copy and copy 3 can be a cloud upload you switch on once and forget — the rule counts copies, not tools. What it does demand is that each copy is complete and that you have checked it: a backup you have never tested is a hope, not a backup, and the check for each copy is in the method that makes it.

What you need: An Android phone with photos on it. The phone is copy 1 — the originals. Check the count before you start: open the Files app, look at the DCIM folder size, and add Pictures (screenshots and saved images live there, not in DCIM) — that total is the library copy 2 has to hold.; A USB drive with enough free space. Count first, buy second: the drive has to hold the whole library for copy 2, and a second drive of the same size for copy 3 if the off-site copy is a drive rather than the cloud. What SnapDisk adds is the oldest-first order across the whole library, the detailed progress notification with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification with .part resume, and this article's rule: copy 2 is the whole library in one tap, with no computer in the chain.

Copy 3: the off-site copy SnapDisk does not do: Here is the honest trade-off, stated up front instead of buried: SnapDisk makes copy 2, and copy 3 is your step. SnapDisk is offline-only — it holds no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave the phone — and it has no cloud step at all. That is a deliberate privacy property, and it is also a limit: an app that cannot reach the internet cannot put a copy anywhere else. So the off-site copy needs a second drive or a cloud step that SnapDisk does not do, and this section is that step. The drive route is the one that keeps the whole routine offline. Take a second USB drive — the same size as the first, formatted exFAT — and copy the library to it the same way: plug it in, tap Backup, let the same oldest-first run copy the whole library. Then keep it somewhere else: a relative's home, a workplace you trust, a safe deposit box. The rule is only satisfied when the copy is really somewhere else — a second drive in the same drawer as the first is not an off-site copy, it is the same fire, the same theft, the same flood taking both. Rotate it on a schedule you will actually keep: once a month is the honest cadence for most people, and always before a major trip, a repair, or a phone replacement. The cost is the second drive and the discipline — the copy itself is the same one tap as copy 2. The cloud route is the one most people actually keep up, because it runs itself once it is switched on — and it is also the one with a trap this article has to name, because the cloud copy is only a real copy 3 if it holds the originals. Google Photos backs up the camera folder, but the default is not Original quality: Google's own help page says Storage saver stores photos and videos "at a slightly reduced quality" — photos larger than 16 MP are resized to 16 MP, and videos higher than 1080p are resized to high-definition 1080p. A 4K photo backed up at Storage saver comes back as a smaller file — still the same picture, but no longer the original. The setting is one tap in Photos settings, easy to have wrong for years without noticing, because the photo still looks right at a glance. And the second trap is sync pretending to be backup: deleting a photo in Google Photos also deletes the copy on the device, and with backup on that deletion carries across every device backing up to the account. So the rule for the cloud route is the same as for every other format in this series: copy to the drive first, at original quality, and check the copy — and only then let the cloud hold whatever it holds. Set the quality to Original, check that the upload has actually finished, and never delete the phone originals on the strength of a cloud badge alone. Copy 3 is only a copy when you have confirmed it holds the originals; a badge that says "backed up" is not the confirmation.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed): If you would rather not install anything, the Files app does the same copy by hand — and for 3-2-1 it has one advantage: you see exactly which files you selected, and you can do copy 3 the same way on the second drive. Plug the drive in, open Files by Google (or your phone's file manager), browse to DCIM/Camera, long-press one photo, tap the rest, tap Copy, navigate to the USB drive, and tap Paste. Repeat for Pictures if you want the screenshots and saved images too. Check the drive afterwards: compare the file counts and sizes against the phone, and open a few photos on the drive yourself. Then do the same again on the second drive, and take that drive somewhere else. Three warnings specific to 3-2-1 on this route. First, copy in the Files app — do not share from the Gallery. Sharing a photo from the Gallery hands the file to another app, and what that app does with it — re-encode it at lower quality, save a fresh file — is out of your control. Copy in the Files app moves the file itself; Share hands the file to another app. Second, do not use Move. The guides that suggest Move are telling you to delete the originals as the copy goes — and a Move that is interrupted halfway leaves some photos on the drive, some on the phone, and no record of which is which. Copy, verify, then delete — that order is what keeps your photos safe, and it is doubly true when the copy is one of three. Third, do not mistake two copies for three. The manual route makes it easy to copy the library to one drive, feel done, and never make the second one — and one drive plus the phone is two copies in the same room, which is not 3-2-1. The routine is not finished until the second drive is copied and somewhere else. What you give up is everything SnapDisk automates. There is no oldest-first order — you copy in whatever order you selected. There is no progress notification with speed and time left, no Pause and Stop, and no resume: if the drive is unplugged mid-copy, you start that file again and work out yourself which photos already arrived. There is no per-file size verification, and no skipped-file list — a file that does not fit, or a copy that silently stops, fails quietly. And there is no skip-if-exists: the second run copies everything again, because the file manager does not remember what arrived last time. For a few hundred photos that is fine. For a library of thousands, the manual route is an afternoon of tapping and checking, repeated every month, and the one-tap route is the honest recommendation. The manual route is also the fallback for the photos MediaStore does not index: the default run covers every photo MediaStore indexes, whatever folder it sits in, so a photo outside DCIM is included — but a photo in a folder MediaStore skips, for example a folder containing a .nomedia file, never reaches the default run, and the way to copy it is to select it by hand in the Files app and copy it the same way.

The 5 GB free cap, and how it shapes the routine: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — verified in the repo as FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB — and runs can be repeated. Files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For 3-2-1, 5 GB per run shapes the routine rather than blocking it: the cap is per run, not per library, so the free version can finish any library if you run it again — and the routine is a repeat, not a single event, so the cap is a count of runs, not a ceiling. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock, verified in the repo's billing code) that auto-starts the backup when a disk is connected and removes the size limit, so a whole library copies in one run — and the auto-start is what makes the monthly repeat actually happen, because the copy starts when the drive connects instead of waiting for you to remember. The count to do before you start is the library size: open the Files app, look at the DCIM folder size, add Pictures, divide by 5 GB, and that is how many free runs copy 2 needs — and the same count again for copy 3 on the second drive, if the off-site copy is a drive. Do the arithmetic before you plug the drive in, not halfway through the copy. A library of 20 GB is four free runs for copy 2 and four more for copy 3; a library of 100 GB is twenty and twenty, and that is the point where Pro's unlimited size stops being a convenience and starts being the routine itself. One more size note: a file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — verified in the repo's BackupService. A single photo never reaches that, but a long 4K video can — and that file is skipped and listed, the photos around it copy normally, and the fix is the same exFAT format recommended above. The skipped-file list is the part of the routine most people skip: read it after every run, because a file the job skipped is a hole in copy 2, and a hole in copy 2 is a hole in the rule.

What this does not do: It does not make the off-site copy for you. SnapDisk is offline-only — no internet permission, no cloud step — so copy 3 is a second drive kept elsewhere or a cloud backup you run yourself. An article that implied SnapDisk alone satisfies 3-2-1 would be wrong, and this one says so.; It does not convert your photos — to anything. SnapDisk copies each file exactly as it is. Converting a photo to a smaller file re-encodes it — and a re-encode is exactly the step that can drop the quality. That is your editor's or your computer's job, on a copy, never on the only original.; It does not copy only the photos you pick on the default run. The default run copies the whole library, oldest-first, photos and videos together in date order. Picking only some photos is the folder pick in Method 1 — and even then, every file in the folder copies — or the manual route in Method 2.; It does not promise a shared copy is the original. Sharing hands the file to another app, which may re-encode it at lower quality. The check is the drive copy, not the shared one.; It does not read or index your photos. There is no photo detection and no search inside the photos — SnapDisk copies files, and finding one photo among thousands is your file manager's job, on the drive, after the copy.; It does not back up anything but photos and videos. No app data, no messages, no system state — and no browser tabs, notes, or clipboard history. Those live in the app's own storage, not in the photo folders, and they need their own backup.; It does not delete anything. SnapDisk only copies — the only delete calls in its source touch .part files, never your photos — so freeing space is a two-step flow you do yourself: copy to the drive, open a few photos and check they arrived, then delete the originals from your phone. That flow is covered step by step in How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive.; It does not promise the copy keeps running with the screen off under battery saver. No wake lock, no battery-saver handling in the repo, no 3-2-1 run ever tested — stated plainly above, not promised. Keep the phone awake for the run.; It does not restore or view your photos. There is no in-app viewer and no restore feature — you open the copied files in a viewer or on your computer yourself. The SnapDisk vs VaultDrive comparison covers what the rivals add here, and what they charge for it.

What to avoid: Counting sync as a backup. A synced photo library is not a second copy — deleting a photo in one place can delete it everywhere. The rule counts copies that survive each other, not copies that mirror each other.; Keeping both drives in the same place. Two drives in the same drawer fail together in the same fire, the same theft, the same flood. Copy 3 is only a copy when it is somewhere else.; Stopping at two copies and calling it 3-2-1. The phone plus one drive is two copies in one room. The routine is not finished until the second drive is copied and somewhere else, or the cloud copy is confirmed at Original quality.; Letting Storage saver shrink the cloud copy. Google Photos Storage saver resizes photos larger than 16 MP to 16 MP and videos higher than 1080p to 1080p — Google's own words. Copy to the drive first, at original quality, and set the cloud quality to Original.; Sharing the photo when you meant to copy it. Sharing from the Gallery hands the file to another app, which may re-encode it at lower quality. Copy in the Files app; Share hands the file to another app.; Using Move instead of Copy in the Files app. Move deletes the originals as the copy goes — an interrupted Move leaves photos split between phone and drive with no record of which is which. Copy, verify, then delete.; Formatting the drive NTFS. Most Android phones cannot open NTFS on their own. Use exFAT — DriveForge's guide is the format reference — and keep FAT32 only for a drive an older device must read.; Buying a drive before counting the library. Count the DCIM folder plus Pictures first, then buy the size — and buy two of them, because copy 3 needs a drive of its own. Divide by 5 GB to know how many free runs each copy needs.; Deleting before verifying. A backup is only a backup once you have confirmed the copy — open a few photos on the drive and check they arrived. Copy, check, then delete from the phone — never the other way round.; Assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off. Unverified — no wake lock, no battery-saver handling. Keep the phone awake for the run or check it.; Starting a multi-gigabyte copy on a nearly dead battery. One USB-C port holds the drive or the charger, not both — charge first, or use a powered hub with pass-through charging, which is standard USB-C behaviour but unverified with SnapDisk.; Searching for the wrong thing. The pages the search returns are thorough 3-2-1 guides whose USB copy needs a PC, a manual file-manager copy, or a cloud account — none of them is a no-computer phone-to-USB guide. Search for the USB copy, not the rule, and the gap is obvious.

On your phone instead: If you would rather tap once than copy by hand, SnapDisk copies your photos and videos to a USB drive — free, no ads, no account, no cloud, and your photos never leave the phone. Leave From unpicked and the default run copies the whole library oldest-first — or pick DCIM as the From folder and the folder route copies every photo in the tree — then tap Backup, and open a few photos on the drive and check they arrived before you delete anything. Then make copy 3: a second drive kept somewhere else, or a cloud backup at Original quality — SnapDisk does not do that step, and this article does not pretend it does. Rule of thumb: three copies, two kinds of storage, one somewhere else — and each copy has to be complete and checked. Phone is copy 1, the USB drive is copy 2 in one tap with SnapDisk, and copy 3 is a second drive kept elsewhere or a cloud copy at Original quality.
