https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/telegram-photos-to-usb.html

Your Telegram photos are files on your phone — in Telegram's own folders, which you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

What the search results actually offer: Search for this job and the results split into four shapes, none of them the one-tap phone-to-USB copy. The closest guide that actually names Telegram's folders is NetworkUstad's "Move Telegram Downloaded Files To A New Phone Manually" — it finds the Telegram folder (Telegram Images, Telegram Video, Telegram Documents, Telegram Audio) or Android/data/org.telegram.messenger on newer Android, but its job is moving files to a new phone through a PC or with the USB drive only as a middleman between two phones. Wondershare MobileTrans' generic phone-to-USB guide copies "DCIM, Pictures, Movies, Music, Download, Documents, and messaging-media folders" by hand in the Files app, with a computer-first fallback — Telegram is never named, no Telegram folder path is given, there is no scoped-storage note, and the copy is manual with no progress, no resume, and no verification. AnExplorer's OTG guide and the YouTube OTG walkthroughs are the same shape: a manual file-manager copy, with DCIM and Download as the examples. RottenWifi's "How to Find Downloaded Files in Telegram" finds the files but stops there, though it makes one distinction this article relies on: a file you only viewed may be cache, not a permanent file, and cache is not a backup. The third shape is apps that save Telegram media to the phone, not to a drive: Telegram Media Saver and Media Saver for Telegram. The fourth shape goes the opposite direction: TeleDrive and Telegrive use your Telegram account as cloud storage — they upload your files into Telegram, which is the reverse of getting Telegram files out onto a drive you hold. Two one-tap whole-library apps do appear — PhotoStick Mobile and Photos to USB: OTG Backup, both of which copy the whole gallery in one tap — but neither names Telegram or its folders, and neither is a guide for the Telegram folders. VaultDrive, the rival this site compares against, also does phone-to-USB with no computer and lets you pick files and folders, and its page, read in full this run, never mentions Telegram either, so there is no Telegram-specific guide there. That is the gap: the folders are named in a phone-to-phone guide, the USB copy is done by hand in generic guides, and nobody puts the two together in one tap.

Where Telegram keeps your photos and videos: Telegram saves every photo and video you download as an ordinary file in a folder on your phone. Older setups: Internal storage > Telegram > Telegram Images (photos), Telegram Video (videos), Telegram Documents, Telegram Audio. Android 11 and later: Telegram's working data lives under Internal storage > Android > data > org.telegram.messenger, and the built-in file manager may refuse to open Android/data — that is the wall the Android/data section is about. Videos live in Telegram Video next to Telegram Images, so picking the parent Telegram folder gets both in one run. If a photo never downloaded (the blurred thumbnail with a download arrow), it is not on your phone yet — open the chat and download it first, or there is nothing to copy. Viewing a photo is not downloading it: Telegram keeps a cache so you can reopen what you viewed, and the cache is fragments keyed to the installation, not your photos in any usable sense — do not copy the cache folder and call it a backup.

What you need: An Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; and enough space on the drive for the Telegram photos and videos you want to keep. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, and a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Check the Telegram folder sizes in the Files app first, and divide by 5 GB — that is how many free runs the copy needs, and the arithmetic belongs before you plug the drive in, not halfway through the copy.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy): Install SnapDisk from the v0.1.2 APK (not on Google Play yet). Open SnapDisk and set the From folder: tap the From folder picker and navigate to the Telegram Images folder, or pick the parent Telegram folder to get images and videos together — SnapDisk walks the folder recursively, and other file types in that folder (documents, voice messages) are simply skipped; only image and video files copy. Set the To folder to the USB drive; the copy mirrors the source folder structure. Plug in the USB drive, tap Backup in the notification, and photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background, with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying. Files that already copied are never copied twice, so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big Telegram folder partway, run it again and it picks up where it left off. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the drive is back. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device. What SnapDisk adds over VaultDrive (Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, "2,000+ installs on the App Store and Google Play") is the oldest-first order, the detailed progress with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification, a free tier of 5 GB per run with no file count, and half the Pro price. VaultDrive's own wins, stated fairly: you can pick just the photos you want, folders are organised by date or album, and Pro copies only what's new since last time.

The Android/data wall — and what to do about it: On Android 11 and later, you cannot use the system folder picker to select files under Android/data or Android/obb — Android's own developer documentation says so, for both picking single files and picking a folder tree. SnapDisk's From picker is that system picker (the Storage Access Framework's folder picker), so if you navigate to Android/data/org.telegram.messenger and tap it, the picker answers "Can't use this folder. To protect your privacy, choose another folder." That is the platform's rule, not the app refusing, and no setting in SnapDisk changes it. Check first in the Files app: if a Telegram folder exists outside Android/data — the top-level Telegram folder with Telegram Images and Telegram Video — pick that one and Method 1 works as written. If the media only exists under Android/data, use one of the two fallbacks: Telegram's own route (in each chat, save the photos and videos you want with Save to Downloads or Save to Gallery, which puts ordinary copies in folders the picker can reach) or the PC route from NetworkUstad's guide (connect the phone to a computer in File Transfer mode, copy the Telegram folders to the computer, then copy them from the computer to the USB drive). Neither fallback is one-tap, and this article does not pretend otherwise.

Method 2: by hand in the Files app (no app needed): Plug in the USB drive, open Files, browse to Internal storage and find the Telegram folder, select the photos (or long-press the Telegram Images folder to select the whole thing), tap Copy to, then choose the USB drive as the destination, and wait for the copy to finish. This works fine for a one-off copy, and it is also the fallback for the one configuration SnapDisk's route gets wrong: if your Telegram media sits under Android/data and the picker refuses it, the Files app at least lets you look — and if it refuses too, the PC route above is the way in. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time Telegram photos pile up.

The 5 GB free cap, and how it shapes the routine: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — verified in the repo as FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB — and runs can be repeated. Files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For Telegram, 5 GB goes further than it does for a camera library: Telegram photos are usually compressed by the sender or by Telegram, and the folder is mostly images, so a whole Telegram Images folder is often one free run. The videos are the part that eats the cap — a Telegram Video folder full of long clips can pass 5 GB on its own, and that is the count to do before you start: open the Files app, look at the Telegram Images and Telegram Video folder sizes, divide by 5 GB, and that is how many free runs the copy needs. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock, verified in the repo's billing code) that auto-starts the backup when a disk is connected and removes the size limit. A file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — verified in the repo's BackupService — and the fix is the same exFAT format recommended above.

What this does not back up: Copying the Telegram Images and Telegram Video folders backs up the files — the photos and videos. It does not back up chat history (your messages live in Telegram's cloud, not in the Images folder, and they reappear when you sign in on any device; for a chat archive, use Telegram Desktop's Export chat history on a computer); secret chats (device-bound, never sync, not files in the Telegram folders); voice messages and audio (voice messages are .opus audio files, and SnapDisk copies image and video files only — verified in the repo: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .heic, .heif, .webp, .gif, .bmp, .dng, .raw for images; .mp4, .mov, .mkv, .webm, .3gp, .m4v, .avi for videos — so audio files are skipped); documents (PDFs and other files in Telegram Documents are not image or video files, so they are skipped — copy them by hand in the Files app if they matter); the cache (files Telegram downloaded only to show you once sit in the cache, not in the media folders, and the cache is rebuilt per installation); or stickers outside the picked folder (they only copy if they sit inside the folder you picked, and only if they are image files).

What to avoid: PC-only tools when you have no computer — the top search results for moving Telegram files assume a computer in between, and MobileTrans is a Windows/Mac program at heart. Cloud backup dressed as USB backup — TeleDrive and Telegrive store your files in Telegram, a cloud shelf, not a USB backup. Deleting before verifying — copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone, never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes. Assuming the chats came along — the photo files are not the conversation; cloud chats reappear on sign-in, secret chats never leave the device, and neither is in the folders this article copies. Copying the cache and calling it a backup — cache files are fragments keyed to the old installation. Unplugging mid-copy — pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight; wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first. Assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off — Unverified, no wake lock, no battery-saver handling in the repo; keep the phone awake for the run or check it.

On your phone instead: If you'd rather tap once than copy a folder by hand, SnapDisk copies your Telegram photos to a USB drive — free, no ads, no account, no cloud, and your photos never leave the phone. You delete the originals yourself, after you check the copy. See also: Back up WhatsApp photos to a USB drive on Android (no computer) for the same folder-route rule on WhatsApp's folders, How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them, Transfer photos to a USB drive automatically (no manual copy), SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared, and How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive.

Rule of thumb: the photos are files in a folder — back up the folder. The chats are in the cloud — they follow your sign-in. The secret chats are on the device — they follow nothing. Do the folder copy, check the copy on the drive before you delete anything, and export the chats on a computer if the conversation itself matters.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/instagram-photos-to-usb.html

Your Instagram photos are files on your phone — in the Instagram folder and the Downloads folder, which you can point a backup app at. Plug a USB drive into the phone and copy them straight to it, no computer, no upload.

What the search results actually offer: Search for this job and the results split into four shapes, none of them the one-tap phone-to-USB copy. The first shape downloads Instagram media to the phone and stops there: en.androidayuda's InstaPP guide downloads one photo at a time into a folder on the phone called "InstaPP", and umatechnology's InstaSave and FastSave guides copy a post link and save the photo or video into the phone's gallery, as do the web downloaders that save a browser download into Downloads or Pictures. The second shape is Meta's official export, covered by HowToGeek and by FastSaveMedia's backup guide: Accounts Center, Download Your Information, choose "Download to your device", wait for the email, and download a zip within four days — the only bulk route Instagram itself offers, but the zip lands on the phone and still has to be unzipped and copied to a drive by hand. The third shape is the generic OTG guide: YouTube walkthroughs and Wondershare MobileTrans' phone-to-USB guide copy by hand in the Files app, Instagram never named, no Instagram folder path given, manual select-copy-paste with no progress, no resume, and no verification. The fourth shape is the bookmark: Instagram's own Save adds a post to a private list inside the app, and several guides present it as "saving" — but it saves nothing to the phone at all. Two one-tap whole-library apps do appear in the wider results — PhotoStick Mobile and Photos to USB: OTG Backup — but neither names Instagram or its folders. That is the gap: the folders are named in download-to-phone guides, the USB copy is done by hand in generic guides, and nobody puts the two together in one tap.

Where Instagram keeps your photos and videos: Instagram saves what it saves on your phone as ordinary files — but in two different folders, depending on how the file got there. Pictures/Instagram is the Instagram folder in your gallery: your own posted photos land there when the Save Original Photos toggle is on (Settings, Archiving and downloading), and photos you save from the app land there too, as do Reels downloaded with Instagram's own Download option in the Share menu on public Reels where the creator allows it. Downloads is where a Reel or photo saved through a browser downloader lands. DCIM is the camera folder — your phone's own photos live there, not Instagram's — so a backup that only copied DCIM would miss your Instagram media entirely — but SnapDisk's default run copies the whole media library via MediaStore, not DCIM only, so your Instagram media is covered. Instagram's Save (the bookmark icon) saves nothing to the phone: it adds the post to a private list inside Instagram, and if the creator deletes the post it vanishes from that list too. Stories you want to keep need the archive on: Settings, Archiving and downloading, Save story to archive — otherwise an expired Story is gone. A photo you only viewed is not on the phone at all. Check the two folders in the Files app first — if Pictures/Instagram does not exist on your phone, nothing has been saved there yet, and the toggle is the fix for future posts, not for past ones.

What you need: An Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; and enough space on the drive for the Instagram photos and videos you want to keep. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup, and a drive formatted exFAT has no such limit. Open the Files app, look at the Pictures/Instagram and Downloads folder sizes, and divide by 5 GB — that is how many free runs the copy needs, and the arithmetic belongs before you plug the drive in, not halfway through the copy.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy): Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then open SnapDisk and set the From folder for an Instagram-only copy. The default run copies your whole media library via MediaStore — not DCIM only — so it covers your Instagram media too, along with everything else; "/sdcard/DCIM" is only the label on the settings screen until you pick a folder. To copy only the Instagram folders instead of the whole library, tap the From folder picker and navigate to Pictures/Instagram and tap it. Run Downloads as a second run: Reels saved through a browser downloader live in Downloads, not in Pictures/Instagram, so after the first run finishes, pick Downloads as the From folder and run it again — files already copied are never copied twice, so the two runs do not duplicate anything. Set the To folder to the USB drive, plug in the drive, tap Backup in the notification, and the photos and videos copy oldest-first in the background with a progress notification showing percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Wait for "Backup complete" — every file is size-verified after copying. If you unplug the drive mid-copy, the backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device. What SnapDisk adds over the rival that also does phone-to-USB — VaultDrive, Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, "2,000+ installs on the App Store and Google Play" — is the oldest-first order, the detailed progress with Pause and Stop, per-file size verification, a free tier of 5 GB per run with no file count, and half the Pro price. VaultDrive's own wins, stated fairly: you can pick just the photos you want, folders are organised by date or album, and Pro copies only what's new since last time.

Method 2: the Meta export — your whole account as a zip: Method 1 copies the Instagram media already on your phone as files. For everything you ever posted — including Stories, Reels, and the originals of posts you never saved to the phone — the only bulk route Instagram itself offers is Meta's official export, and it is a two-step job. Request the export: in Instagram, open your profile, tap the menu, tap Accounts Center, then Your information and permissions, then Export your information (some versions say Download your information). Tap Create export, pick your Instagram profile, and choose Export to device — not the transfer to Google Drive or Dropbox. Pick what goes in it (Content covers your posts, Reels, and Stories), all time, and high media quality, then start the export and enter your password when asked. Wait for the email: Meta prepares the archive and emails you when it is ready — most arrive within hours to a few days, Meta allows up to 30 days — and the download link is valid for four days, so download the zip as soon as the email arrives. Download and unzip the zip on your phone: the zip downloads to your phone, usually the Downloads folder, and you open it in the Files app and extract it. The zip itself is not an image or video file, so SnapDisk would skip it — unzipping is the step that turns the export into a backup. Point SnapDisk at the unzipped folder and run Method 1 on it. Two honest notes: the export is slow and partial by nature — you wait on Meta, the link expires, and what arrives is your content plus messages, comments, and account data, and SnapDisk copies only the image and video files, so the messages and comments stay on the phone; and the export is the only route that reaches posts you never saved to the phone — Method 1 can only copy files that are already there.

Method 3: by hand in the Files app (no app needed): Plug in the USB drive, open Files, browse to Internal storage, Pictures, Instagram — and, for the browser-saved Reels, Internal storage, Download — select the photos (or long-press the Instagram folder to select the whole thing), tap Copy to, then choose the USB drive as the destination, and wait for the copy to finish. This works fine for a one-off copy, but it has no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time Instagram photos pile up — and you have to remember both folders, because the Files app will not tell you that DCIM is not where Instagram keeps its files.

The 5 GB free cap, and how it shapes the routine: SnapDisk's free version backs up manually up to 5 GB per run — verified in the repo as FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT, 5 GiB — and runs can be repeated. Files already copied are never copied twice, so a second run picks up where the first stopped. For Instagram, 5 GB goes further than it does for a camera library: Instagram photos are compressed by the app when you post them, and the folder is mostly images, so a whole Pictures/Instagram folder is often one free run. The videos are the part that eats the cap — a Downloads folder full of Reels can pass 5 GB on its own, and that is the count to do before you start. Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (product id pro_unlock, verified in the repo's billing code) that auto-starts the backup when a disk is connected and removes the size limit. A file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped with its reason and the job continues — verified in the repo's BackupService — and the fix is the same exFAT format recommended above.

What this does not back up: Copying the Pictures/Instagram and Downloads folders backs up the files — the photos and videos. It does not back up your Instagram account (your profile, your follower list, and your account itself live on Instagram's servers, not in a folder on your phone); messages and comments (text in Instagram's database, not files in the Instagram folder — the Meta export includes them in the archive as text, and SnapDisk copies image and video files only); bookmarked posts (Instagram's Save is a bookmark inside the app, not a file — a saved post from someone else's account is not on your phone at all, and it vanishes from your Saved list if the creator deletes it); other people's posts (saver apps like InstaSave and FastSave download other people's posts onto your phone, one link at a time — this article covers your own media already on your phone, and downloading someone else's posts without their permission is against Instagram's terms); Stories you never archived (a Story that expired without Save story to archive turned on is gone — no folder on the phone holds it); or anything still only on Instagram's servers (a post you never saved to the phone, never downloaded, and never exported is not a file on your phone — Method 1 copies what is there, Method 2 is the route for the rest).

What to avoid: Running the default and thinking it copied Instagram only — the default run copies your whole media library via MediaStore, Instagram included, along with everything else. Treating the Save bookmark as a backup — the bookmark icon saves a post to a list inside Instagram, not to your phone. Downloading the export and stopping there — the Meta export zip on your phone is not a backup, it is one file on the same phone that could be lost, and its download link expires in four days; unzip it and copy the files to the drive. Copying the zip and calling it a backup — SnapDisk copies image and video files, not zip archives, so the export zip would be skipped; unzip first, then copy the folder. Deleting before verifying — copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone, never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes. Assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off — Unverified, no wake lock, no battery-saver handling in the repo; keep the phone awake for the run or check it. Unplugging mid-copy — pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight; wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first. Backing up other people's posts and calling it your archive — saver apps make it easy to pull anyone's public post onto your phone, but your archive is your own media.

On your phone instead: If you'd rather tap once than copy a folder by hand, SnapDisk copies your Instagram photos to a USB drive — free, no ads, no account, no cloud, and your photos never leave the phone. You delete the originals yourself, after you check the copy. The bookmark is a link — it follows nothing. It does not back up your Snapchat account (your profile, friends, Snap score, and account itself live on Snapchat's servers); chats and messages (text in Snapchat's database, not files in a folder — the My Data export includes your data as an archive, and SnapDisk copies image and video files only); Memories still only in Snapchat (a Memory you never exported is not a file on your phone — if you delete Snapchat or log out before Backup Progress says Complete, the un-backed-up Memories are gone); My Eyes Only, as it sits (protected by a passcode, not in the export — unlock them and move them out first, keeping in mind that exporting removes the extra privacy layer); other people's Snaps (a Snap someone sent you, or a Story you only viewed, is not yours to export); or anything Snapchat archives in January 2027 that you never downloaded (archived Memories stay as thumbnails, and opening one takes a paid plan — the download in Method 2 is free, but only if you do it before the archive takes effect).
What to avoid: Running the backup before exporting anything — Memories live in Snapchat's cloud, not on your phone, and a backup run over a phone with no exported Snaps copies nothing and finishes green. Trusting one guide's folder and skipping the check — the guides disagree, and your phone decides; open the gallery and the Files app and look before you start. Deleting before verifying — copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone, never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes. Downloading the export and stopping there — the My Data export ZIP on your phone is not a backup, it is one file on the same phone that could be lost, and its download link expires in 7 days; unzip it and copy the files to the drive. Copying the ZIP and calling it a backup — SnapDisk copies image and video files, not zip archives, so the export ZIP would be skipped; unzip first, then copy the folder. Assuming the copy keeps running with the screen off — Unverified, no wake lock, no battery-saver handling in the repo; keep the phone awake for the run or check it. Unplugging mid-copy — pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight; wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first. Forgetting My Eyes Only — Snaps in My Eyes Only are not in the export and not in the gallery; unlock them and move them out before you export.

SnapDisk has no restore button — the backup on your drive is plain files in plain folders. Copy them back with the Files app, put them where the Gallery looks, and check they show up before you unplug.
What the search results actually offer: Search for this job and the results split into five shapes, none of them a restore for a SnapDisk backup. The first shape is the Samsung-only guide: Samsung's "Download Media Files from a USB to my Galaxy Device" walks through My Files — plug in the drive with an OTG adapter, select the file on the USB drive, Copy, go back to Internal storage, pick a folder, Copy here — and its example pastes into Downloads. It works, and it is the closest thing to a real answer, but it is Galaxy-only by its own note ("designed for Australian variant devices"), it says nothing about where camera photos belong, and it never mentions SnapDisk or any backup app. The second shape is the generic USB guide: How-To Geek's "How to Use a USB Flash Drive With Your Android Phone or Tablet" is a phone-to-USB guide first, and the reverse direction gets a single line — "You can use this same method in reverse to move files from your USB drive to your Android device" — with Samsung My Files screenshots and no word about the Gallery. Tom's Guide's "How to Connect USB Storage Devices to Your Android Phone" is the same shape: connect the drive, browse it, copy files to the phone — generic, no backup, no Gallery step. The third shape is the platform help page: Google's "Use USB storage devices" for Files by Google gives the exact copy steps — Storage devices, tap the USB drive, find the file, Copy to, choose where, Copy here — but it is a file-manager manual, not a restore guide: it says nothing about which folder the photos belong in or how the Gallery finds them. The fourth shape is the photo-stick comparison: the umatechnology and mefmobile "Photo Stick vs. USB Flash Drive" pages both say the copy is manual — file manager, or through a computer — and stop there; a photo stick is a product label, not a restore workflow. The fifth shape is the wrong job entirely: Unerased and the deleted-file recovery tools recover files deleted from the phone itself — a different problem from copying a backup back off a drive you hold. That is the gap: the copy-back is taught as a generic file move for one phone brand, or in one line, and nobody puts together the SnapDisk backup, the folder it belongs in, and the Gallery step.
What SnapDisk does — and does not do — for restore: Say it plainly, because this is the fact the whole article turns on: SnapDisk does not restore. Version 0.1.2 copies photos and videos one way, from the phone to the USB drive, and has no restore button, no import button, and no copy-back path of any kind. This was verified in the code this run, not assumed: a search of the backup engine, the photo query, the main activity, the backup service, the settings screen, and the manifest at the current base finds no restore function — the only matches for "restore" or "import" are the word import at the top of Kotlin files, which is how the language loads libraries, not a feature. The app's job is the backup half, and it is honest about that. The restore half is a plain file copy, and the Files app already does it. Two consequences follow. First, there is nothing to install, buy, or sign into for the restore: the drive, the phone, and the file manager you already have are the whole toolkit, and the free 5 GB per-run cap and the $9.99 Pro purchase are backup facts, not restore facts — restoring costs nothing either way. Second, the rival does not restore either, and that is worth stating fairly: VaultDrive's own guide, "How to Back Up Your Photos Before Switching to a New Phone" on coticsy.com, says "VaultDrive doesn't currently restore photos back into your photo library itself" — because, like SnapDisk, its backups are plain files, and you copy them back onto the phone yourself. VaultDrive's prices, re-verified from its own site this run: Pro is $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup. So neither app sells you a restore button; the difference between them is in the backup, not the way back.
Where your backup actually sits on the drive: Before you copy anything back, look at what is on the drive — because the restore copies the folders, not the app, and the folders tell you where everything goes. SnapDisk's default run copies your whole media library via MediaStore — every photo and video the gallery sees, oldest first — not DCIM only. And the copy mirrors the source tree on the drive: a photo that lived in DCIM/Camera on the phone sits in DCIM/Camera on the drive, a photo from Pictures sits in Pictures, a download sits in Download. Both facts are verified in the code this run — the photo query reads MediaStore images and videos with no folder filter, and the backup engine carries the source relative path through to the destination. So the restore rule is simple: copy each folder back to the same relative folder it came from. DCIM/Camera on the drive goes back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera. Pictures on the drive goes back to Pictures. That is what puts the photos back in the albums they came from, instead of in one flat pile. Three things on the drive are not photos. First, files ending in .part — an in-progress copy writes to <name>.part and is renamed to the real name only after the size verification passes, so a .part file is an unfinished copy, not a photo: do not copy it back, and delete it or leave it. Second, a video that is missing from the drive was probably never copied: files of 4 GB or more cannot sit on a FAT32 drive, and SnapDisk skips them with the reason listed instead of failing the whole backup — check the skipped list from the backup run before concluding a video is lost. Third, the drive holds the files, not your gallery's organisation: albums, favourites, people tags, and edits live in the gallery app or the cloud, not in the file.
Method 1: copy back with Files by Google (the restore): This is the restore. No app to install, no computer, no account — the phone, the drive, and the file manager. It works on any Android phone, not just Samsung, because Files by Google is the platform's own file manager. Plug the USB drive into the phone — a USB-C flash drive goes straight in, a regular USB drive needs a USB-C OTG adapter; a notification should offer the drive, and if nothing appears, open Files by Google and look under Storage devices. Find the backup on the drive: in Files by Google, tap the USB drive under Storage devices and browse to the folder you want back — DCIM/Camera for camera photos, Pictures for the rest, or the folder you pointed SnapDisk's From picker at if you backed up a single folder. Select what is missing — not the whole drive: long-press one photo, then tap the rest, or long-press a folder to select the whole thing; copy back only the photos you lost, because if the phone still holds half of a folder and you copy the whole folder back over it, you can end up with two copies of the same photo. Copy, don't move: tap the menu and choose Copy to — not Move; the drive is your backup, so keep it intact until the restore is checked, because Move deletes from the drive as it goes and a failed move is how a backup becomes a loss. Choose the same folder on the phone: navigate to Internal storage and into the same relative folder the files came from — DCIM, then Camera, for camera photos; Pictures for the rest — and tap Copy here. Wait for the copy to finish, and don't unplug the drive until it says it is done — pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight. Open the Gallery and check: the restored photos should be back in their albums, and if they are not there, do not copy again yet — see the Gallery section below, because the files are almost certainly on the phone, just not indexed yet. Check a few photos before you touch the drive: open two or three restored photos full-screen and confirm they render; only then is the restore done, and the drive stays your backup until then. On a Samsung phone the same steps run in My Files instead: plug in the drive, open My Files, tap USB storage, long-press to select, tap Copy, go back to Internal storage, open the matching folder, and tap Copy here. The buttons have different names and the example in Samsung's own guide pastes into Downloads — but the rule is the same: copy to the folder the photos came from, not to Downloads, or they land in a Downloads album instead of with your camera photos. Either file manager does the job; the folder you choose is what matters, not the app you choose it in.
Method 2: restore a whole folder — or a whole phone: Method 1 restores the photos you lost. This method is for the bigger cases: a folder wiped by accident, or a new phone. The steps are the same, the scale is different. For a whole folder — say every photo in DCIM/Camera is gone — long-press the DCIM folder on the drive, Copy to, Internal storage, and paste it back as DCIM: the folder structure inside comes with it, so the photos land in the albums they came from. For a new phone, the backup is plain files on a plain drive, so nothing ties it to the old phone: plug the drive into the new phone, copy the folders back to the same relative folders, and the photos are the new phone's photos. No account to sign into, no proprietary archive to unlock, no transfer code. Two honest notes. First, the new phone's camera photos will land in the same DCIM/Camera folder, so a restore and a new camera roll mix cleanly — but copy the backup back before the new phone's own photos pile up, or you will be sorting old from new by hand. Second, after the restore, run SnapDisk on the phone you restored to: it protects the restored photos again, and files already on the drive at the same size are skipped — verified in the backup engine, a destination file that already exists with the same size is never copied twice — so a re-run only copies what is actually new. The switching-phones guide covers the new-phone case from the backup side; this article is the restore half of it.
When the photos don't appear in the Gallery: This is the step people get wrong, because it looks like the restore failed when it didn't. The Gallery does not read folders — it reads a database called the MediaStore. A background scanner fills that index: it runs when the phone boots, when storage is mounted, when an app saves a file through the proper APIs, and when an app explicitly asks for a scan. A file copied by a file manager is on the disk but may not be in the index yet, and until something tells the index about it, the Gallery has no reason to know it exists. That is the mechanism, and it decides the fix. Usually the restored photos appear within seconds — the file manager's copy does trigger a scan — but if they don't, do not copy them a second time. Instead, in order: restart the phone — the scanner runs at boot, so a restart is the reliable nudge; give it a few minutes after booting, then open the Gallery; this is the fix to try first, and it needs no app and no computer. Check the folder has no .nomedia file — a file named .nomedia in a folder tells the scanner to skip that folder and everything under it; in your file manager, turn on Show hidden files, look in the folder you copied back to, and delete any .nomedia you find there, then restart the phone. Check the Gallery's permission — on Android 13 and later, the gallery needs Photos and videos permission: Settings, Apps, your Gallery app, Permissions, Photos and videos, Allow all, not a partial selection; then reopen the Gallery. Check the Files app itself — open Files by Google and look in the folder you copied to; if the photos are there, the files are safe and the problem is indexing only, so work through the steps above, not another copy; if they are not there either, the copy itself did not land, and that is a different problem: repeat Method 1 and watch for the copy to finish before unplugging. One more check, and it settles the date question at the same time: open a restored photo and look at its Details. The taken date should read the original — the file itself is unchanged by a copy, so the date stored inside the photo is the one from when it was taken. What changes is the arrival date: the gallery's Recently added view sorts by when the file arrived on the phone, so restored photos may sit under the restore date there, while the timeline view by taken date should still show the original date.
What restore does not bring back: A restore brings back files. It does not bring back everything around them, and the honest version of that list is: albums, favourites, and people tags — those live in the gallery app's database, or in the cloud, not in the photo file; the restored file is the photo, and the album it sat in, the star you gave it, and the face tag are not in it. Edits made after the backup — the drive holds the file as it was at backup time; a crop, a filter, or an adjustment you made in the gallery or in Google Photos after that backup is not in the file on the drive, and a later backup of the edited file is a different file, not the same one with the edit attached. Photos that were only in the cloud — a photo that lived only in Google Photos, freed from the phone and never downloaded as a file, was never on the phone for SnapDisk to copy, so it was never on the drive; the restore can only bring back what the backup actually held. Videos the backup skipped — a video of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive was skipped at backup time with its reason listed; it is not on the drive to restore, and the fix for next time is a drive formatted exFAT, which has no such limit. App data and messages — chats, app settings, and account data are not files in a photo folder; the backup is photos and videos, and everything else needs its own backup. None of this makes the restore a failure — it makes it a file restore, and the files are the irreplaceable part. But it is why the backup should run before the loss, not after: a backup made yesterday cannot hold an edit made today, and a photo that was never a file on the phone cannot be copied back from a drive.
What to avoid: Looking for a restore button in SnapDisk — there isn't one in v0.1.2, verified in the code; tapping around the settings for an import that does not exist wastes the time the copy-back would have taken, and the Files app is the restore. Using Move instead of Copy — Move deletes from the drive as it goes, and if the move fails halfway, the photos are neither on the phone nor on the drive; copy, check, and only then decide what the drive is for. Copying everything back over a phone that still has half of it — copy back only what is missing, because a whole-folder copy over a half-full folder can leave two copies of the same photo, and sorting duplicates out is slower than selecting the missing ones in the first place. Copying the .part files back — a .part file is an unfinished copy, not a photo; it will not open, and it is not a backup of anything, so leave it on the drive or delete it. Copying back to Downloads because Samsung's example does — Downloads is a folder the Gallery indexes, so the photos would show up, but under a Downloads album, not with your camera photos; copy camera photos back to DCIM/Camera, where they came from. Concluding the restore failed because the Gallery is empty — the files are probably on the phone and unindexed, so check the Files app first, then restart the phone so the scanner runs at boot; a second copy over the first one is how duplicates happen. Deleting the drive copy before checking the restore — the drive is the only other copy until the restore is verified, so open a few restored photos full-screen first, then decide what to do with the drive. Unplugging mid-copy — pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight; wait for the copy to finish, or the restore creates the damage it was meant to fix. Expecting the albums and edits to come back with the files — they live in the app or the cloud, not in the file; the restore brings back the photos, and rebuilding the albums is a separate, manual job. Treating a deleted-file recovery app as a restore — Unerased and its kind recover files deleted from the phone, a different job with its own limits; if you hold the backup on a drive, the copy-back is faster, surer, and free.
On your phone instead: If you'd rather tap once than copy a folder by hand, SnapDisk copies your photos to a USB drive — free, no ads, no account, no cloud, and your photos never leave the phone — and the copy back is the Files app's job, described above. You delete the originals yourself, after you check the copy. See also: Switching phones? Back up your photos to USB first for the new-phone case from the backup side, Back up photos before a factory reset for the backup to make before you wipe the phone, How to back up photos to a USB drive without uploading them, Transfer photos to a USB drive automatically (no manual copy), SnapDisk vs VaultDrive: USB photo backup on Android, compared, and How to free up space by moving photos to a USB drive.
Rule of thumb: there is no restore button — the backup is plain files, so the restore is a plain copy. Copy back only what is missing, to the same folder it came from, with Copy — never Move — and check the Gallery before you touch the drive. If the photos don't show, restart the phone: the scanner runs at boot. The files are the irreplaceable part; the albums and edits around them are not in the file, and they don't come back with it.

Your WeChat photos are not in your gallery until you save them there — WeChat keeps them inside the app. Save them first, then copy them straight to a USB drive, no computer, no upload.
What the search results actually offer: Search for this job three ways and the results split into four shapes, none of them a WeChat-to-USB guide for the phone. The first shape is the generic OTG guide: a YouTube walkthrough ("How to Connect USB Drive to Android Phone to Move Photos & Videos", PYcbV25CczI) and written guides from mefmobile and AnExplorer — plug the drive in with an OTG adapter, open the file manager, select photos in DCIM, copy them to the drive. They work, and they are the honest manual route, but they are generic: they copy camera photos, and WeChat is never named in any of them. The second shape is the one-tap generic app: "Photos to USB: OTG Backup" copies the whole photo library in one tap — again generic, WeChat never named, and a whole-library copy, not a WeChat copy. The third shape is the WeChat backup guide that needs a computer: Coolmuster's WeChat backup guide covers WeChat for Windows/Mac, iTunes, Google Drive, and chat-log migration to a new phone — PC, cloud, or a new phone, and no phone-to-USB route anywhere in it. The fourth shape is the forum thread: Zhihu answers about backing up WeChat describe the same PC backup and migration routes. And our own SnapDisk articles — the generic transfer guide and the WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram, Facebook, Snapchat, and TikTok articles in the same series — cover those apps' folders, not WeChat's. That is the gap: the saved WeChat photos, copied oldest-first in one background run, phone straight to USB, with progress, resume, and verification, and no computer in between.
Save first, then back up: WeChat does not save received photos to your gallery on its own — unlike WhatsApp, which does. Save inside WeChat first: long-press a photo and save it to your phone, or save up to 9 at once from a chat's Search Chat History, then Media, screen. Moments and Channels posts give no save option, so those stay inside WeChat. Once the photos are in your gallery they are ordinary files, and SnapDisk's default run already includes them: with no From folder picked, the app reads the phone's whole MediaStore library — every photo and video the gallery sees, oldest-first — not DCIM only, verified in the code this run (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, BackupService.kt:635-639). To copy only the WeChat album, pick the WeChat folder under Pictures in the From picker instead. What the picker cannot do is reach WeChat's own storage: Android 11 and later will not grant a folder inside Android/data, and the tencent/MicroMsg cache files are not plain photos anyway.
Where WeChat keeps your photos — the disagreement, stated plainly: the sources do not agree on one folder, so the article names all three and tells the reader to check the gallery, not one guide's path. Saved copies land in the gallery under a WeChat album (the phone's Pictures area, in the Pictures/[app] pattern). WeChat's own storage is /sdcard/tencent/MicroMsg/[account]/, with image and video subfolders and a diskcache of concatenated cache.data files that are not plain photos. The app's private folder under Android/data/com.tencent.mm is closed to other apps on Android 11 and later — the system file picker cannot grant a tree there, verified from Android's own storage documentation and the umatechnology scoped-storage guide this run. SnapDisk copies media files only: it does not back up chat history (WeChat's own backup route is to a computer, through WeChat for Windows or Mac — it has no Google Drive chat backup, unlike WhatsApp), voice messages (.opus/.amr audio is not a copied file type), stickers kept inside WeChat, or documents. SnapDisk v0.1.2 has no restore function, verified in the code. The free version covers 5 GB per run (ProPrefs.FREE_BACKUP_BYTES_LIMIT = 5L*1024^3, verified in the code); Pro is a one-time $9.99. VaultDrive's figures, re-verified live this run from the full vendor page (coticsy.com/vaultdrive.html): Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and the vendor's own page says 2,000+ installs across the App Store and Google Play. No AppBrain install figure is used in this article — it was not re-verified this run.
Rule of thumb: the photos are files in a folder only once you save them — save them to the gallery first, then back up the folder. The chats are a database — back them up in WeChat, to a computer. Do both, and check the copy on the drive before you delete anything from the phone.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/encrypted-photos-to-usb.html
SnapDisk does not encrypt — it copies your photos exactly as they are. The protection has to come from the drive itself, or from encrypting the files before they leave the phone. Here are the routes that actually work.
SnapDisk does not encrypt — the honest centre, verified in the code: the copy is a byte copy (BackupEngine.copyWithResume, BackupEngine.kt:131) with a size check only (verify, BackupEngine.kt:107), and a search of the whole app source for encrypt, cipher, AES, and decrypt returns zero matches. The default run reads the whole MediaStore library, images and videos, oldest-first, with no folder filter (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, PhotoQuery.kt:23; BackupService.kt:634-641); the From-picker route walks the folder and keeps only recognised photo and video extensions (PhotoQuery.kt:89-105, 124-135). An encrypted .zip or .rar archive, or a vault container, is not an image or a video, so SnapDisk skips it on both routes — the archive goes to the drive by hand in the Files app.
What the search results actually offer: Search for this job three ways and the results split into seven shapes, none of them the narrow job. HowToGeek covers the opposite direction — the phone as an encrypted flash drive. The WITNESS blog (2020) says to password-protect the drive and encrypt files first with ZArchiver or RAR, then move them — manual, no automation. UltraVault is the near-miss: an on-phone AES-256-GCM vault with an encrypted backup to a folder you choose, cloud, USB or SD card, restored with a recovery phrase — a vault container, restored only inside UltraVault, not a whole-library one-tap copy of plain files. MeBackup is a second near-miss app: offline backup to USB with optional encryption, batch backup and progress tracking, but no Pause and Stop, resume or per-file verification in its listing, and its encryption is the app's own backup, not plain files on the drive. Huawei Backup writes an encrypted archive that only a Huawei phone can restore. AndroidAuthority names DroidFS and Photok, which encrypt on the phone and take no USB backup step. The EAGET FU80 is a fingerprint-encrypted SSD sold as a product, not a guide, and the LESOGE 128 GB drive is a second product pitch — Touch ID and passcode encryption with a one-click backup app, sold by a retailer, not a guide. Behind all seven sit the generic OTG guides, which copy plain files to a plain drive and never mention encryption.
The four routes: Method 1, a hardware-encrypted drive — the iStorage datAshur PRO2, read from the maker's own page this run: 7-15 digit PIN on the drive, AES-XTS 256-bit, FIPS 140-2 Level 3, "use as a normal flash drive" once unlocked, no software required, Android listed as a compatible host, auto-locks when unplugged, 4 GB to 512 GB; USB-A, so a USB-C phone needs an OTG adapter. Method 2, encrypt first on the phone (ZArchiver/RAR, DroidFS/Photok) and copy the archive by hand — SnapDisk skips it, and losing the password loses the photos forever. Method 3, UltraVault's encrypted backup to USB — a vault container, restore only in UltraVault. Method 4, Huawei Backup's encrypted archive — Huawei only. Method 5 is SnapDisk's one-tap copy to the unlocked drive: unlock the PIN drive first, tap Backup, oldest-first in the background with progress, Pause and Stop, size-verified, free 5 GB per run, Pro $9.99 once.
Whether SnapDisk can write to a hardware-encrypted drive's unlocked partition is unverified — the maker says it works on Android and behaves as a normal flash drive once unlocked, but no real-device test of SnapDisk against one has been run, so the article states the combination as expected-to-work, not proven, and names the encrypt-first fallback. Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no WakeLock/Doze code in the repo). VaultDrive's figures, re-verified live this run from the full vendor page (coticsy.com/vaultdrive.html): Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and the vendor's own page says 2,000+ installs across the App Store and Google Play. No AppBrain install figure is used in this article — it was not re-verified this run.
Rule of thumb: the backup app copies plain files — the protection is the drive or the archive, never the copy. Pick a hardware-encrypted drive if you want the protection without thinking about it, encrypt first if you want it for free, and never trust either until you have opened the copy on another device.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/no-otg-photos-to-usb.html
Without OTG the phone cannot see a USB drive at all — nothing to copy to, and no app that fixes it. The photos still get to the drive, but the route goes through a computer, a Wi-Fi drive, or a phone that does support OTG.
The honest centre, verified in the code: SnapDisk v0.1.2 copies to a connected drive — it offers the backup when the phone reports a drive attached (StorageReceiver listens for media-mounted / USB-device-attached broadcasts) and writes to the mounted volume, so on a phone without OTG the one-tap route is closed and no setting changes that. The default run reads the whole MediaStore library, images and videos, oldest-first, with no folder filter (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, PhotoQuery.kt:23); the copy is a byte copy with a size check only (BackupEngine.copyWithResume, BackupEngine.kt:130; verify, BackupEngine.kt:107). A Wi-Fi drive never appears as a mounted volume, so SnapDisk cannot write to one at all.
What the search results actually offer: three phrasings, four shapes, none of them the narrow job. The generic OTG guides (our own external-drive and auto-backup articles, eztoolset) assume the drive plugs in; eztoolset notes some older phones do not support USB host mode and moves on. The PC-first guides (rottenwifi, mobiletrans, sekin.in) say to copy phone to computer, then computer to drive — rottenwifi calls it the most dependable method, mobiletrans says "use a computer when OTG is unavailable", sekin.in gives a Windows-PC method for phones that don't support OTG. Our own articles describe the one-tap copy and assume the drive plugs in. Nobody checks the phone first, names the Wi-Fi drive, or says plainly that the automated whole-library backup is closed on a no-OTG phone.
The check and the three routes: check first with a free OTG checker app — it reads the USB manager, the android.hardware.usb.host.xml host feature flag, and any connected OTG device, and only reports, it cannot enable OTG; a "cannot confirm" is not a "no". Try a USB-C drive plugged in directly, try a USB mouse through the same adapter (a cursor means host mode works), and check power and cable — a thirsty drive or a charging-only cable looks exactly like "no OTG". Method 1, through a computer: unlock the phone, choose File transfer (MTP), copy DCIM and Pictures to the computer, then to the drive, verify before deleting. Method 2, a Wi-Fi flash drive: the SanDisk Connect Wireless Stick creates its own Wi-Fi network and auto-backs-up the camera roll — but it is a 2015 product, SanDisk retired the Connect Wireless Flash Drive app effective March 18, 2021, and it tops out at 256 GB, so check the companion app is still available before buying. Method 3, a different phone that does support OTG: Quick Share the photos across, then run SnapDisk there — best for a small batch, not a whole library. Method 4 is SnapDisk's one-tap copy itself, for the reader whose checker says yes: plug in, tap Backup, oldest-first in the background with progress, Pause and Stop, size-verified, free 5 GB per run, Pro $9.99 once.
Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no WakeLock/Doze code in the repo). VaultDrive's figures, re-verified live this run from the full vendor page (coticsy.com/vaultdrive.html): Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and the vendor's own page says 2,000+ installs across the App Store and Google Play — and its Android route needs OTG too. No AppBrain install figure is used in this article — it was not re-verified this run.
Rule of thumb: check the phone before you route around it — most "no OTG" verdicts are a bad adapter, a charging-only cable, or a thirsty drive. If the phone truly has no host mode, the copy needs a host: a computer, a Wi-Fi drive, or another phone — and no app can be that host for it.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/ntfs-photos-to-usb.html
Most Android phones can't write to NTFS drives. Check the format, reformat to exFAT, or copy by hand with an NTFS app — then SnapDisk works.
The honest centre, verified in the code: SnapDisk v0.1.2 has no NTFS detection at all — the word "ntfs" does not appear anywhere in the app's code, and there is no check for a read-only mount; the only format check in the app is the FAT32 one (a file of 4 GB or more on a FAT32 drive is skipped up front with "use exFAT"). On a drive the phone does not mount at all — the common case on most phones — SnapDisk offers the backup when the phone reports a drive attached (StorageReceiver listens for media-mounted / USB-device-attached broadcasts, StorageReceiver.kt:34-35), so no offer appears and there is nothing to tap. On a drive the phone mounts read-only, the offer appears and tapping Backup fails on the first file: the write to the .part file is refused, the copy returns Failed with the full error (BackupEngine.copyWithResume, BackupEngine.kt:130; verify, BackupEngine.kt:107), the service records it in the skipped list and continues (BackupService.kt:489-497), the retry-once rule does not fire (it fires only on size-verification failures, BackupService.kt:540-541, 581), and the run ends DONE with every file skipped and nothing copied — and a read-only error matches none of the detach keywords (BackupService.kt:655-661), so it is not treated as a detach. Whether a given phone mounts an NTFS drive read-only or not at all is unverified — no real-disk test of SnapDisk against an NTFS drive has been run, and the follow-up for exactly that test is still open in the Work Log. The default run reads the whole MediaStore library, images and videos, oldest-first, with no folder filter (PhotoQuery.queryMediaStoreOldestFirst, PhotoQuery.kt:23); the copy is a byte copy with a size check only. A Wi-Fi drive never appears as a mounted volume, so SnapDisk cannot write to one at all.
What the search results actually offer: three phrasings, three shapes, none of them the narrow job. The NTFS-writer apps (Paragon exFAT/NTFS for USB, NTFS Reader: USB+Bitlocker, USB File Manager, AnExplorer) bring their own filesystem drivers so the phone can read and write a drive Android itself cannot — Paragon as a SAF document provider with NTFS as an in-app purchase, NTFS Reader with NTFS read free and NTFS write a one-time in-app purchase and exFAT/FAT32 read and write free, USB File Manager reading and writing NTFS, exFAT, FAT32 and ext4 with manual import, AnExplorer reading and writing NTFS without root — and all four copy by hand in a file manager, one selection at a time: no whole-library one-tap run, no oldest-first, no background progress with Pause and Stop, no resume, no per-file verification. The format explainers (DriveForge "exFAT vs FAT32 vs NTFS", KnowTechie) answer the format question well — Android reads and writes FAT32 and exFAT on most current phones and NTFS "not on most phones without an app", formatting erases the drive, a phone can format a drive itself with an OTG adapter via a formatting app — and then stop: none gets to the backup. Our own articles describe the one-tap copy and assume the drive is writable. Nobody checks the format first, gives the reformat route, the NTFS-writer route, and the honest statement that SnapDisk's one-tap run needs a writable drive, in one place.
The check and the three routes: check first — on Windows, right-click the drive and read Properties ("File system: NTFS"); on the phone, the drive's Properties in a USB file-manager app lists the file system; if the phone shows nothing at all when the drive is plugged in, that is itself the answer. Method 1, reformat to exFAT: copy the drive's contents off first (formatting erases it), then format — Windows right-click Format, Mac Disk Utility Erase, or a formatting app such as DriveForge from the phone with an OTG adapter (exFAT free) — pick exFAT, not FAT32, because FAT32 caps a single file at 4 GB while exFAT has no such limit, and then SnapDisk's one-tap backup works. Method 2, an NTFS-writer app plus manual copy: the four apps above, copy by hand, no automation — and SnapDisk cannot use another app's private NTFS mount, so this route and SnapDisk do not combine. Method 3 is SnapDisk's one-tap copy itself, once the drive is writable: plug in, tap Backup, oldest-first in the background with progress, Pause and Stop, size-verified, free 5 GB per run, Pro $9.99 once.
Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no WakeLock/Doze code in the repo). VaultDrive's figures, re-verified live this run from the full vendor page (coticsy.com/vaultdrive.html): Pro $19.99 once, free up to 200 files or 2 GB per backup, and the vendor's own page says 2,000+ installs across the App Store and Google Play — and its Android route is headed "Back up Android photos to a USB drive with OTG", it recommends exFAT and warns about FAT32, so the format gate applies to it exactly as it applies to SnapDisk. No AppBrain install figure is used in this article — it was not re-verified this run.
Rule of thumb: check the format before you blame the app — most "won't back up to this drive" cases are NTFS, and the fix is a format change, not a different backup app. exFAT is the format a phone and a PC both write to, with no 4 GB limit — reformat once, and the one-tap backup works every time after.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/veracrypt-bitlocker-photos-to-usb.html
Back up photos from Android to a VeraCrypt or BitLocker USB drive: mount it with OTG Master, then copy by hand. What works, and where SnapDisk fits.
The honest centre, verified live this run (November 23, 2026) and from the code at base 048414c: Android reads no VeraCrypt, LUKS, or BitLocker volume natively. OTG Master (app.fayaz.otgmaster, free, open source GPL-3.0, F-Droid + Google Play, v0.5.2, updated November 17, 2026, Android 8.0+, no root) mounts VeraCrypt, LUKS1, LUKS2, and BitLocker (password, 48-digit recovery key, .BEK key file) and exposes the unlocked volume via DocumentsProvider so Files and other apps can browse it; filesystems inside: FAT32, exFAT, NTFS, ext4. No kernel mount on non-rooted Android — userspace USB mass storage (libaums), per the project's own docs page. SnapDisk v0.1.2 cannot unlock an encrypted drive — 0 matches for encrypt/cipher/AES/decrypt in the app source — and whether its To folder picker can write to an OTG Master-mounted volume is unverified: the backup maps the picked SAF tree URI back to a raw /storage/<volume>/<path> path (BackupService.destinationBaseDir, BackupService.kt:592-608) and writes plain files there, so a DocumentsProvider volume is expected not to work — but that is a reading of the code, not a test; what would prove it is picking a mounted VeraCrypt volume as the To folder on a real phone and running a backup. SnapDisk copies photos and videos only, oldest-first by date taken from the MediaStore library (PhotoQuery.kt:23-35), size-verified after copying (BackupEngine.kt:107), Pause and Stop in the notification (BackupService.kt:113-115), free up to 5 GB per run (ProPrefs.kt:43), Pro $9.99 once (ProPrefs.kt:40). SnapDisk copies, it never deletes.
What the search results actually offer: three phrasings, scored live this run. Phrasing 1, "back up photos to encrypted USB drive from Android phone OTG" (supervisor): our own Huawei article, Dr.Fone's generic OTG manual copy, a LESOGE product page, and the OTG Master F-Droid page — a tool page, not a guide. Phrasing 2, "transfer photos to VeraCrypt BitLocker encrypted USB drive Android phone" (supervisor): OTG Master, the rottenwifi EDS NG guide, the androidcrypt F-Droid page, and the NTFS Reader page. Phrasing 3, "backup photos to BitLocker USB drive from Android without computer" (lead): the top four results are all our own articles — Samsung, automatic transfer, Pixel, Xiaomi — generic USB guides that never mention BitLocker. No dedicated guide for whole-library photo backup to a VeraCrypt or BitLocker drive exists in any phrasing.
The check and the routes: mount with OTG Master, copy by hand in the Files app — the only route that writes plain photo files onto a VeraCrypt or BitLocker drive with no computer and no root. NTFS Reader decrypts BitLocker To Go and copies to internal storage, but NTFS is read-only on the free tier (NTFS write is a one-time purchase; exFAT/FAT32 inside BitLocker is read and write, free). EDS NG and androidcrypt open VeraCrypt containers and copy a few files by hand; a filesystem mount needs root. LESOGE's one-click backup belongs to its iOS app — on Android there is no app, and the manual says to copy by hand. Huawei Backup writes an encrypted archive only a Huawei phone restores. Rule of thumb: unlock first, copy second, verify third — and never plan the backup around a combination nobody has tested. The mount is proven; the manual copy is proven; SnapDisk onto a mounted volume is not.

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/work-profile-photos-to-usb.html
A personal-profile app can't see work-profile photos. Copy them inside the work profile, share to personal, or use cloud — then back up to USB, no computer.
The honest centre, verified live this run (November 23, 2026), from Android's developer documentation and from the code at base e5c6b56: work and personal profiles have separate storage areas — "a file URI that is valid on one profile is not valid on the other" (developer.android.com/work/managed-profiles) — so SnapDisk installed in the personal profile reads only the personal MediaStore library and cannot see work-profile photos at all. SnapDisk v0.1.2 copies photos and videos only, oldest-first by date taken (PhotoQuery.kt:23-35), size-verified after copying (BackupEngine.kt:107-108), Pause and Stop in the notification (BackupService.kt:113-115), free up to 5 GB per run (ProPrefs.kt:43), Pro $9.99 once (ProPrefs.kt:40). SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — the only .delete() calls in the code are on its own half-finished .part files. No internet permission, no encryption code in the app source (0 matches).
What the search results actually offer: three phrasings, scored live this run. Phrasing 1, "back up photos from work profile Android to USB drive" (supervisor): generic OTG copy guides — Dr.Fone, Pixoneye, FotoSafe, our own automatic-transfer article — none mentions a work profile. Phrasing 2, "move photos from work profile to personal profile Android copy files between profiles" (supervisor): profile-sharing explainers — the Intune MDM manual, the How-To Geek profiles explainer, the appitika work-profile setup guide, the Maine IT migration doc — none is a photo-backup-to-USB guide; the USB leg is missing everywhere. Maine IT confirms the motive: removing a work profile deletes all its data, "ensure that any needed data is backed up before removing the work profile." Phrasing 3, "back up work profile photos Android to USB drive before removing work profile" (lead): the top result is a Samsung-specific guide about backing up before removing a work profile (umatechnology.org) whose USB method is a cable to a computer, not a drive plugged into the phone; the other results are Dr.Fone's generic OTG guide, our own backup-photos-to-usb article, and an AndroidPolice generic backup guide. No dedicated phone-direct USB-drive guide for work-profile photos exists in any phrasing.
The check and the routes: first find which profile holds the photos — work apps carry a briefcase badge. Copy inside the work profile with its own file manager (plug the drive in, open the work Files app, look for the drive) — but whether the drive appears there is unverified from Android's documentation, so try it and fall back if it doesn't show up; an organisation can also block USB file transfer entirely. Share from the work app to a personal app — the Personal tab appears only if IT policy allows it; sharing work to personal is blocked by default on personally-owned devices and copy/paste work to personal is blocked on many managed devices. Work-profile cloud (OneDrive or Google Drive inside the work profile) is a bridge, not a USB backup — verify the upload from another device, and know the copy dies with the work account. Installing SnapDisk inside the work profile is not a route to plan on: the work Play Store is managed, SnapDisk is not on Google Play, and side-loading is usually IT-blocked. Leaving the job: Android Enterprise warns that after the work profile is deleted, all local data on the device within that profile is deleted — back up and verify before removal.
Screen-off continuation under battery saver is unverified (no WakeLock/Doze code in the repo).
Rule of thumb: the profile is the boundary — the backup has to start inside the work profile, or the photos have to cross to personal first. Check which profile holds the photos before you trust any backup, and back them up before the profile is removed, not after.
